guides.t: Bolt error 500 (Internal Server Error): how to fix it
guides.d: A 500 in your Bolt app means a server hit an error it didn't handle. Find which one from the failing request, read the real error, and fix the usual causes.
guides.x:
Fix guide · updated 2026-11-09

## Bolt error 500 (Internal Server Error): find which part of your app failed and fix it

500 (Internal Server Error) · Edge Function returned a non-2xx status code · Database error saving new user · infinite recursion detected in policy

Your Bolt app shows 500 or Internal Server Error, or a red line in the browser console says the server responded with a status of 500. A 500 only says that a server hit an error it didn't handle. It doesn't say which server, or why. In a Bolt app, several different places can send one, and the address of the failing request tells you which. Find that first, then read the real error behind it.

## 1. Find the request that failed

In Chrome, open the console (Ctrl + Shift + J on Windows, Cmd + Option + J on a Mac) and make the error happen again. Look for a red line like this one:

Failed to load resource: the server responded with a status of 500 (Internal Server Error)

Next to it is the address that failed. The Network tab lists the same requests with their status codes. Match the address:

- It contains /functions/v1/, or your app says Edge Function returned a non-2xx status code: one of your server functions failed. Go to step 2.

- It contains /auth/v1/, usually when someone signs up: Supabase Auth failed. Go to step 3.

- It contains /rest/v1/: a database query failed. Go to step 4.

- It ends with one of your project's files, like /src/App.tsx, and the preview is blank or shows an error panel: that file doesn't compile. Go to step 5.

- Bolt itself is failing, not your app: the editor, the chat or the preview won't work. Go to step 6.

## 2. A server function returned 500

Server functions (Supabase calls them Edge Functions) run the backend part of your app: payments, emails, calls to AI services. When one crashes or returns an error, the Supabase client in your app only reports Edge Function returned a non-2xx status code. The function's own error message is in the response it sent back. There are two ways to read it:

- The logs. On a Bolt database, click the database icon at the top of your project, then Server Functions, then View Logs on the function. Bolt only shows the last hour, so make the error happen first and look right away. On your own Supabase project, open the function from the Edge Functions page of the dashboard and check its logs.

- The response itself. Supabase's docs show how to print the function's error from your app's code:

import { FunctionsHttpError } from '@supabase/supabase-js'

const { data, error } = await supabase.functions.invoke('my-function', { body })
if (error instanceof FunctionsHttpError) {
console.error('Function error', await error.context.json())
}

Ask Bolt to add that check, make the error happen again, and the console shows what the function actually said. The usual causes:

- A missing secret. Functions read keys like STRIPE_SECRET_KEY or RESEND_API_KEY from secrets. If one doesn't exist, the function fails as soon as it calls that service. Bolt warns you with a message like The following secrets are used in the code but don't exist yet: RESEND_API_KEY. Add it under database icon → Secrets, with the name spelled exactly as in the message: names are case-sensitive.

- A wrong or expired key. The secret exists, but the outside service rejects it, and the log shows that service's own error. Copy a fresh key from the service's dashboard and save it as the secret's value.

- A crash in the function's code, for example reading a field the app didn't send. The log shows the error and where it happened. Paste that log entry into Bolt and ask it to fix the function. Bolt redeploys server functions for you after each change.

If the message is Failed to send a request to the Edge Function instead, your app couldn't read any answer from the function. From a browser, the usual reason is CORS: the function doesn't answer the browser's OPTIONS check, sent before the real request, or its answer lacks the CORS headers. Edge Function returned a non-2xx status code covers that fix and every status code a function can return.

## 3. Sign-up fails with "Database error saving new user"

This 500 comes from Supabase Auth while it creates the account. The cause is usually not Auth itself but a trigger: many apps run a function for every new user that copies them into a profiles table. When that function fails, the sign-up fails with it, and Auth only returns this generic message. Supabase's docs warn about exactly this: a failing trigger can block sign-ups.

To see the real error, open the logs right after a failed sign-up. On a Bolt database, that's database icon → Logs, then PostgreSQL or Authentication in the dropdown. On your own Supabase project, it's the Logs page of the dashboard. Then compare your function with Supabase's example:

create function public.handle_new_user()
returns trigger
language plpgsql
security definer set search_path = ''
as $$
begin
insert into public.profiles (id, first_name, last_name)
values (new.id, new.raw_user_meta_data ->> 'first_name', new.raw_user_meta_data ->> 'last_name');
return new;
end;
$$;

- security definer makes the function run with its owner's rights. Without it, the function runs as Supabase Auth's own database role, which can't write to your tables.

- set search_path = '' means every table needs its schema: public.profiles, not profiles. Without the schema, the log says the table doesn't exist.

- The columns must match your table. A required (not null) column the function doesn't fill, or a column that was renamed since, makes every sign-up fail.

Each error the log can show here, with its fix, is in Database error saving new user.

## 4. A database query returns 500

Most database errors come back as a 400, 401 or 403. A 500 from /rest/v1/ is rarer, and in apps like these it's usually one of two errors:

- infinite recursion detected in policy for relation "...": a security policy reads its own table, or two tables' policies read each other, so Postgres can never finish checking. It's common with sharing and admin features.

- canceling statement due to statement timeout: the query ran too long, often a page that loads a whole table at once. Ask Bolt to load the rows in pages, with .range(), and to select only the columns the page shows.

For the recursion, Supabase's documented fix moves the lookup into a security definer function in a private schema, then calls that function from the policy. Here's their example, for lists shared with members. Drop the old policy first, since the new one takes its name:

create schema if not exists private;

create function private.user_list_ids()
returns setof uuid
language sql
security definer
set search_path = ''
stable
as $$
select list_id from public.list_members
where user_id = (select auth.uid())
$$;

revoke execute on function private.user_list_ids() from public;
grant usage on schema private to authenticated;
grant execute on function private.user_list_ids() to authenticated;

create policy "members read lists" on lists for select
to authenticated
using ( id in (select private.user_list_ids()) );

Keep that function out of the public schema. A security definer function in a schema your API exposes can be called by anyone, with its owner's rights. You can paste this example into Bolt and ask it to apply the same pattern to your own tables. How to find the policy behind the loop, the admin and team versions of the fix, and the errors that can follow it are in Infinite recursion detected in policy.

If you get a 403 or permission denied for table instead, that's a different problem with its own fix: see Supabase permission denied for table (42501).

## 5. The preview is blank and one of your files returns 500

Bolt's preview runs a development server inside your browser. When one of your files has an error that stops it from compiling, that server answers with a 500 for that file, and the page stays blank. We reproduced it with a missing closing tag in src/App.tsx. The console showed the 500 for /src/App.tsx, and the error panel over the page gave the real message, with the line and column:

[plugin:vite:react-babel] …/src/App.tsx: Unterminated JSX contents. (6:10)

So the fix is in that file, at that line, not on a server. Copy the panel's message, or the red text from the Terminal tab in Code view, into Bolt and ask it to fix that line. That's also Bolt's own advice for a blank preview: give it the exact error. Running npm run build in the terminal shows compile errors too. Most Bolt and Lovable web apps are built with the same tool, Vite, so the messages are the same: Lovable build unsuccessful shows how to read the common ones.

## 6. Bolt itself is failing

If Bolt's editor, chat or preview fails rather than your app, check status.bolt.new first. During an incident, wait and try again later. If there's no incident, Bolt's troubleshooting guide suggests turning off ad blockers and other extensions, and your VPN, then trying again. If Bolt says your project is too large for a prompt, its docs suggest removing unused files and splitting large files into smaller ones.

## Still stuck?

Write down three things: the failing address, its status code, and the real error from the logs or the response. That's what anyone helping you will ask for first, and for a server function, the real error often points straight to the line to fix.

## Bolt preview not working: blank screen, stuck loading, or WebContainer error

Your preview will appear here · blank, white or gray preview · Out of memory · Building a hosted preview of your app

Your Bolt project opens, but the preview is a blank white or gray box, stays on Your preview will appear here, crashes with an out-of-memory error, or never starts. Each symptom has a different cause, and the browser you use changes how the preview works. Check status.bolt.new first: if Bolt has an incident, wait for it to clear and try again.

## First: which browser are you in?

- Chrome or another Chromium browser (Edge, Brave, Vivaldi, Opera): the preview runs inside your browser on WebContainers, StackBlitz's in-browser runtime. It uses your computer's memory, and extensions, ad blockers and VPNs can break it.

- Safari on a Mac: the preview is built on Bolt's side and hosted, not run in your browser. It behaves differently (see the Safari section below).

- Firefox: not on Bolt's list of supported desktop browsers. Open the project in Chrome, Edge or Brave instead.

## Stuck on "Your preview will appear here"

The project never started, usually because of a port conflict or an error that stops it. Asking "the preview isn't working" won't get you far. Give Bolt the exact error instead:

- Click the code icon (<>) at the top center to switch to Code view.

- At the bottom, look through the three tabs (Bolt, Publish Output, Terminal) for text in red.

- Copy that output, paste it into the chat, and ask Bolt to fix it: "The preview isn't loading. Here's the output from the terminal:" followed by what you copied.

## The preview is blank, white or gray

Here the project starts but the page shows nothing. Work down this list:

- Hard refresh: Cmd+Shift+R on a Mac, Ctrl+Shift+R on Windows. Then try the project in a new tab.

- Ask once: "The preview is not showing, fix this." Bolt's docs say that if this works, it works on the first try. Sending the same prompt again rarely helps.

- Read the console. A white screen often hides a runtime error Bolt can't see. Open the browser console (Cmd+Option+J on a Mac, Ctrl+Shift+J on Windows), refresh until the white screen shows, then copy the red errors into the chat.

- Run a build. In Code view, open Terminal, type npm run build and press Enter. A build shows compile errors that don't appear while the preview runs.

- Check environment variables. Projects often show a white screen when a required variable is missing. Ask: "List every environment variable the application requires and where each value can be found." Then add them through the Secrets menu or a .env file.

If the console errors mention a Supabase URL, the project expects a database connection that isn't set up. Connect your Supabase database from the Advanced database settings. If you see Supabase URL errors while connected to a Bolt database, Bolt's docs say to contact their support.

## Out of memory

In Chromium browsers the whole development environment runs on your computer, so a full machine can't start it, or it crashes mid-session. Close other tabs and apps, keep only one Bolt or StackBlitz project open, refresh, and restart your computer if it keeps happening. A browser with fewer extensions helps too.

## The preview environment won't start

When WebContainers themselves fail to start:

- Use Chrome or another Chromium browser.

- Clear your browser cache.

- Turn off extensions for a moment, ad blockers first.

- Turn off your VPN.

- Try Chrome's Guest mode, which rules out extensions and settings in one go.

## In Safari

- "Building a hosted preview of your app" is normal: Safari previews are built and hosted by Bolt.

- Project made in Chrome, opened in Safari, no preview: Safari doesn't load it on its own. Prompt "Load the preview" or "Show my project's preview".

- "This preview may be outdated": Bolt is rebuilding the hosted preview after your latest change. It refreshes when the deploy finishes.

- No terminal, read-only files: Safari's Code view can't edit files or run commands. For the terminal steps above, open the project in Chrome.

- A hosted preview is not your live site. To put the app online, you still have to publish it.

Still stuck after all this? Bolt's docs point to their support team, or you can send the project to us.

Sources: Bolt help center, Preview issues and Supported browsers; WebContainers.

## Edge Function returned a non-2xx status code: read the real error and fix it

Edge Function returned a non-2xx status code · FunctionsHttpError · Failed to send a request to the Edge Function

Your app shows Edge Function returned a non-2xx status code, often in a red pop-up after you click a button that sends an email, takes a payment or calls an AI service. Your function didn't write that message. The Supabase client in your app did, and it only means the function answered with an error code instead of a success (2xx means 200 to 299). The function's real answer, the one that names the problem, is one step away. Read it first.

## 1. Read the status code and the real error

In Chrome, open the developer tools (Ctrl + Shift + I on Windows, Cmd + Option + I on a Mac), click the Network tab, then make the error happen again. Click the request whose address contains /functions/v1/ followed by your function's name. The status code is at the top of its Headers tab, and what the function sent back is in the Response tab. The console shows the same code in a red line that starts like this:

Failed to load resource: the server responded with a status of 500

Error responses can also carry an sb-error-code header with a name for the problem, such as BOOT_ERROR or UNAUTHORIZED_NO_AUTH_HEADER.

To print the function's answer from your app instead, check the error's type and read error.context, which holds the function's response:

import { FunctionsHttpError } from '@supabase/supabase-js'

const { data, error } = await supabase.functions.invoke('send-email', { body })
if (error instanceof FunctionsHttpError) {
console.error('Function answered', error.context.status, await error.context.text())
}

Supabase's docs read the answer with .json(). That fails when the answer is plain text, such as Internal Server Error, so .text() is the safer choice. We tested both with the current Supabase client in Chrome. Then open the function's logs, which hold the full error and the line it came from:

- Lovable: More → Database → Manage → Edge functions, click the function, then View logs. Logs don't update by themselves, so click Refresh after the error.

- Bolt: the database icon at the top of your project, then Server Functions, then View Logs on the function. Bolt only keeps the last hour.

- Your own Supabase project: the Edge Functions section of the dashboard, then your function. Invocations lists each request with its status code, and Logs shows crashes and your function's own messages.

Then match the status code below. A 400, 403 or 422 usually comes from your function's own code, which refused the request on purpose, and its answer says why.

## 2. 401: the function refused the caller

If the answer is Missing authorization header (full guide), Invalid JWT or Invalid Token or Protected Header formatting, your code never ran. By default, Supabase checks every call for a signed-in user's token before it reaches your function, and this call didn't pass. The usual reasons:

- Nobody is signed in, or the session expired. Sign out and back in, then try again. If the function serves visitors who aren't signed in, like a contact form, it shouldn't require a user at all: see the last point.

- The app calls the function with fetch instead of supabase.functions.invoke. The Supabase client adds the user's token for you, and a plain fetch doesn't. Ask your AI tool to switch the call to supabase.functions.invoke.

- The caller isn't your app: Stripe, another webhook, a scheduled job. They don't have a user's token. Turn the check off for that function only, and make the function check the caller itself, the way Stripe webhooks are checked with their signature. In a Supabase project, the setting is on the function's page in the dashboard, or in supabase/config.toml:

[functions.stripe-webhook]
verify_jwt = false

Turning the check off makes the function public: anyone who finds its address can call it. Only do it for a function that checks its caller in its own code. If every call gets a 401 even with a signed-in user, Supabase's troubleshooting page for 401s covers key formats the built-in check rejects. Its fix is the same: turn the check off for that function and verify the user in the function's code.

If the 401 comes with a message your own code wrote, the function ran and refused the request on purpose. Its code says why.

## 3. 500: the function's code failed

A 500 means your function ran and hit an error. If the answer is just Internal Server Error, the code crashed on an error it didn't catch. Otherwise the answer is your function's own error message. Either way, the log has the details. The usual causes:

- A missing secret. Functions read keys like RESEND_API_KEY or STRIPE_SECRET_KEY from secrets. A missing one comes back empty, and the call to that service fails. Add it with the exact name the code uses: in Lovable, More → Settings → Secrets; in Bolt, database icon → Secrets; in Supabase, Edge Functions → Secrets. After you remix a Lovable project, only the names of your secrets are copied, so enter each value again.

- A key the outside service rejects: wrong, expired, from test mode, or out of credit. The log shows that service's own error. Copy a fresh key from the service's dashboard into the secret.

- A crash in the code, often from data it didn't expect: the app sent a different body, or an outside service answered with something else. The log gives the error and the line, like this example from Supabase's docs:

TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'some_func')
at Object.handler (file:///var/tmp/sb-compile-edge-runtime/source/index.ts:15:26)

Here, line 15 of the function's index.ts is where it broke. Paste the whole log entry into Lovable or Bolt and ask it to fix that function.

## 4. 503, 504 or 546: the function couldn't start or finish

- 503 with BOOT_ERROR and Function failed to start (please check logs): the function didn't even start, usually because of a syntax error or an import that fails, like a package version that doesn't exist. Its log has a line with worker boot error that names the problem. Paste it into the chat. Where to find that line and the usual fixes: Edge Function 503 BOOT_ERROR "Function failed to start (please check logs)". A 503 without BOOT_ERROR can also mean Supabase itself is having trouble: check status.supabase.com.

- 504: the function didn't answer within 150 seconds. That's usually a slow call to an outside service, like a long AI generation, or a loop over many items. Ask for a time limit on the slow call, and split big jobs into smaller ones.

- 546 with WORKER_RESOURCE_LIMIT: the function ran out of memory (256 MB) or CPU time (2 seconds of actual computing per request; waiting for other services doesn't count). The log says Memory limit exceeded or CPU Time exceeded. It's common when a function processes big files or images, or loads a whole table at once. Process smaller pieces at a time. Which limit it was, and why it fails only sometimes: Edge Function 546 "not having enough compute resources" (WORKER_RESOURCE_LIMIT).

## 5. "Failed to send a request to the Edge Function"

This message is different: your app never got an answer it could read, so there's no status code to match. In our test, the console showed why, with one of these two lines:

Access to fetch at '…/functions/v1/send-email' from origin '…' has been blocked by CORS policy: Response to preflight request doesn't pass access control check: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource.

Access to fetch at '…/functions/v1/send-email' from origin '…' has been blocked by CORS policy: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource.

Both are CORS errors. Before a browser sends the real request, it asks the function for permission with an OPTIONS request, and it only lets your app read answers that carry the right CORS headers. The first line, the one with Response to preflight request in it, means the function doesn't answer that OPTIONS request. The second means it answered, often with an error, but without the headers, so the browser hid the answer from your app. The fix is the same for both: answer OPTIONS, and put the CORS headers on every response, errors included. Here's Supabase's example:

import { corsHeaders } from 'npm:@supabase/supabase-js@^2/cors'

export default {
fetch: async (req) => {
// Handle the CORS preflight request.
if (req.method === 'OPTIONS') {
return Response.json({ ok: true }, { headers: corsHeaders })
}
try {
const { name } = await req.json()
return Response.json({ message: `Hello ${name}!` }, { headers: corsHeaders })
} catch (error) {
const message = error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error)
return Response.json({ error: message }, { status: 400, headers: corsHeaders })
}
},
}

If your function starts with Deno.serve(async (req) => { or serve(async (req) => { instead, the same lines go inside it. The other causes of this message:

- The function doesn't exist: the app and the function use different names, the function was never deployed, or the app points at a different Supabase project than the one with the function. Supabase's docs note that browsers report this 404 as a CORS error, so it looks like the cases above. The function's logs stay empty, since the request never reached it. Compare the name in the failing address with your list of functions. Every cause, tested: Edge Function 404 "Requested function was not found".

- The request never left the browser: no connection, or an extension like an ad blocker stopped it. Try a private window with extensions off.

Every other CORS line, like It does not have HTTP ok status or Request header field x-client-info is not allowed, and why a function can pass on your machine and fail once deployed: Supabase Edge Function "blocked by CORS policy".

If the message is Relay Error invoking the Edge Function instead, Supabase's docs describe it as a network problem between your app and Supabase, not a bug in your function. Try again, and check status.supabase.com.

## Still stuck?

Write down three things: the function's name, the status code (or the CORS line from the console), and the error from the response or the logs. That's what anyone helping you will ask for first, and the log line often points straight to the fix. In Lovable, also check that the project isn't paused: edge functions don't run while it is.

## Google login "Error 400: redirect_uri_mismatch": the fix for Supabase and Lovable apps

Access blocked: This app's request is invalid. Error 400: redirect_uri_mismatch

You click Sign in with Google and Google stops you with Access blocked: This app's request is invalid, and under it Error 400: redirect_uri_mismatch. Your users see the same page. It always means one thing: the address your app asked Google to send people back to is not on the list your Google OAuth client allows. Google only accepts an exact match, so the fix is to put that exact address on the list.

## What the error means

When someone signs in with Google, your app sends them to Google with a redirect_uri: the address Google should send them back to afterwards. Google compares it with the Authorized redirect URIs saved on your OAuth client and refuses if it isn't there exactly. Google's own docs say the scheme (http or https), letter case and a trailing slash must all match.

To see the address Google received, click see error details on the error page. The line redirect_uri=… is the exact value to add.

In an app that uses Supabase for login, that address is not your app. Google sends users to Supabase first, at https://<your-project-ref>.supabase.co/auth/v1/callback. Supabase signs them in, then sends them on to your app. So Google needs Supabase's address, and the most common mistake is adding your app's address (https://yourapp.lovable.app, https://yourapp.com) instead.

- Your app uses your own Supabase project (Lovable connected to Supabase, Bolt, Cursor, v0, Next.js): see section 1.

- Your app runs on Lovable Cloud, Lovable's built-in backend: see section 2.

- It worked, then broke after a domain change: see section 3.

- The error code is different (origin_mismatch, invalid_client, access_denied): see section 4.

## 1. Supabase apps: add Supabase's callback address in Google

- In Supabase, open Authentication → Sign In / Providers → Google (just Providers in older dashboards). Copy the callback URL shown there. It looks like https://abcdefghijklmnopqrst.supabase.co/auth/v1/callback.

- In Google Cloud, open Google Auth Platform → Clients (in older menus, APIs & Services → Credentials). Click the OAuth client whose Client ID is the one in your Supabase Google settings.

- Under Authorized redirect URIs, click Add URI and paste the callback URL exactly as you copied it: https, no slash at the end, nothing added. Click Save.

- Under Authorized JavaScript origins, check that your app's address is there too, as an origin only: https://yourapp.com, no path. Supabase's setup guide asks for both lists.

- Try again in a private window. Google warns that a change can take from five minutes to a few hours to apply. If it still fails right away, wait before changing anything else.

Still failing after the wait? It is almost always one of these:

- You edited a different client. A Google Cloud project can hold several OAuth clients, and you may have more than one project. Compare the Client ID in Supabase with the one on the client page you edited. They must be the same.

- Wrong client type. The client must be a Web application. Android, iOS and desktop clients have no redirect list, and a sign-in that goes through Supabase needs one.

- A near miss. http instead of https, a slash at the end, a typo in the project ref, or your app's address instead of Supabase's. Google allows no wildcards (*), so every address goes in whole.

- Testing locally with the Supabase CLI. The callback is then http://127.0.0.1:54321/auth/v1/callback, and it needs its own line.

## 2. Lovable Cloud apps

On Lovable's built-in backend, Google sign-in is Managed by Lovable by default: Lovable runs the Google client, and you set nothing up in Google Cloud. The error comes up when you switched to Your own credentials:

- In Lovable, open More → Users → Settings → Google. Lovable lists the redirect addresses your app can use: one for your lovable.app address, and one for each custom domain.

- Add every one you use to Authorized redirect URIs on your Google client, copied exactly. Lovable's docs say scheme, domain, path and trailing slash all matter.

- Back in Lovable, select the addresses you added and click Save. Lovable only sends users back through the addresses you select there.

Don't need your own branding on the Google consent screen? Switching back to Managed by Lovable removes the Google Cloud setup completely.

## 3. It worked, then broke after a domain change

- Supabase custom domain (like api.yourapp.com): sign-ins now announce a new callback, https://api.yourapp.com/auth/v1/callback. Supabase's docs say to add it in Google in addition to the original ….supabase.co one, not instead of it. The same goes for a vanity subdomain like yourbrand.supabase.co.

- A new custom domain on Lovable Cloud, with your own credentials: add its redirect address in Google and select it in Lovable (section 2).

- A new address for your app (a new domain, or a move from Lovable to Vercel or Netlify) with Supabase login: Google's redirect list doesn't change, because it still points at Supabase. Add the new address to Authorized JavaScript origins in Google, and to Supabase's Authentication → URL Configuration, or users come back to the wrong place.

## 4. Similar Google errors

- Error 400: origin_mismatch, or The given origin is not allowed for the given client ID in the browser console: the Google button or One Tap checks your app's address against Authorized JavaScript origins instead. Add it there, as an origin only (https://yourapp.com).

- Error 401: invalid_client (The OAuth client was not found): the Client ID in Supabase or Lovable is wrong, or that client was deleted. Copy it again from the client page in Google Cloud.

- Error 403: access_denied while your Google app is in testing: only the test users listed under Google Auth Platform → Audience can sign in. Add them, or publish the app.

- Unsupported provider: provider is not enabled on a page of JSON, before any Google page: Supabase stops before asking Google, because Google sign-in is off, or saved without its secret, in the project your app uses. See Supabase "Unsupported provider: provider is not enabled".

## Still stuck?

If Google now lets users through but they land on {"error":"requested path is invalid"} or on localhost, the Google side is fixed and the problem is in Supabase's URL settings: see Supabase "requested path is invalid" and Supabase login redirecting to localhost. Supabase → Authentication → Logs shows each sign-in attempt and where it went.

## Lovable app: blank page or Vercel 404 after deploy

404: NOT_FOUND · supabaseUrl is required.

Your app works perfectly in the Lovable preview. You deploy it to Vercel or Netlify, and you get one of these: a blank white page, a 404 as soon as you refresh a page, or a build that fails. It's almost always one of the four causes below. Check them in order.

## 1. A 404 when you refresh a page or open a link directly

The home page loads, you click around, everything works. Then you refresh on /dashboard and get 404: NOT_FOUND (Vercel) or Page not found (Netlify).

Why: Lovable builds a single-page app. There is only one real file, index.html, and the app draws every page itself in the browser. When you refresh /dashboard, the host looks for a file called dashboard, doesn't find one, and gives up before your app can load.

Fix: tell the host to send every unknown path to index.html.

On Vercel, add a file called vercel.json at the root of the project:

{
"rewrites": [{ "source": "/(.*)", "destination": "/index.html" }]
}

On Netlify, add a file called _redirects inside the public folder:

/* /index.html 200

On Cloudflare Pages there's nothing to add, as long as your project has no 404.html at its root: Pages then serves index.html for unknown paths by itself.

Commit, redeploy, and refresh a deep page to check.

## 2. A blank white page with "supabaseUrl is required"

The page is completely white. Open the browser console (right-click → Inspect → Console) and you see:

Uncaught Error: supabaseUrl is required.

Why: your code reads the Supabase address from an environment variable, and that variable doesn't exist on your host. Vite, the tool Lovable uses to build, copies these values into the app at build time, and only variables whose names start with VITE_. If the variable was missing during the build, the app ships with nothing in it and crashes on the first line.

Fix:

- Open src/integrations/supabase/client.ts (or search the project for createClient(). Note the exact variable names after import.meta.env., for example VITE_SUPABASE_URL.

- In your host's settings (Vercel: Settings → Environment Variables; Netlify: Site configuration → Environment variables), add each variable with the same name and the value from your Supabase dashboard (the Connect button at the top shows the Project URL and the key).

- Redeploy. Adding the variable alone changes nothing: the app has to be built again to pick it up.

Only put the public anon or publishable key here. The service_role key must never be in a VITE_ variable: everything in those ends up readable by anyone who opens your site.

See it live. We reproduced this on a demo app: the broken deploy opens blank (press F12, then Console: supabaseUrl is required.), and the fixed deploy is the same code built with the two variables. The 34-second video shows both.

## 3. The build succeeds but the site is empty or shows old files

Why: the host is publishing the wrong folder. Vite puts the finished site in dist.

Fix: in your host's build settings, use build command npm run build and output (publish) directory dist. Then redeploy.

## 4. "Build failed: Could not resolve './components/Header'"

It builds in preview and fails on the host.

Why: the file is named header.tsx but imported as ./components/Header. Your computer and the preview ignore the difference in capitals; the Linux servers that build your site don't.

Fix: make the import match the file name exactly, letter for letter, or rename the file. If you rename only the capitals with Git, do it in two steps (git mv header.tsx tmp.tsx, then git mv tmp.tsx Header.tsx) so Git notices the change.

## Still blank?

Open the console and copy the first red error. That line names the real problem. If it doesn't match anything above, it's usually a crash in one specific component, and that's the kind of thing we fix every day.

## Lovable build unsuccessful: find the real error and fix it without burning credits

Fix build errors · failed to resolve import · is not exported by · Publishing failed

Your Lovable build failed. The chat shows an error with a Try to fix button, the Publish dialog says Fix build errors instead of letting you publish, or a publish ends with Publishing failed. Pressing Try to fix over and over is the expensive way out. A failed build often comes down to one line in one file, and the error message says which. Here's how to read it and fix the cause.

## Before you press Try to fix again

Try to fix is a good first move: Lovable scans the logs, finds the issue and attempts a fix. Your account gets 10 free fixes, shared between Try to fix and the fixes in the Security view, across all your workspaces and projects. Each one comes back 24 hours after you use it. Once all 10 are used, Try to fix still works, but it costs credits like any other build request. Where else the button shows up, and which problems it can't fix: Lovable Try to fix button.

Lovable's own debugging guide says to use it once or twice. If the same error comes back, or a new one takes its place, the fix isn't reaching the cause. Stop there and read the error yourself.

## 1. Find the real error

- Look for a file path and a line number, like src/App.tsx:8. That's where the build stopped. In Lovable projects, @/ in an import means the src/ folder: @/components/Button is the file src/components/Button.tsx.

- Fix the first error. One broken line can produce several errors. In our tests, a single missing closing tag gave two.

- Publishing blocked? When a publish fails on a build error, the Publishing failed banner shows a short summary of that build error.

Then go to that line:

- On a paid plan, open the Code tab, go to the file and line, and fix it yourself. Editing code by hand costs no credits, and each save becomes a version you can revert. On the Free plan the editor is read-only. You can still read the file and point Lovable at the exact line: hover the line number and click + to put a reference like App.tsx:8 in the chat.

- If the project syncs with GitHub, run the same build on your computer to see the full output (you need Node.js). Fix the file, commit, and push to the synced branch:

npm install
npm run build

If your pushes never show up in Lovable, see Lovable GitHub connection not working.

Red underlines alone don't fail the build. Both Lovable templates build with vite build, which strips TypeScript types without checking them. We checked the build script in 40 public Lovable repositories, then planted a type error in a test app: it built. A failed build means Vite hit something it can't get past. Here are four common ones, with their exact wording. Most older Lovable projects build with Vite 5. Newer projects, on TanStack Start (the default since May 13, 2026), build with Vite 8, which words the same errors differently. We reproduced each one on both versions.

## 2. "Could not load" or "Could not resolve" one of your files

[vite:load-fallback] Could not load …/src/components/button (imported by src/App.tsx): ENOENT: no such file or directory
Could not resolve "./components/button" from "src/App.tsx"

The first comes from an @/ import, the second from a relative one like ./components/button. On newer projects: [UNLOADABLE_DEPENDENCY] Could not load src/components/button and [UNRESOLVED_IMPORT] Could not resolve './components/button' in src/App.tsx.

A file imports another file that isn't there under that name. Usually a file was renamed, moved or deleted, and an import somewhere still uses the old path. Compare the import with the file list in the Code tab, letter by letter: capital letters count. For the build, button and Button.tsx are different files, even though Mac and Windows treat them as the same.

That difference bites when you edit on a Mac or a Windows PC and push to GitHub. Rename Button.tsx to button.tsx in Finder or Explorer and Git keeps recording the old name, because on those systems it treats the two names as one file. The app runs on your computer, and Lovable's build fails. Rename with Git instead, then commit and push:

git mv src/components/Button.tsx src/components/button.tsx

## 3. "Failed to resolve import" for a package

[vite]: Rollup failed to resolve import "date-fns" from "…/src/App.tsx".
This is most likely unintended because it can break your application at runtime.

On newer projects, the same message starts with Rolldown failed to resolve import.

The code uses a package that isn't installed: it's missing from package.json. That happens when an edit adds the import but not the package, or when someone removes a package that's still in use. Ask Lovable to add that exact package to the project. With GitHub, run npm install date-fns (with your package's name), then commit package.json and the lock file.

Check the name first. If the package doesn't exist on npmjs.com under exactly that name, the import was a mistake. Fix the import instead of installing a look-alike: anyone can publish a package under a name that sounds right.

## 4. "Transform failed", "Unexpected token" or "Unexpected end of file"

[vite:esbuild] Transform failed with 2 errors:
…/src/App.tsx:8:0: ERROR: The character "}" is not valid inside a JSX element
…/src/App.tsx:9:0: ERROR: Unexpected end of file before a closing "main" tag

On newer projects: Unexpected token. Did you mean {'}'} or }?, followed by the file and line.

A file isn't valid code anymore: a missing closing tag, bracket or quote, often from an edit that stopped halfway. The file and line in the message are where the parser gave up, so the real slip is often on that line or just above it. In our test, the missing </main> belonged on line 7. If the file was fine one version ago, open History, use View code changes on the last version to see what changed, and put the missing piece back. Or revert that version (section 6).

## 5. "is not exported by"

"Buton" is not exported by "src/components/Button.tsx", imported by "src/App.tsx".

On newer projects: [MISSING_EXPORT] "Buton" is not exported by "src/components/Button.tsx".

The file exists, but the name you import isn't in it. A function or component was renamed or removed in one file, and another file still imports the old name. Fix the import to the current name, or bring the export back. If one name changed everywhere but one file, search the project for the old name (Search code in the Code tab finds every place that still uses it).

## 6. When fixes go in circles: plan, then roll back

If every fix brings a new error, ask before you build. Switch to Plan mode, which investigates without touching your code (one credit per message, plus any research it runs), and use the prompt Lovable's docs suggest:

What is the root cause of this build error? Show me the relevant code and explain what is going wrong before proposing a fix.

Rolling back is often faster than untangling a pile of fixes. Open History in the top bar, find the last version that built, and click Revert. The version that's live on your site carries a Published badge: it built, so it's a safe point to return to. Then ask for the change again, in smaller steps. Three things to know:

- Revert restores your code only, and redeploys your edge functions to match. It doesn't undo database changes made since that version.

- Credits spent on the messages you roll back aren't refunded.

- Very old versions can be previewed but not restored: the button says Cannot revert this far back in history.

## 7. The preview works, but publishing fails

The Publish dialog names the kind of failure in its Publishing failed banner. Each one has its own way out:

- Temporary issue (a timeout, a rate limit): click Try again. Retries usually succeed.

- Error in your app: a build error or an edge function that couldn't be deployed. Click Try to fix, or fix it yourself with the sections above.

- Configuration issue in your project, for example a file too large to include: click Try to fix.

- External connection or secret, such as an expired Supabase connection or a connected service that hit its plan limit. Lovable can't change those for you: reconnect the integration or raise the limit, then click Try again.

- A database change conflicts with existing data: click Ask Lovable. It confirms with you before touching anything, because the fix changes real data. Read that step carefully.

- Internal error: the problem is on Lovable's side. Try again in a few minutes. If it keeps failing, contact Lovable Support with your project link.

If the build passes but the app shows a blank page or a 404 once deployed, for example on Vercel, that's a different problem: see Lovable app: blank page or Vercel 404 after deploy.

## Still stuck?

Check status.lovable.dev: during an incident in Lovable's build pipeline, builds can fail for everyone until it's fixed. If you're on a paid plan and believe the problem is on Lovable's side, contact Lovable Support. Otherwise, write down the first error, the file and line, and what you've tried. That's what anyone helping you will ask for first.

## Lovable custom domain not working: DNS, SSL and Cloudflare fixes

Looking for your DNS records · Issuing certificate · Error 1034: Edge IP Restricted · Error 1001: DNS resolution error

You connected your domain in Lovable and it doesn't work. It's stuck on Looking for your DNS records or Issuing certificate, it still shows your old website, the browser shows a security error, or you get a Cloudflare error page. Almost every time, the problem is in the DNS records at the company that manages your domain, not in your app. Here's how to find which one and fix it.

## First, two quick checks

- Is the project published? A custom domain shows nothing until you publish the project. Custom domains also need a paid Lovable plan.

- What does Lovable say? Open Project → Settings → Domains and read the line under your domain:

- Looking for your DNS records, or Some DNS records for this domain are missing or wrong: sections 1 to 3.

- DNS records found, waiting for them to take effect: nothing is wrong. Other networks are catching up. Most do within a few hours; Lovable says to allow up to 72.

- Issuing certificate for hours: section 4.

- Active, but the site is wrong or doesn't load for everyone: section 5.

- Domain unavailable or Domain already in use: another project has the domain. Disconnect it there first.

## 1. Make sure you're editing the right place

DNS records only count at the company that runs your domain's DNS. That's usually where you bought the domain, unless it was moved to a service such as Cloudflare or a website builder you used before. Records added anywhere else are simply ignored, with no error.

To find the right place, look up your domain's NS records on dnschecker.org, or in a terminal:

dig +short NS yourdomain.com

The names that come back (for example …ns.cloudflare.com) tell you which company to log in to. Lovable's automatic setup finds it for you.

## 2. Stuck on "Looking for your DNS records"

Lovable can't see the records it asked for yet. Open Setup instructions from the three dots menu next to your domain and compare each record, letter for letter, with what's at your DNS provider:

- A record: name @ (the root domain), value = the IP address Lovable shows for your domain. Copy it from your own setup window, not from a tutorial or a forum post: Lovable gives the address for each domain, and it can ask you to change yours later.

- AAAA record: only if Lovable lists one. Add it the same way, with the IPv6 address shown.

- TXT record: name _lovable, value starting with lovable_verify=. Copy the whole value: it's unique to your domain.

- www: if you kept the Redirect www option, www needs its own pair, an A record named www and a TXT record named _lovable.www. It's easy to add the root's records and miss these.

Three traps catch most people:

- The Name field. Most providers want only the part before your domain: _lovable, not _lovable.yourdomain.com. If yours doesn't accept @, leave the name blank or enter the full domain. Amazon Route 53 works that way.

- Old records at the same name. Delete every other A, AAAA or CNAME record at @ and at www, whether it's from a parking page, a previous host or a website builder. A name can't have a CNAME and other records at the same time, so a leftover CNAME on www must go. Keep your MX records: they carry your email.

- A proxy is turned on. If your DNS is on Cloudflare, read section 3.

Then check what the rest of the internet sees:

dig +short A yourdomain.com
dig +short AAAA yourdomain.com
dig +short TXT _lovable.yourdomain.com

On Windows, use nslookup -type=TXT _lovable.yourdomain.com, or look up the same names on dnschecker.org. The A answer must be exactly the address Lovable shows, with nothing else listed. When everything matches, open the three dots menu and select Check again.

## 3. Your DNS is on Cloudflare

In Cloudflare, each DNS record has a cloud icon. An orange cloud (Proxied) means Cloudflare answers with its own addresses instead of the one you typed. So Lovable can't find its A record, and visitors get a Cloudflare error page instead of your app.

We tested it with a spare subdomain of our own: an A record pointing to Lovable's address, set to Proxied. Public DNS answered with a Cloudflare address instead of Lovable's, and the page showed Error 1034: Edge IP Restricted. Lovable's docs mention errors 1001 and 1003 for the same mistake, and Cloudflare's docs list this setup under Error 1000: DNS points to prohibited IP. The reason: Lovable's own addresses also run on Cloudflare's network (we checked the public IP registry). Cloudflare only lets your domain through once Lovable has set it up, and Lovable can't set it up while the proxy hides its records.

Two ways out:

- Simplest: in Cloudflare → DNS, click the orange cloud on your Lovable records (@ and www) so it turns grey (DNS only). Wait a few minutes, then select Check again in Lovable.

- To keep Cloudflare's proxy: disconnect the domain in Lovable, connect it again, and under Advanced turn on Uses Cloudflare or similar proxy. Lovable then asks for one CNAME record per address, pointing to your project's lovable.app address, and no TXT record. In Cloudflare, set SSL/TLS encryption to Full or Full (strict), never Flexible: Lovable redirects plain http to https (we checked), and Cloudflare's docs warn that Flexible plus that redirect gives an endless loop, ERR_TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS.

## 4. Stuck on "Issuing certificate"

Lovable creates the HTTPS certificate for you once your records are right. You don't need to buy one, and a certificate from your registrar isn't used. Until the domain is Active, opening it over https fails with a security or connection error, and that's expected: we checked, and a domain that points at Lovable but isn't set up yet gets no certificate at all. Don't judge your setup by it before Lovable says Active.

If it stays on Issuing certificate, look for CAA records. They list which companies may issue certificates for your domain, and they can lock Lovable out:

dig +short CAA yourdomain.com

If that prints nothing, CAA isn't your problem. If it prints anything, add these three records at your DNS provider (type CAA, flag 0, tag issue):

0 issue "pki.goog"
0 issue "letsencrypt.org"
0 issue "ssl.com"

Connecting a subdomain like app.yourdomain.com? Check the root domain too: a subdomain with no CAA records of its own follows the root's. Then select Check again. If there's still no certificate after 72 hours, contact Lovable support.

## 5. Active, but it shows your old site or only works for some people

Lovable says Active, yet some visitors see your previous website, a parking page, or nothing at all. A leftover record is sending them elsewhere:

- An extra A record from your old host: each visitor gets one address or the other.

- An AAAA (IPv6) record your provider added on its own: phones and networks that prefer IPv6 go there instead of to Lovable.

Run the dig lines from section 2 and delete every A, AAAA or CNAME at that name that Lovable didn't give you. Then test in a private window: your browser may still have the old site cached.

## 6. The site loads, but login fails on the new domain

Sign-in worked in preview and breaks on your domain? Your new address isn't on the list of addresses your login may send people back to. On Lovable's built-in backend, Lovable adds the domain itself once it's Active; if login still fails, ask Lovable in the project chat to add it. With your own Supabase project, add it yourself under Authentication → URL Configuration: see Supabase login redirects to localhost. With your own Google sign-in keys, also add the new redirect URL in Google Cloud Console.

## Still stuck?

Ask Lovable about your domain in the project chat. It tells you the domain's state, how long it has been there, which records it expects and whether it can see them. Compare that with your dig results: the difference is your fix.

## Lovable code won't run locally after export or GitHub sync

npm run dev fails · blank page on localhost · supabaseUrl is required · listen EAFNOSUPPORT :::8080 · bunx: not found

You downloaded your Lovable project, or cloned it from GitHub, and it won't start on your computer: npm install or npm run dev fails, or the page stays white. The code is usually fine. A Lovable project expects a few things that Lovable's servers provide, and your computer has to provide them instead. Here they are, in the order they usually break.

## First: which kind of Lovable project is it?

Lovable builds two kinds of apps, and they run a little differently on your computer. Open package.json:

- Newer apps (created from May 13, 2026) use TanStack Start. package.json lists @tanstack/react-start, and vite.config.ts imports @lovable.dev/vite-tanstack-config. Part of the app runs as server code.

- Older apps use React + Vite. vite.config.ts imports from vite, usually with lovable-tagger. The app runs in the browser, and server work happens in Edge Functions on the backend.

The steps below apply to both. Where they differ, the step says so.

## Step 1: use Node.js 22

Lovable's own instructions for running and hosting a project outside Lovable use Node.js 22. Newer projects come with a recent Vite that refuses old Node versions. Check yours:

node -v

If it's lower than 22, install 22. With nvm:

nvm install 22
nvm use 22

Then delete the node_modules folder if a failed install left one, and install again.

## Step 2: install with the lockfile your project has

Look at the files next to package.json:

- package-lock.json is there: run npm install.

- Only bun.lock (common in newer projects): run bun install, or npm install, which creates a package-lock.json for you. Skip npm ci here: it needs a package-lock.json and stops without one.

"bunx: not found" when you start the app? Some projects call Bun inside their scripts, for example a "predev": "bunx tsx scripts/generate-sitemap.ts" line in package.json that runs before every npm run dev. Install Bun from bun.sh and run the command again.

## Step 3: start it, then open the address it prints

npm run dev

Older projects don't use Vite's usual port 5173. Their vite.config.ts sets port: 8080, so the app is at http://localhost:8080. If 8080 is busy, Vite moves to the next free port. Newer projects get their port from Lovable's config. Either way, open the exact address the terminal prints after Local:.

Error: listen EAFNOSUPPORT: address family not supported :::8080: older projects also set host: "::", an IPv6 address. On a computer or container with IPv6 turned off, nothing can listen there. Start the app on a normal local address instead, without editing the file Lovable syncs:

npm run dev -- --host 127.0.0.1

## Step 4: blank page or "supabaseUrl is required": the .env file

If the app starts but the page stays white, open the browser console (F12). supabaseUrl is required. means the app found no backend address. The Supabase client Lovable generates (src/integrations/supabase/client.ts) reads that address and its public key from the .env file at the project root:

VITE_SUPABASE_URL=https://xxxx.supabase.co
VITE_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=...
VITE_SUPABASE_PROJECT_ID=...

Lovable keeps .env in the repository on purpose, and its docs say never to add it to .gitignore. It goes missing when a template or a tool ignores it, or when the files were copied without hidden files (names that start with a dot). Copy .env from the code editor in Lovable to your local project, next to package.json. Then stop npm run dev and start it again: Vite reads .env only when it starts.

These VITE_ values are sent to the browser, which is fine for the URL and the publishable key. Never add a service role key or any other secret to them.

## Step 5: it runs, but sign-in or some features fail

A clone gives you the code, not everything around it. Lovable's docs list what stays behind:

- Sign-in. Login providers only send users back to addresses they know. Add your local address (http://localhost:8080, or the port you use) to the redirect URLs where your sign-in provider is set up. If users land on the wrong address or an error page, see login redirects and "requested path is invalid".

- Secrets you stored in Lovable (Stripe, Resend or OpenAI keys) never go into the repository. In older apps, the code that uses them runs in Edge Functions on your backend, so it still works from your computer. In newer apps, that server code runs on your machine, so it needs those values set there too.

- Lovable AI and app connectors use credentials that Lovable manages and that can't be copied out. In newer apps, those calls fail locally. Test them in the Lovable preview or in your published app.

One warning before you click around: with the same .env, your local app reads and writes the same live database as your published app. Records you create or delete locally change real data, so test with test accounts.

## If you change code locally

- Work on your own branch and merge it into the branch Lovable syncs, usually main. Don't force-push or rebase that branch: Lovable keeps its own copy, and rewriting the history replaces Lovable's work (the project owner can restore it from Project settings → Git).

- Syncing doesn't deploy backend changes. A changed Edge Function or a new migration file does nothing until you ask Lovable in the project chat to deploy it, or run the SQL yourself.

## Still stuck?

Run the four checks in order: node -v shows 22, the install finished without errors, you opened the address the terminal printed, and .env sits next to package.json. Then read the first red line in the terminal or the browser console: it names the step that failed. Sources: Lovable's docs on hosting outside Lovable, Git sync and working locally and secrets, and the settings in public Lovable repositories (checked in November 2026).
