Fix guide · updated 2026-11-16

## Supabase "Database error deleting user"

{"code":500,"error_code":"unexpected_failure","msg":"Database error deleting user"}

You delete a user, in the dashboard under Authentication → Users or with supabase.auth.admin.deleteUser(), and it fails with "Database error deleting user". Or, from recent versions of Supabase Auth, with the database's own message: update or delete on table "users" violates foreign key constraint "profiles_id_fkey" on table "profiles". Something in your database still points at that user, and Postgres won't leave it pointing at nothing. We ran Supabase Auth itself (version 2.198, November 2026) with the usual table setups to see what blocks a delete and what each fix does.

## What the error means

Deleting a user removes their row from auth.users. Supabase's own tables, like sessions and identities, follow by themselves. Your tables don't: each foreign key that references auth.users says what happens to the rows that point at the deleted user, and with no rule, which is the default, Postgres refuses the delete. In our test:

- profiles.id referencing auth.users with no rule: the delete failed with the foreign-key message above (code 23503, HTTP 500),

- the same key with on delete cascade: the delete worked, and the profile went with the user,

- a trigger on auth.users that hit a permission error: the delete failed with "Database error deleting user".

Supabase Auth passes constraint errors on as they are, so if your message names a table, that's the table to fix. Other database errors, like a failing trigger, come back as the generic "Database error deleting user".

## The one-minute check

In the SQL Editor, list your tables that point at users:

select conrelid::regclass as your_table, conname as constraint_name, pg_get_constraintdef(oid) as definition
from pg_constraint
where confrelid = 'auth.users'::regclass and contype = 'f'
and connamespace <> 'auth'::regnamespace;

A definition that ends with ON DELETE CASCADE or ON DELETE SET NULL has a rule. One that ends with just REFERENCES auth.users(id) blocks the delete of any user who has a row in that table.

If the error names a table that isn't in this list, it points at one that is: posts pointing at profiles, for example. In our test, a profiles table with on delete cascade still couldn't go, because posts pointed at it with no rule. Run the same query with 'public.profiles'::regclass in place of 'auth.users'::regclass to see those.

## 1. Rows that belong only to the user: on delete cascade

For a profile, settings, or anything that means nothing without its user, let the rows go with the user. Supabase's docs recommend on delete cascade for a profiles table. Replace the key, with the constraint name from the check:

alter table public.profiles
drop constraint profiles_id_fkey,
add constraint profiles_id_fkey foreign key (id) references auth.users (id) on delete cascade;

Do the same for every table in the chain: if posts points at profiles, it needs a rule too. Cascade deletes those rows for good, so check the list before you run it.

## 2. Rows you must keep: on delete set null

Orders, invoices, or messages in a shared thread may have to outlive the user. Keep the row and forget who it belonged to. The column has to accept null: in our test, set null on a not null column failed with null value in column "user_id" of relation "invoices" violates not-null constraint (23502).

alter table public.orders alter column user_id drop not null;
alter table public.orders
drop constraint orders_user_id_fkey,
add constraint orders_user_id_fkey foreign key (user_id) references auth.users (id) on delete set null;

In our test, the order stayed, with an empty user_id.

## 3. A trigger that runs when a user is deleted

Some projects have a trigger on auth.users that cleans up or logs when a user goes. If it fails, the delete fails with "Database error deleting user". List the triggers on that table:

select tgname, pg_get_triggerdef(oid) from pg_trigger
where tgrelid = 'auth.users'::regclass and not tgisinternal;

Look for one with DELETE in its definition. In our test, a trigger function that wrote to a public table failed with "permission denied for table deleted_users": Supabase Auth works through its own database role, which can't write to your tables. Make the function run with its owner's rights:

alter function public.on_user_deleted() security definer set search_path = '';

After that, the delete worked and the trigger logged it. With search_path empty, the function must name every table with its schema, like public.deleted_users.

## 4. Files in Storage

If the message names storage.objects or storage.buckets, the user still owns files. Supabase's docs say to delete that user's files, or give them to another user, before deleting the user.

## Soft delete is not a fix

Calling supabase.auth.admin.deleteUser() from the browser fails earlier, with "User not allowed": it needs your secret key, so it belongs on your server or in an Edge Function.

supabase.auth.admin.deleteUser(id, true) soft-deletes. In our test it succeeded despite the blocking key, because the row stays in auth.users, with its email replaced by a scrambled value and deleted_at set. Your rows keep pointing at that row, so use it only if that's what you want.

## If an AI tool built your app

Give your AI tool this prompt:

Write a SQL migration for the foreign keys in the public schema that reference auth.users(id): use ON DELETE CASCADE for tables that only hold that user's own data (profiles, settings), and ON DELETE SET NULL, with the column made nullable, for rows that must be kept (orders, invoices). Do the same for foreign keys that reference those tables. List every change and wait for my OK before applying it. Don't change anything else.

Read its list before you say yes: a cascade deletes those rows along with the user, for good.

## Not quite your error?

- Deleting a row of your own table fails with "update or delete on table … violates foreign key constraint": Supabase "violates foreign key constraint" (23503).

- Creating a user fails, not deleting: Database error saving new user (Supabase): find the real error and fix sign-up.

- Your app's own delete query fails with "permission denied": Supabase "permission denied for table" (42501) since October 30: the safe fix.

## Still stuck?

Open the Auth logs in your dashboard at the time of the failed delete. The entry for the delete request carries the database's own error, with the table or function to fix, even when the answer only said "Database error deleting user". In our test it read ERROR: permission denied for table deleted_users (SQLSTATE 42501).

guides.d: Sign-in fails with Database error granting user (500)? A trigger on auth.users or auth.sessions broke. Find it and fix it, tested on real Supabase Auth.
p: error update user.{1,2}s last_sign_in field(: error: .{1,200}?\(sqlstate \w{5}\))?

Fix guide · updated 2026-11-17

## Supabase "Database error granting user" (500 at sign-in): find the trigger and fix it

Database error granting user · AuthRetryableFetchError 500 · unexpected_failure

People can sign up, but signing in fails. Your app shows Database error granting user, supabase-js reports AuthRetryableFetchError with status 500, and the Network tab shows a 500 on /auth/v1/token. The password was fine. The failure comes right after it: every sign-in writes to your database, and something your database runs on one of those writes failed. Almost always, that's a trigger you or your AI tool added on auth.users or auth.sessions.

## What the error means

When Supabase Auth signs someone in, it makes three writes in one transaction: a new row in auth.sessions, a new row in auth.refresh_tokens, and an update of the user's last_sign_in_at in auth.users. If the database refuses any of them, Auth undoes all three and answers:

500 {"code":500,"error_code":"unexpected_failure","msg":"Database error granting user","error_id":"…"}

The update is the write that usually trips. In our test, Postgres logged it as:

UPDATE "users" AS users SET "last_sign_in_at" = $1, "updated_at" = $2 WHERE users.id = $3

So a trigger after update on auth.users runs at every sign-in, not only when someone edits their profile. If its function fails, nobody can sign in. A trigger after insert on auth.sessions, such as a login log, also runs at every sign-in.

Two more things we saw in our test. Nothing is half-done: the failed sign-in left no session and didn't change last_sign_in_at, so once the trigger is fixed, the next sign-in works with no cleanup. And supabase-js 2.119 reports this 500 as AuthRetryableFetchError, with error.code undefined: the message is all your app gets.

## 1. Find the real error

The app only gets the 500. The reason is in the logs. Make a sign-in fail once more, then open them:

- Lovable: More → Settings → Logs, then Authentication logs or PostgreSQL logs in the log type selector. Click Refresh, since the logs don't update by themselves.

- Bolt: the database icon at the top of your project, then Logs, then PostgreSQL or Authentication in the dropdown.

- Your own Supabase project: the Logs page of the dashboard, then the Auth or Postgres logs.

In the Auth logs, the failed sign-in carries the database's error at the end of its line. In our test, a broken trigger on auth.users gave:

error update user`s last_sign_in field: ERROR: relation "profiles" does not exist (SQLSTATE 42P01)

and a broken trigger on auth.sessions gave:

error creating new session: … ERROR: relation "login_history" does not exist (SQLSTATE 42P01)

The Postgres logs show the same error, with the function and the line that raised it:

CONTEXT: PL/pgSQL function public.sync_profile() line 1 at SQL statement

To list every trigger on Auth's tables, run this in the SQL Editor:

select c.relname as on_table, t.tgname as trigger_name, pg_get_triggerdef(t.oid) as definition
from pg_trigger t
join pg_class c on c.oid = t.tgrelid
join pg_namespace n on n.oid = c.relnamespace
where n.nspname = 'auth' and not t.tgisinternal
order by 1, 2;

In our test it listed:

sessions | log_login | CREATE TRIGGER log_login AFTER INSERT ON auth.sessions FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION log_login()
users | handle_new_user | CREATE TRIGGER handle_new_user AFTER INSERT ON auth.users FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION handle_new_user()
users | sync_profile | CREATE TRIGGER sync_profile AFTER UPDATE ON auth.users FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION sync_profile()

The usual sign-up trigger (AFTER INSERT ON auth.users) doesn't run at sign-in. Look at anything AFTER UPDATE ON auth.users and anything on auth.sessions or auth.refresh_tokens. To read a function's code, run select pg_get_functiondef('public.sync_profile'::regproc); with your function's name.

## 2. If people are locked out right now

Drop the trigger first. In our test, the next sign-in worked right away:

drop trigger sync_profile on auth.users;

Use the trigger's name and table from the list above. Dropping a trigger keeps its function and your data. Then fix the function and create the trigger again (step 3).

## 3. Match the error and fix it

These are the errors we got in the logs with the triggers that AI tools and tutorials usually write, and what fixed each one.

### relation "profiles" does not exist (42P01)

The trigger's function runs inside Auth's own query, as Auth's database user (supabase_auth_admin), whose search path is the auth schema. A table name without its schema, like profiles, is looked up in auth and isn't found. Adding security definer alone didn't help in our test: the function still used Auth's search path. What worked was both: security definer set search_path = '' and the full name public.profiles.

### permission denied for table profiles (42501)

The function names public.profiles correctly but isn't security definer, so it runs with Auth's rights, and Auth's database user has no rights on your tables. Make it security definer, with set search_path = ''.

The fixed function for both cases, the one that let sign-in through in our test:

create or replace function public.sync_profile()
returns trigger
language plpgsql
security definer set search_path = ''
as $$
begin
update public.profiles
set email = new.email, updated_at = now()
where id = new.id;
return new;
end;
$$;

A login log on auth.sessions needs the same two things: security definer set search_path = '', and insert into public.login_history … with the schema. In our test, that version logged the sign-in and let it through.

### duplicate key value violates unique constraint "profiles_pkey" (23505)

The trigger fires after insert or update, and its body inserts the profile row. Sign-up created the row, so every sign-in tries to insert it again. Keep two triggers: one after insert that inserts the row for new users, and one after update that only updates it, like the function above.

### Your own error message (P0001)

Some apps block sign-ins with a trigger that runs raise exception 'Account suspended'. That message only reaches the logs: in our test, the app got "Database error granting user". To block someone, use Auth's ban instead, from your server with the secret (service_role) key:

await supabase.auth.admin.updateUserById(userId, { ban_duration: '24h' }) // 'none' lifts the ban

In our test, the banned user's sign-in got a clear answer instead of a 500: AuthApiError 400, code user_banned, "User is banned".

### Make the trigger run only when it matters

A sign-in only sets last_sign_in_at and updated_at. If your trigger only cares about the email or the user's metadata, name those columns. In our test, even with a broken function behind this trigger, sign-in still worked:

drop trigger if exists sync_profile on auth.users;
create trigger sync_profile
after update of email, raw_user_meta_data on auth.users
for each row execute function public.sync_profile();

A condition, when (old.email is distinct from new.email), worked the same way. Fix the function anyway: in our test, changing the email still hit the broken function and failed with "Error updating user".

## 4. What else the same trigger breaks

A broken after update on auth.users trigger doesn't only stop password sign-ins. With one in place, each of these failed with a 500 in our test, under other messages:

- Sign-up with email confirmation off: "Database error updating user", and no user was created.

- Magic links and confirmation links (verifyOtp): "Database error updating user".

- Anonymous sign-in: "Database error creating anonymous user".

- Profile changes (updateUser, auth.admin.updateUserById): "Error updating user".

- People already signed in: their token refresh failed with "Unexpected failure, please check server logs for more information". supabase-js retried it several times, then gave up. Once their access token expires (after an hour by default), their requests fail too: see "JWT expired".

They all come from the same trigger, so the same fix applies.

## Other messages from the same failure

- Database error updating user's last_sign_in_at and Database error creating new session: the same two triggers, on a Supabase Auth set up with its newer refresh token format. In our test, with Auth's refresh token algorithm set to 2, the broken auth.users update trigger gave the first message and the broken auth.sessions trigger gave the second. Same fixes.

- Database error querying schema at sign-in, at the same time as Database error saving new user at sign-up, with no change on your side: check your disk. When disk use reaches 95%, Supabase puts the database in read-only mode (Supabase docs, read-only mode). In our test, read-only mode gave exactly those two messages, token refreshes failed with "cannot execute SELECT FOR UPDATE in a read-only transaction (SQLSTATE 25006)", and turning read-only off brought sign-in back. If only some users get that sign-in message, see our guide to "Database error querying schema".

## If an AI tool built your app

Give your tool this prompt:

Sign-in to my Supabase app fails with "Database error granting user" (500). Every sign-in updates auth.users (last_sign_in_at) and inserts into auth.sessions, so a trigger on one of those tables is failing. Give me SQL for the Supabase SQL Editor that lists every trigger on tables in the auth schema (pg_trigger with pg_get_triggerdef), and show me the code of each trigger function that runs after update on auth.users or on auth.sessions. Then fix each function: make it security definer with set search_path = '', and write every table with its schema (public.profiles, not profiles). Don't insert a row that sign-up already created; update it instead. Don't raise exceptions to block sign-ins; use auth.admin.updateUserById with ban_duration from the server. If a trigger only needs email or metadata changes, recreate it as "after update of email, raw_user_meta_data on auth.users". Then test a sign-in.

## Not quite your error?

- "Database error saving new user" at sign-up: the sign-up trigger is the one failing.

- "Invalid login credentials": the five cases behind that one message.

- "Error running hook URI" at sign-in: your Custom Access Token hook failed.

- "Database error deleting user": something still points at the user.

- "relation … does not exist" from your own queries: find the function or policy, then fix the name.

## Still stuck?

Run the trigger list from step 1 and open the Auth log line of one failed sign-in. The text after its last ERROR: is the real reason, and the Postgres log names the function and the line. If the list shows no trigger of yours on auth.users updates or on auth.sessions, that log line still names what refused the write: start from it.

## Supabase "Database error querying schema" (500 at sign-in): find the broken rows and fix them

Database error querying schema · AuthRetryableFetchError 500 · unexpected_failure · converting NULL to string is unsupported

Some of your users can't sign in. Your app shows Database error querying schema, supabase-js reports AuthRetryableFetchError with status 500, and the Network tab shows a 500 on /auth/v1/token. Most of the time, those users were added to auth.users by SQL (a seed script, an import, or an AI tool) instead of through Supabase Auth, and their rows hold an empty value (NULL) where Auth expects text. One SQL statement fixes them all. If every user gets the error at once, look at your disk first (section 5).

## What the error means

To sign someone in, Supabase Auth first reads their row from auth.users. Auth reads some of its columns as text and fails on a NULL there. Auth then stops and answers:

500 {"code":500,"error_code":"unexpected_failure","msg":"Database error querying schema","error_id":"…"}

This happens before the password is checked. In our test, the broken account got the same 500 with a wrong password, while an email that doesn't exist got the usual 400 Invalid login credentials. So the message says nothing about the password, and other users' accounts are not affected.

In our test, users created through Auth's API had none of those NULLs. A SQL insert that leaves four columns out does: confirmation_token, recovery_token, email_change_token_new and email_change have no default value, so they stay NULL. In our test, the usual seed insert (email, crypt() password, email_confirmed_at, metadata, no token columns) gave exactly those four.

## 1. Find the real error

The app only gets the 500. The reason is in the logs. Make a sign-in fail once more, then open them:

- Lovable: More → Settings → Logs, then Authentication logs in the log type selector. Click Refresh, since the logs don't update by themselves.

- Bolt: the database icon at the top of your project, then Logs, then Authentication in the dropdown.

- Your own Supabase project: the Logs page of the dashboard, then the Auth logs.

The failed sign-in's line ends with the real reason. In our test we got one of three:

error finding user: sql: Scan error on column index 3, name "confirmation_token": converting NULL to string is unsupported

A NULL in a text column: sections 2 to 4. The column named may differ, the fix is the same.

error locking user: ERROR: cannot execute SELECT FOR NO KEY UPDATE in a read-only transaction (SQLSTATE 25006)

Your database is in read-only mode: section 5.

error finding user: ERROR: permission denied for table users (SQLSTATE 42501)

Auth lost its rights on its own table: section 6.

## 2. Find the broken rows

Eight text columns of auth.users are the ones that end up NULL. In our test, a NULL in any one of them gave this error, each time with that column's name in the log. Run this in the SQL Editor to list the accounts that have at least one:

select id, email, created_at
from auth.users
where confirmation_token is null or recovery_token is null
or email_change_token_new is null or email_change is null
or email_change_token_current is null or phone_change is null
or phone_change_token is null or reauthentication_token is null;

In our test it listed the account made by the seed insert and nothing else. Accounts created through Auth never showed up.

## 3. Fix them in one statement

Supabase's own troubleshooting page fixes one column at a time (Supabase, "Database error querying schema"). That works, but the next sign-in can then fail on the next column. This covers all eight at once:

update auth.users set
confirmation_token = coalesce(confirmation_token, ''),
recovery_token = coalesce(recovery_token, ''),
email_change_token_new = coalesce(email_change_token_new, ''),
email_change = coalesce(email_change, ''),
email_change_token_current = coalesce(email_change_token_current, ''),
phone_change = coalesce(phone_change, ''),
phone_change_token = coalesce(phone_change_token, ''),
reauthentication_token = coalesce(reauthentication_token, '')
where confirmation_token is null or recovery_token is null
or email_change_token_new is null or email_change is null
or email_change_token_current is null or phone_change is null
or phone_change_token is null or reauthentication_token is null;

It only touches rows that have a NULL, and only those columns. An empty text is what Auth itself stores there. In our test, after it, the query from step 2 returned nothing, the account signed in, and its magic link worked again.

## 4. What else the same row breaks

With the broken account still in place, our test got these answers:

- Magic link or email code (signInWithOtp) for that email: Database error finding user.

- Password reset email (resetPasswordForEmail): Unable to process request, status 500.

- Sign-up with that email: Database error finding user.

- Listing users from a server (auth.admin.listUsers()): Database error finding users. One broken row breaks the whole list, for every user.

- Reading, updating or deleting that user from a server (auth.admin.getUserById, updateUserById, deleteUser): Database error loading user. So setting a new password for that account fails too, until step 3 is done.

If you'd rather delete the account than repair it, do it in the SQL Editor: delete from auth.users where id = '…'; worked in our test where deleteUser failed.

## Stop it from coming back

Create users through Supabase Auth, from a server with your service role key (never in browser code). This is how our test made the accounts that never broke:

const { error } = await admin.auth.admin.createUser({
email: 'person@example.com',
password: 'a-long-password',
email_confirm: true,
});

If a seed file must use SQL, give those four columns an empty text. In our test, this account signed in with its password:

insert into auth.users (instance_id, id, aud, role, email, encrypted_password, email_confirmed_at,
raw_app_meta_data, raw_user_meta_data, created_at, updated_at,
confirmation_token, recovery_token, email_change_token_new, email_change)
values ('00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000', gen_random_uuid(), 'authenticated', 'authenticated',
'person@example.com', crypt('a-long-password', gen_salt('bf')), now(),
'{"provider":"email","providers":["email"]}', '{}', now(), now(),
'', '', '', '');

Keep instance_id at all zeros. Auth only looks for users with that value. In our test, an account inserted with a random instance_id got Invalid login credentials with the right password, and a magic link or a sign-up with its email failed with Database error saving new user, because Auth didn't see the account and tried to create a second one. update auth.users set instance_id = '00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000' where instance_id <> '00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000'; fixed it.

## 5. Every user gets it, and you changed nothing

Check your disk. When disk use reaches 95%, Supabase puts the database in read-only mode (Supabase docs, read-only mode). A sign-in locks the user's row before it creates the session, and a read-only database refuses that lock. In our test, read-only mode gave Database error querying schema to every account with the right password, while a wrong password still got Invalid login credentials. Sign-up fails at the same time, with Database error saving new user (we tested it for our "Database error granting user" guide). Once read-only mode was off, sign-in worked again. Supabase's page explains how to free space or grow the disk.

## 6. After restoring a backup or moving a database

permission denied for table users means auth.users now belongs to another role, for example after a dump was restored as postgres. Auth connects as supabase_auth_admin. In our test, giving the table to postgres broke every sign-in with this message, and this brought it back:

alter table auth.users owner to supabase_auth_admin;

On a hosted Supabase project, if the SQL Editor refuses this, ask Supabase support: the auth schema is theirs to manage.

## If an AI tool built your app

Give your tool this prompt:

Sign-in to my Supabase app fails with "Database error querying schema" (500). The Auth log says "converting NULL to string is unsupported": some users were inserted into auth.users by SQL and have NULL in text columns. Give me SQL for the Supabase SQL Editor that sets confirmation_token, recovery_token, email_change_token_new, email_change, email_change_token_current, phone_change, phone_change_token and reauthentication_token to '' where they are NULL, in one update. Then change every place in my project that inserts into auth.users with SQL so it creates users with supabase.auth.admin.createUser from server code instead.

## Not quite your error?

- "Database error saving new user" at sign-up: the sign-up trigger is the one failing.

- "Database error granting user" at sign-in: a trigger that runs at every sign-in is failing.

- "Invalid login credentials" for accounts you created with SQL: the password may be stored as plain text.

- "Database error deleting user": something still points at the user.

## Still stuck?

Open the Auth log line of one failed sign-in. The text after error finding user: or error locking user: is the real reason. If step 2 lists no account but the line still names a column, find the rows with select id, email from auth.users where <that column> is null; and give that column a value.

## Database error saving new user (Supabase): find the real error and fix sign-up

Database error saving new user · AuthApiError 500 · unexpected_failure

Nobody can sign up: your app shows Database error saving new user, and the Network tab shows a 500 for the request to /auth/v1/signup. Supabase Auth itself is rarely the cause. When it creates an account, your database also runs whatever your app attached to new users, usually a trigger that copies each new user into a profiles table. If that step fails, the whole sign-up is cancelled, no account is created, and Auth only reports this generic message. The real error is in the logs.

## 1. Read the real error

Make a sign-up fail once more, then open the logs:

- Lovable: More → Settings → Logs, then Authentication logs or PostgreSQL logs in the log type selector. Click Refresh, since the logs don't update by themselves.

- Bolt: the database icon at the top of your project, then Logs, then PostgreSQL or Authentication in the dropdown.

- Your own Supabase project: the Logs page of the dashboard, then the Auth or Postgres logs.

In the Auth logs, the failed sign-up carries the database's error at the end of a longer line. Here's Supabase's own example:

failed to close prepared statement: ERROR: current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block (SQLSTATE 25P02): ERROR: relation "profiles" does not exist (SQLSTATE 42P01)

Only the last ERROR matters. The Postgres logs show the same error, with the function and the line that raised it:

PL/pgSQL function public.handle_new_user() line 3 at SQL statement

Adding or inviting a user from the Supabase dashboard runs the same trigger, so it can fail with the same message.

## 2. Match the error

We reproduced the usual mistakes on Postgres 16, with Supabase's roles. The sign-up was written as Supabase Auth's own database role, supabase_auth_admin, the way Auth does it. Each mistake gave one of these errors:

permission denied for table profiles (SQLSTATE 42501). The function was created without security definer, so it runs as Supabase Auth's role, which has no rights on your tables. Recreate it with security definer, as in Supabase's example:

create or replace function public.handle_new_user()
returns trigger
language plpgsql
security definer set search_path = ''
as $$
begin
insert into public.profiles (id, first_name, last_name)
values (new.id, new.raw_user_meta_data ->> 'first_name', new.raw_user_meta_data ->> 'last_name');
return new;
end;
$$;

Keep the column list matched to your own profiles table. create or replace keeps the trigger attached to the new version.

relation "profiles" does not exist (SQLSTATE 42P01). With set search_path = '', every table needs its schema: public.profiles, not profiles. If the name already has its schema, the table really is missing: it was renamed, dropped or never created. Create it, or update the function to use the right name.

null value in column "username" of relation "profiles" violates not-null constraint (SQLSTATE 23502). The table requires a column the function doesn't fill, often a column added after the trigger was written. Or the app doesn't send that field when people sign up. Make the column optional, give it a default value, or make sure the app always sends it.

value too long for type character varying(50) (SQLSTATE 22001). The function copies a sign-up value into a column with a length limit, and someone's value is longer. In our test of this error, a 55-character full name and a full_name varchar(50) column stopped the new user from being created. The message gives the limit but not the column: see Supabase "value too long for type character varying" (22001) to find it and widen it.

duplicate key value violates unique constraint "profiles_username_key" (SQLSTATE 23505). A column that must be unique, like a username, got a value someone already has. This happens when the function builds it from the person's name or from the first part of their email. Let people choose a username after they sign up, or add a random part to the generated one.

invalid input value for enum public.app_role: "Admin" (SQLSTATE 22P02). The function turns sign-up data into a fixed list of values, here a role, and the app sent a value that isn't on the list. This one also points to a security hole: never take a role from sign-up data. That data comes from the person signing up, so anyone can send admin. Supabase's docs say users can change their own raw_user_meta_data, so it's no place for anything that grants access. Give every new user the default role in the function, and change roles from the dashboard or from an admin-only function.

## 3. Apply the fix and test it

To see the function as it is now, run this in the SQL editor (Supabase's query), or ask your AI tool to show you the code of handle_new_user:

select pg_get_functiondef(oid)
from pg_proc
where proname = 'handle_new_user';

After the fix, sign up with a new email address and check that a matching row appears in profiles. If people need to sign up before you can fix the function, you can remove the trigger for now:

drop trigger on_auth_user_created on auth.users;

Sign-ups work again, but new users get no profile until you put the trigger back, so ask your AI tool to create the missing profiles once it's fixed.

## 4. Less common causes

- A constraint you added on auth.users, or a foreign key pointing to it, isn't met. The log names the constraint. Supabase's troubleshooting page suggests dropping it, or recreating a foreign key with on delete set null or on delete cascade.

- must be owner of … in the log: a migration tool such as Prisma changed who owns the objects in the auth schema. Supabase's page "Resolving 500 status authentication errors" shows how to give them back to supabase_auth_admin.

- Changes to the auth schema itself, like row level security on its tables or edited columns. Supabase manages that schema, and these changes break Auth. Undo them.

If the message is Database error querying schema instead, and the log says converting NULL to string is unsupported, users were added to auth.users by a SQL insert rather than through Auth, which some AI tools do. Supabase's fix is to set the column named in the log to an empty string, for example update auth.users set confirmation_token = '' where confirmation_token is null;. For one statement that fixes all eight columns that can be NULL, and what else those rows break, see our guide to "Database error querying schema".

If sign-up works but sign-in fails with Error running hook URI, the function that fails is your Custom Access Token hook: see our guide to "Error running hook URI".

If sign-up works but sign-in fails with Database error granting user, a trigger that runs at every sign-in is failing, usually one after update on auth.users: see our guide to "Database error granting user".

## Still stuck?

Write down the last ERROR from the log, the function's code and your profiles table's columns. That's what anyone helping you will ask for first, and comparing the function with the table often shows the problem right away.

guides.t: Supabase "duplicate key value violates unique constraint"
guides.d: insert() or upsert() fails with "duplicate key value violates unique constraint" (23505). Find the existing row, then upsert, fix onConflict or reset the id.
p: duplicate key value violates unique constraint
there is no unique or exclusion constraint matching the on conflict specification

Fix guide · updated 2026-11-16

## Supabase "duplicate key value violates unique constraint" (23505)

{"code":"23505","details":"Key (id)=(1) already exists.","hint":null,"message":"duplicate key value violates unique constraint \"items_pkey\""}

Saving a row fails with duplicate key value violates unique constraint "profiles_pkey", code 23505, HTTP 409 Conflict. A row with that key already exists, and that column must be unique. The constraint's name and the details line say which column and which value clashed. We ran Supabase's Data API (PostgREST 13) with the requests supabase-js sends (version 2.119, November 2026) for each case below.

## What the error means

Every primary key and every unique column has a constraint, usually named table_pkey or table_column_key. Postgres refuses a second row with the same value there, and the answer tells you exactly what clashed:

"message": "duplicate key value violates unique constraint \"profiles_username_key\"",
"details": "Key (username)=(ana) already exists."

Then the question is what your app wanted: replace the existing row, skip it, or save a different value.

## 1. The row already exists: update or upsert

The clash is on _pkey, often with the user's id: your app inserts a row that was already created. One setup does it twice: a database trigger creates the profile at sign-up, and the app inserts the profile again right after. A button pressed twice does the same when the id comes from your app. In our test, inserting the same id twice gave this 409.

If the row may already be there, update it, or use upsert(), which inserts or replaces. In our test, an upsert on the primary key replaced the row:

const { error } = await supabase.from('profiles').upsert({ id: user.id, name })

On a table with Row Level Security, an upsert also needs an UPDATE policy. In our test, with only select and insert policies, upserting an existing row failed with "new row violates row-level security policy (USING expression)".

## 2. upsert() without onConflict

upsert() checks the primary key unless you name another column. Take a settings table with its own id and a unique user_id: upsert({ user_id, theme }) has no id, so Postgres tries a new row, and user_id clashes. In our test that gave 23505 on settings_user_id_key. With onConflict, the same call updated the row:

const { error } = await supabase
.from('settings')
.upsert({ user_id: user.id, theme }, { onConflict: 'user_id' })

onConflict must name a column, or several separated by commas, that has a unique constraint. On a column without one, our test got 42P10 "there is no unique or exclusion constraint matching the ON CONFLICT specification". To add one (it fails if duplicates are already in the table):

alter table public.settings add constraint settings_user_id_key unique (user_id);

## 3. A value someone else already has

The clash is on a column the user chooses, like profiles_username_key with Key (username)=(ana). Nothing is broken: the name is taken. Catch that code and say so:

const { error } = await supabase.from('profiles').update({ username }).eq('id', user.id)
if (error?.code === '23505') {
// show: "This username is already taken"
}

## 4. The id counter is behind the rows

The clash is on _pkey with a small number, like Key (id)=(1) already exists, on a table whose ids the database numbers by itself. Rows added with their own ids, from a CSV import, a migration or a seed file, don't move that counter. In our test, after importing ids 1 to 3, the next three inserts failed with ids 1, 2 and 3, and the fourth worked: each failed try still moves the counter, which is why the error can seem to come and go. Move the counter past the highest id, in the SQL Editor:

select setval(pg_get_serial_sequence('public.items', 'id'), (select max(id) from public.items));

## Skip duplicates instead of failing

For imports where existing rows should stay as they are, pass ignoreDuplicates: true. In our test the request succeeded and the existing row didn't change:

const { error } = await supabase.from('profiles').upsert(rows, { ignoreDuplicates: true })

## If an AI tool built your app

Give your AI tool this prompt, with your table and constraint name:

Saving to the profiles table fails with duplicate key value violates unique constraint "profiles_pkey". If the row can already exist (for example a profile created by a sign-up trigger), use upsert, with onConflict set to the unique column when it isn't the primary key, or update the row. For values users choose, like usernames, catch error.code === '23505' and show "already taken". Disable the save button while a request runs. Don't change anything else.

If the clash is on an id after an import (case 4), run the setval query yourself.

## Not quite your error?

- Sign-up itself fails with "Database error saving new user": Database error saving new user (Supabase): find the real error and fix sign-up.

- Signing up an email that's already in use: Supabase "User already registered" error.

- The upsert fails with a policy error: Supabase RLS: "new row violates row-level security policy".

- "new row for relation … violates check constraint": Supabase "new row for relation … violates check constraint" (23514).

## Still stuck?

Take the details line, Key (column)=(value), and look up the row that already holds that value: select * from public.profiles where username = 'ana'; in the SQL Editor. The existing row, and its created_at if the table has one, usually shows which of the cases above you're in.

guides.t: Supabase Edge Function 404: Requested function was not found
guides.d: Your Supabase Edge Function call gets 404 NOT_FOUND, or only a CORS error in the browser: Supabase doesn't know that name. Find the mismatch and fix it.
guides.x:
Fix guide · updated 2026-11-17

## Edge Function 404 "Requested function was not found" (NOT_FOUND)

{"code":"NOT_FOUND","message":"Requested function was not found"}

Your app calls a Supabase Edge Function and gets status 404 with "Requested function was not found", code NOT_FOUND. Or, in the browser, you only see a CORS error and "Failed to send a request to the Edge Function". Either way, Supabase doesn't know a function by that name in that project: the name in your app doesn't match the deployed one, the function was never deployed, or your app points at another project. The local server, supabase functions serve, answers "Function not found" for the same thing. We reproduced it with the Supabase CLI's local function server on Supabase's edge-runtime 1.79.1, Chromium 145 and supabase-js 2.119, November 2026.

## What your app sees

It depends on where the call comes from:

- From a server, a terminal or Postman: status 404 and the body {"code":"NOT_FOUND","message":"Requested function was not found"}.

- From a browser, on Supabase's servers: Supabase's 404 article warns that browsers report this 404 as a CORS error, so supabase-js can only say "Failed to send a request to the Edge Function". Before the real call, the browser sends a check request (the preflight) to the same address, and an address with no function behind it fails that check. In our test, where the preflight hit the 404 the same way, the app got FunctionsFetchError with TypeError: Failed to fetch in error.context, and Chrome's console showed:

Access to fetch at '…/functions/v1/send-email' from origin 'http://localhost:3000' has been blocked by CORS policy: Response to preflight request doesn't pass access control check: It does not have HTTP ok status.

- From a browser, on your computer with supabase start: the local gateway answers the preflight itself, so the 404 gets through. In our test, functions.invoke() returned FunctionsHttpError: Edge Function returned a non-2xx status code, with status 404 and the plain-text body Function not found in error.context.

So the same wrong name can show up as a clear 404 on your computer and as a CORS error once deployed.

## Make sure it's this 404

The browser hides this answer, but a terminal doesn't. Call the exact address your app calls (copy it from the failing request in your browser's Network tab), with the anon or publishable key your app uses, sent the way supabase-js sends it:

curl -i 'https://YOUR_PROJECT_REF.supabase.co/functions/v1/send-email' \
-H 'apikey: YOUR_KEY' -H 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_KEY' \
-H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{}'

- 404 with NOT_FOUND in the body: Supabase doesn't know that name in that project. This guide.

- 404 with another body: your function ran and answered 404 itself, often for a record it couldn't find. Search your function for 404. In our test, a function that answered its own {"error":"Order not found"} came back with its own body, readable in the browser too, since that function handled CORS.

- Another status: not this 404. See Edge Function returned a non-2xx status code: read the real error and fix it.

Your function's own logs stay empty for this 404, since the request never reached it. Supabase's article gives a log query that lists these 404s: a request with an empty execution_id never found a function.

## Fix 1: make the name match exactly

The name in functions.invoke('…') has to match the deployed function's name character for character. In our test, each of these got the 404 when the function was hello-world:

- Hello-World: capital letters count.

- hello–world: an en-dash instead of a hyphen, often pasted from a document or a chat. It travels as hello%E2%80%93world, so a % code in the failing address is the giveaway.

- hello_world: an underscore instead of a hyphen.

- send-email: a name that was never created.

To see the exact names, run supabase functions list (the SLUG column is the name that goes in the address) or open Edge Functions in the Supabase dashboard.

Two typos didn't matter in our test: a trailing space (supabase-js builds the address with the standard URL parser, which drops it), and, on the local server, a leading or trailing slash ('/hello-world' or 'hello-world/' still reached the function). Supabase's article still lists extra slashes among the typos behind this 404 on its servers, so remove them.

## Fix 2: deploy the function to the project your app uses

A function in your code isn't on Supabase until it's deployed:

supabase functions deploy send-email

Then check that it shows up in supabase functions list. Also check the Supabase address your app uses, such as VITE_SUPABASE_URL or NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL: it must be the project you deployed to. Supabase's docs list this first for a 404: verify the function name and the project reference in the request URL. If you just deployed, give it a few minutes: Supabase's advice for this code is to redeploy and wait until every region has the update.

On your computer, the CLI only serves folders that have an index.ts (unless config.toml names another entrypoint), and it skips a function set to enabled = false in config.toml, printing Skipped serving Function: send-email. In our test, a folder with only an index.js and a function switched off that way both got the same Function not found.

## Fix 3: it's listed but still 404s

A second 404, NOT_FOUND_FUNCTION_BLOB, means Supabase knows the name but can't find the deployed code, even when the dashboard shows the function as ACTIVE. Supabase's pages disagree on its message (one shows "Function deployment bundle not found", the other says it's the same "Requested function was not found"), so read the sb-error-code header in the curl -i answer above: it says NOT_FOUND or NOT_FOUND_FUNCTION_BLOB.

Supabase names two causes: two deploys of the same function running at once, such as overlapping GitHub Actions runs, and a batch deploy whose metadata update failed. First, make a test call from the dashboard (open the function, then test it). If it fails too, or the header says NOT_FOUND_FUNCTION_BLOB, deploy the function again with the latest Supabase CLI, and don't let two deploys of the same function overlap. If the 404 stays, Supabase's support can re-sync the function.

## If an AI tool built your app

Two mix-ups to look for in generated code: invoke('sendEmail') for a function deployed as send-email, and a function whose code exists but was never deployed. Give your AI tool this prompt, with your function list:

My app calls a Supabase Edge Function and gets 404 NOT_FOUND ("Requested function was not found"), or "Failed to send a request to the Edge Function" with a CORS error in the browser. Here is the output of "supabase functions list": [paste it here]. Find every supabase.functions.invoke() call and every fetch to /functions/v1/ in the code, and make each function name match a SLUG from that list exactly: same letters, same case, plain hyphens, no slashes. If the code needs a function that isn't in the list, tell me which one and give me the command to deploy it. Check that the Supabase URL the app uses is the project from that list. Show me each change before making it.

## Not quite your error?

- Another status, such as 401 or 500: Edge Function returned a non-2xx status code: read the real error and fix it.

- A CORS error, and the terminal call above doesn't return 404: Supabase Edge Function "blocked by CORS policy": every message, fixed.

- 503 with BOOT_ERROR: Edge Function 503 BOOT_ERROR "Function failed to start (please check logs)".

## Still stuck?

Paste the failing address from the Network tab and the SLUG from supabase functions list one above the other, and compare them letter by letter, project reference included. Look-alike characters hide easily: a % code in the address means one crept in.

## Edge Function 503 BOOT_ERROR "Function failed to start (please check logs)"

{"code":"BOOT_ERROR","message":"Function failed to start (please check logs)"}

Your app calls a Supabase Edge Function and gets status 503 with "Function failed to start (please check logs)", code BOOT_ERROR. Your function never ran: its code couldn't even load, usually because of a mistake in the code or an import that fails. The local server, supabase functions serve, says "Worker failed to boot (please check logs)" for the same thing. We reproduced the usual causes with the Supabase CLI's local function server on Supabase's edge-runtime 1.79.1 and supabase-js 2.119, November 2026.

## What your app sees

functions.invoke() returns an error named FunctionsHttpError with the message "Edge Function returned a non-2xx status code". The 503 and the body are inside error.context:

const { data, error } = await supabase.functions.invoke('send-email', { body });
if (error?.context?.status === 503) {
console.log(await error.context.text());
}

On Supabase's servers the body is {"code":"BOOT_ERROR","message":"Function failed to start (please check logs)"}. On your computer, the local server answers {"code":"BOOT_ERROR","message":"Worker failed to boot (please check logs)"}: we got exactly that for all five boot failures below, within a fraction of a second, on every call.

## Make sure it's a boot error

Supabase's 503 article lists three kinds of 503 from a function:

- The body says BOOT_ERROR: the code couldn't load. This guide.

- The body is your own, like {"error":"upstream unavailable"}: your code ran and answered 503 itself, often passing on an outside service's error. Search your function for 503. In our test, a function that returned its own 503 came back with its own body, untouched.

- Neither: Supabase itself may be having trouble. Check status.supabase.com.

## Find the line that broke

In the Supabase dashboard, open the function, then its Logs tab, and search for worker boot error. That line names the problem, and on Supabase's servers it ends with the file and the line number, like this example from Supabase's article:

worker boot error: Uncaught SyntaxError: Identifier 'some_var' has already been declared
at file:///var/tmp/sb-compile-edge-runtime/source/index.ts:6:7

Here, line 6 of the function's index.ts is the culprit. The local server prints the same worker boot error lines in the terminal, so you can see them without deploying.

## Cause 1: a mistake in the code

The code isn't valid, so it can't load at all. The two our test reproduced, with the exact log lines:

- A name declared twice, often after pasting a block of code: worker boot error: Uncaught SyntaxError: Identifier 'some_var' has already been declared.

- await inside a function that isn't async, often Deno.serve((req) => { … await req.json() … }): worker boot error: Uncaught SyntaxError: Unexpected reserved word. The fix is Deno.serve(async (req) => { … }).

## Cause 2: an import that doesn't match

The code imports a name the module doesn't have, or a file that isn't there:

- A named import the module doesn't export, after a rename or a package update: worker boot error: Uncaught SyntaxError: The requested module './lib.ts' does not provide an export named 'doesNotExist'.

- A file that isn't there, because it was renamed, moved, or isn't deployed with the function: worker boot error: failed to bootstrap runtime: failed to create the graph: Module not found "file:///…/utils/helper.ts". Check the path from the function's own folder.

## Cause 3: a package that can't be loaded

Packages imported with npm: or jsr: have to load with the function. The local server downloads them when the function boots: in our test, with no network, the line was worker boot error: failed to bootstrap runtime: failed to create the graph: Failed loading https://registry.npmjs.org/zod for package "zod", followed by the network error. Supabase's article adds the package update that breaks an import: if the package worked before, check its latest release for breaking changes and pin the version that worked, like npm:zod@3.23.8.

## Two failures that aren't boot errors

- A check at the top of the file that throws, like if (!Deno.env.get('STRIPE_SECRET_KEY')) throw new Error(…) outside the handler. In our test, that wasn't a 503: the local server answered 500 with {"code":"WORKER_ERROR","message":"Function exited due to an error (please check logs)"}, and the log said event loop error: Error: STRIPE_SECRET_KEY is not set. Add the missing secret, and do such checks inside the handler so they return a clear error.

- No Deno.serve, such as an export default handler copied from another platform. The function loads fine but never answers. In our test the call waited until the local server's time limit and got a 546: see Edge Function 546 "not having enough compute resources" (WORKER_RESOURCE_LIMIT). Wrap your handler in Deno.serve(handler).

## Fix: reproduce it on your computer first

Supabase's own advice for a BOOT_ERROR is to check the logs and run the function locally with supabase functions serve. Call it once: if it can't boot, the terminal shows the same worker boot error line right away, and you can fix and retry in seconds instead of deploying each guess.

The local server doesn't add the sb-error-code header to these answers, as we saw in its source and its answers, so in your app check the status and the body's code, not the header.

## If an AI tool built your app

Give your AI tool this prompt, with the log line from your function:

My Supabase Edge Function "send-email" fails with 503 BOOT_ERROR ("Function failed to start (please check logs)"). The function's log says: [paste the full "worker boot error" line here]. Fix the line or import it names: a name declared twice, await outside an async function (Deno.serve must get an async handler), a named import the module doesn't export, an import path that doesn't exist from the function's folder, or an npm:/jsr: package version that doesn't exist or doesn't run in Deno. Keep secret checks inside the handler, and make sure the file calls Deno.serve. Show me each change before making it.

## Not quite your error?

- Another status, such as 401 or 500: Edge Function returned a non-2xx status code: read the real error and fix it.

- 546, "not having enough compute resources": Edge Function 546 "not having enough compute resources" (WORKER_RESOURCE_LIMIT).

- The browser blocks the call with a CORS error: Supabase Edge Function "blocked by CORS policy": every message, fixed.

## Still stuck?

Undo the function's last change and deploy again. If it boots, the error is in what you changed: add it back piece by piece until the 503 returns.

guides.t: Fix Supabase Edge Function 546 (WORKER_RESOURCE_LIMIT)
guides.d: Your Supabase Edge Function returns 546 WORKER_RESOURCE_LIMIT or WORKER_LIMIT. Find which limit stopped it (CPU, memory, time) and why it fails only sometimes.
p: function failed due to not having enough compute resources(?: \(please check logs\))?
worker failed to respond due to a resource limit(?: \(please check logs\))?
guides.x:
Fix guide · updated 2026-11-16

## Edge Function 546 "not having enough compute resources" (WORKER_RESOURCE_LIMIT)

{"code":"WORKER_RESOURCE_LIMIT","message":"Function failed due to not having enough compute resources (please check logs)"}

Your app calls a Supabase Edge Function and gets status 546 with "Function failed due to not having enough compute resources (please check logs)", code WORKER_RESOURCE_LIMIT. The function was stopped because it computed too long, used too much memory, or ran past its time limit. Older messages and the local server, supabase functions serve, use the code WORKER_LIMIT for the same thing. We reproduced each case with the Supabase CLI's local function server on Supabase's edge-runtime 1.79.1 and supabase-js 2.119, November 2026.

## What your app sees

supabase-js doesn't show the 546 at first. functions.invoke() returns an error named FunctionsHttpError with the message "Edge Function returned a non-2xx status code". The status and the body are inside error.context:

const { data, error } = await supabase.functions.invoke('make-thumbnail', { body: { path } });
if (error?.context?.status === 546) {
const body = await error.context.json().catch(() => null);
console.log(body);
}

On Supabase's servers, body is {"code":"WORKER_RESOURCE_LIMIT","message":"Function failed due to not having enough compute resources (please check logs)"}. On your computer, the local server answers {"code":"WORKER_LIMIT","message":"Worker failed to respond due to a resource limit (please check logs)"}: we got exactly that for all three limits.

Supabase's servers also add an sb-error-code header with the code. The local server doesn't add it to a 546 (we checked its source and its answers), so test the status, not the header.

## The three limits

Each call runs in a small worker with three limits. Going over one stops the function at once, and the caller gets the 546.

- CPU time: 2 seconds of actual computing per call. Waiting for the database, an AI model or another API doesn't count.

- Memory: about 256 MB. Supabase's limits page says 256 MB, its 546 article 250 MB.

- Wall clock: 150 seconds on the Free plan, 400 seconds on paid plans. It's the worker's whole lifetime, waiting included.

Separately, a call that hasn't started its answer after 150 seconds gets a 504 instead of a 546. You can't raise these limits on Supabase's servers.

## Find which limit it was

In the Supabase dashboard, open the function, then its Logs tab, and look at the lines around the failed call:

- CPU Time exceeded: too much computing, cause 1.

- Memory limit exceeded: too much memory, cause 2.

- wall clock time limit reached together with a 546: the call ran too long, cause 3. Without a 546, that line is harmless: Supabase prints it every time a worker shuts down, even well before the limit.

Supabase's 546 article has log queries that list each 546 with its log line and show what share of calls fail.

The local server prints its own lines in the terminal: CPU time soft limit reached then CPU time hard limit reached, memory limit reached for the worker, or wall clock duration reached, each followed by "worker error WorkerRequestCancelled: request has been cancelled by supervisor".

## Cause 1: too much computing in one call

Loops over many items, resizing images, reading PDFs or spreadsheets, encryption, big JSON transforms. In our test, a function that computed for 5 seconds was stopped after 2 seconds of CPU, and the caller got the 546 about 3 seconds after calling.

Spreading the work with await doesn't help, because CPU time adds up over the whole call. A function doing 10 seconds of computing in 20 ms slices, with an await between slices, was stopped after 2.7 seconds just the same.

## Cause 2: too much memory

Loading a whole table, a large file or many images at once, or filling a big array in a loop. In our test, a function that kept 1 MB blocks in an array was stopped as it passed 256 MB, a fraction of a second after the call, before it could answer.

## Cause 3: too long, waiting included

Waiting doesn't use CPU, so a slow AI model or API never causes a CPU stop. It runs into the time limits instead: no answer after 150 seconds gives the 504, and work still running when the worker's wall clock ends is cut off, with a 546 if the call was still waiting for it. A background task that keeps going after the answer is cut off the same way.

In our test, with the local server's wall clock set to 10 seconds, a function waiting 20 seconds for a timer used no CPU, was stopped at 10 seconds and answered 546. The local server has no 150-second 504: a slow call there ends as a 546 when its wall clock, 400 seconds by default, runs out.

## Why it fails only sometimes

A worker isn't thrown away after one call. On Supabase's servers it serves the next calls to the same function, one at a time, and its CPU time adds up across them. Supabase's 546 article gives the rule: once a worker has used half of a limit, it finishes the call in progress and shuts down, and the next call gets a fresh worker. If that call uses up the rest first, the worker is stopped at once and the call gets the 546.

We reproduced this with edge-runtime itself, keeping workers like Supabase's servers do and with the local server's CPU settings (1 second to retire, 2 seconds to stop). Two calls with 0.3 seconds of computing each, then a call with 1.5 seconds on the same worker: that call was stopped. The same 1.5-second call on a fresh worker answered normally, and since it had used more than half, the next call went to a new worker. So a call that uses more than about 1 second of CPU passes on a fresh worker and fails on one that has already worked: the same input can pass in testing and fail for real users.

The local server can't show this, because it starts a new worker for every call: its main script passes forceCreate: true, and in our runs 8 calls in a row went to 8 different workers. It gives an early warning instead. When one call uses more than half the CPU budget, it prints CPU time soft limit reached even though the call succeeds. In our runs, every 1.5-second call printed it and none of the 0.3- or 0.8-second calls did. A call that prints it is the one to fix.

## The local server's own surprise

Sometimes the local server answers a CPU or wall-clock stop with 503 and an empty body instead of the 546, and the terminal shows connection aborted (uri: "/your-function"). supabase-js then gives error.context.status 503, and error.context.json() fails on the empty body. It looks like a function that failed to start, but the CPU or wall-clock line just before it tells the real story. In our runs, 10 of 58 CPU and wall-clock stops came back that way, including the first CPU stop after every start of the server. All 12 memory stops gave the 546.

## Fix 1: less computing per call

- Do data work in the database: a filter, sort, count or sum in SQL, or in a database function you call with rpc(), instead of loading rows and looping over them in the function.

- Send heavy jobs to a service built for them: image resizing, PDF work, headless browsers, AI embeddings.

- Split a big job into several calls. Each call does one batch, say 100 items, and returns where it stopped; your app, or a queue, calls again with the next batch. More awaits inside one call don't count as splitting (cause 1).

- Use a lighter library, and don't redo the same work on every call: compute it once and save the result in a table.

## Fix 2: less memory at once

- Read rows in pages with .range(0, 999), then the next thousand, instead of the whole table at once.

- Select only the columns you use, .select('id, title'), not *.

- Don't pass large files through the function. Let the browser upload straight to Storage, and do heavy file work in a service built for it.

## Fix 3: finish sooner

- Run independent calls at the same time with Promise.all instead of one after the other.

- Give every outside call a time limit and handle the error: fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(20000) }).

- For long work, answer right away and keep going in a background task with EdgeRuntime.waitUntil(promise). That avoids the 504, but the task still has to end within the wall clock. Longer jobs belong in a queue or on a server.

## Fix 4: tell the user

A 546 shouldn't leave a blank screen or a spinner that never stops. Catch it and say something useful, and don't retry it in a loop: the same call with the same input usually fails the same way.

if (error?.context?.status === 546) {
showError('This file is too big to process. Try a smaller one.');
}

## If an AI tool built your app

Give your AI tool this prompt, with your function's name:

My Supabase Edge Function "make-thumbnail" fails with status 546 WORKER_RESOURCE_LIMIT ("Function failed due to not having enough compute resources"). The limits are 2 seconds of CPU per call, about 256 MB of memory, and 150 seconds (Free) or 400 seconds (paid) of wall clock. Read the function and list every place that computes a lot, holds a lot in memory, or waits a long time. Then change it so each call stays well under the limits: do filtering and sums in SQL or an rpc() function instead of loops, read rows in pages with range(), select only needed columns, send image or PDF work to an outside service, split big jobs into batches across several calls, run independent requests with Promise.all, and give outside requests a timeout with AbortSignal.timeout(). Splitting a loop with await does not reduce CPU time, so don't do that. In the app, catch error.context.status 546 and show a clear message instead of retrying. Show me each change before making it.

## Not quite your error?

- Another status, such as 401, 500 or 503 with BOOT_ERROR: Edge Function returned a non-2xx status code: read the real error and fix it.

- The browser blocks the call with a CORS error: Supabase Edge Function "blocked by CORS policy": every message, fixed.

- "Missing authorization header": Supabase Edge Function "Missing authorization header" (401).

## Still stuck?

Copy the request body of a failing call from your browser's Network tab, run the function locally with supabase functions serve, and send it that body. Watch the terminal for CPU time soft limit reached or a memory line. Then cut the input in half until the line goes away: that size is how much one call can safely do, and anything bigger needs splitting.
