## Supabase Edge Function "blocked by CORS policy": every message, fixed

Access to fetch at '…/functions/v1/…' has been blocked by CORS policy · Response to preflight request doesn't pass access control check · FunctionsFetchError

Your app calls a Supabase Edge Function and Chrome's console says "has been blocked by CORS policy", maybe only since you deployed. The end of that line names the mistake. We ran Supabase's real Edge runtime with 13 small functions, most with one CORS mistake each, and called them from Chrome with supabase-js 2.119 in two ways: straight to the function, the way a deployed project works, and through the gateway that supabase start runs on your machine. The surprise: all 16 calls that Chrome blocked went through on the local gateway, because it answers the browser's CORS check itself. Your function's CORS code never gets tested on your machine.

## What the error means

supabase-js adds its own headers to each call, like apikey, authorization and x-client-info. Because of them, Chrome first asks your function for permission with an OPTIONS request, called the preflight. Your function has to answer it with status 200 and headers that allow your site, those headers and the method. After that, every real answer, errors included, needs an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header, or Chrome hides it from your app.

When Chrome blocks a call, your app gets nothing to read. In our test, every blocked call gave the same error in supabase-js, whatever the cause:

FunctionsFetchError: Failed to send a request to the Edge Function
error.context: TypeError: Failed to fetch

The cause is in the browser's console, at the end of a line like this one:

Access to fetch at 'https://….supabase.co/functions/v1/hello' from origin 'https://myapp.com' has been blocked by CORS policy: …

- Response to preflight request doesn't pass access control check: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource: your function doesn't answer the preflight (section 1).

- Response to preflight request doesn't pass access control check: It does not have HTTP ok status: it answers the preflight with an error status (section 2).

- Request header field x-client-info is not allowed by Access-Control-Allow-Headers in preflight response, or another header name: your list of allowed headers is missing it (section 3).

- Method DELETE is not allowed by Access-Control-Allow-Methods in preflight response, or PUT or PATCH: your list of allowed methods is missing it (section 4).

- No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource, without the word preflight: the function ran, but its answer had no CORS headers. Usually it's an error answer, or the function crashed (section 5).

- The 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header has a value '…' that is not equal to the supplied origin, or contains multiple values: the function allows a different site than yours (section 6).

The line also tells you whether your function ran. When it says "preflight" or names a header or a method, the real request never reached it: in our test, those functions only ever saw the OPTIONS request. When it doesn't, your function ran, so whatever it did before answering (sending an email, writing a row) has happened, even though your app shows an error.

## Why it worked on localhost

With the Supabase CLI (supabase start, supabase functions serve), your app calls functions at http://127.0.0.1:54321/functions/v1/…. That address is a gateway, Kong, and the CLI's own Kong config turns on Kong's CORS plugin for /functions/v1/. With its default settings, the plugin answers every preflight itself, allows any header and any method, and puts Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * on every answer, replacing the one your function sent.

We ran Kong 2.8.1, the version the CLI uses, with that config in front of the same functions. All 16 calls that Chrome blocked went through, and no function ever saw an OPTIONS request. Even the function that allows only http://localhost:5173 worked from another address. A deployed project has no such gateway in the way: Supabase's docs say your function has to handle the preflight itself. So test CORS against the deployed function, from the browser or with the terminal check further down.

## 1. "No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header" on the preflight: answer OPTIONS

Your function doesn't answer the OPTIONS request, so the runtime's own error goes back, without CORS headers. In our test, a function with no CORS code read the body first, crashed on the empty OPTIONS request (Unexpected end of JSON input in its logs), and Chrome got a 500 with no headers.

Answer OPTIONS before anything else: before reading the body, checking the user or checking the method. This is Supabase's current example. In our test, it passed Chrome's checks for POST and DELETE calls, and its 400 answer reached the app with the error message:

import { corsHeaders } from 'npm:@supabase/supabase-js@^2/cors'

export default {
fetch: async (req) => {
// Handle the CORS preflight request.
if (req.method === 'OPTIONS') {
return Response.json({ ok: true }, { headers: corsHeaders })
}

try {
const { name } = await req.json()
return Response.json({ message: `Hello ${name}!` }, { headers: corsHeaders })
} catch (error) {
const message = error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error)
return Response.json({ error: message }, { status: 400, headers: corsHeaders })
}
},
}

If your function starts with Deno.serve(async (req) => { instead, the same lines go inside it. corsHeaders comes with supabase-js 2.95.0 and later. If your function pins an older version, Supabase's docs give the list to paste into supabase/functions/_shared/cors.ts, the same one supabase-js 2.119 sends:

export const corsHeaders = {
'Access-Control-Allow-Origin': '*',
'Access-Control-Allow-Headers':
'authorization, x-client-info, apikey, content-type, x-retry-count, traceparent, tracestate, baggage',
'Access-Control-Allow-Methods': 'GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, OPTIONS',
}

## 2. "It does not have HTTP ok status": the OPTIONS answer is an error

Your function answers the preflight with the CORS headers, but with an error status. Chrome refused all three of ours:

- Supabase's example with its OPTIONS branch removed: the empty OPTIONS request fell into the catch, which answered 400.

- A method check above the OPTIONS branch, which answered 405.

- A check for the user's token above the OPTIONS branch, which answered 401. A preflight never carries your token, so this check fails on every preflight.

if (req.method !== 'POST') {
return new Response('Method not allowed', { status: 405, headers: corsHeaders })
}
if (req.method === 'OPTIONS') { … } // never reached

If that error status is a 404, your code isn't the problem: Supabase doesn't know that function name, so the request never reached it. See Edge Function 404 "Requested function was not found".

Move the OPTIONS branch to the very top of the function and answer it with 200, as in section 1. Your method and token checks go after it.

## 3. "Request header field … is not allowed": add the header to your list

The call sends a header that your Access-Control-Allow-Headers list doesn't name. Chrome names one header at a time. In our test, it named one of these:

- x-client-info (or apikey): your list is a generic one, like Content-Type, Authorization. supabase-js also sends apikey and x-client-info on every call. Our function with that list was missing both, and Chrome only named x-client-info, so add all four.

- x-region: the call picks a region, like invoke('hello', { region: 'us-east-1' }). supabase-js then adds an x-region header, and the corsHeaders in supabase-js 2.119 doesn't list it, so Supabase's own example failed this way in our test.

- A header you added in invoke('hello', { headers: … }), like x-app-version in our test.

- traceparent, tracestate or baggage: Supabase's docs say supabase-js only sends these when you turn on tracePropagation, and that corsHeaders lists them since supabase-js 2.112.3. Redeploying the function picks up the newer list.

Add the missing names to the list. This passed in our test with a region and a custom header:

import { corsHeaders as supabaseCors } from 'npm:@supabase/supabase-js@^2/cors'

const corsHeaders = {
...supabaseCors,
'Access-Control-Allow-Headers': supabaseCors['Access-Control-Allow-Headers'] + ', x-region, x-app-version',
}

## 4. "Method … is not allowed by Access-Control-Allow-Methods": list your methods

supabase-js calls functions with POST, unless you pass a method. The list from Supabase's older docs has no Access-Control-Allow-Methods line:

export const corsHeaders = {
'Access-Control-Allow-Origin': '*',
'Access-Control-Allow-Headers': 'authorization, x-client-info, apikey, content-type',
}

With it, POST and GET calls worked in our test, because browsers allow those two without the line. PUT, PATCH and DELETE calls, like invoke('hello', { method: 'DELETE' }), were refused. Add the line, or switch to the corsHeaders from supabase-js, which has it:

'Access-Control-Allow-Methods': 'GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, OPTIONS',

## 5. "No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header" without "preflight": your answer has no headers

The preflight passed and your function ran, but its answer had no CORS headers, so Chrome hid it from your app. In our test, two functions did this, and both worked when the request was fine:

// the error answer forgets the headers
if (!name) return Response.json({ error: 'name is required' }, { status: 400 })

// or the function throws: the runtime answers "500 Internal Server Error", without your headers
if (!name) throw new Error('name is required')

So the CORS error only shows up when something else goes wrong, and it hides what. The function's logs still show it: Error: name is required in our test. In your Supabase dashboard, that's Edge Functions, then your function, then Logs.

Put the CORS headers on every answer, and catch errors so a crash also answers with them, like the try/catch in section 1. With the headers on its error, Supabase's example came back as FunctionsHttpError with status 400 and the error message in the body. To read that message in your app, see Edge Function returned a non-2xx status code.

## 6. "not equal to the supplied origin" or "contains multiple values": allow your site

The function allows a different site than the one calling it. In our test:

'Access-Control-Allow-Origin': 'http://localhost:5173'
→ The 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header has a value 'http://localhost:5173' that is not equal to the supplied origin.

'Access-Control-Allow-Origin': 'http://localhost:3000, https://myapp.com'
→ The 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header contains multiple values 'http://localhost:3000, https://myapp.com', but only one is allowed.

The first pins the address where the function was first tested, a dev server or a preview link, and fails everywhere else. The second can't work: the header takes one origin, or *. Supabase's own corsHeaders sends *, which suits a function your app calls with supabase-js, since it sends the user's token in a header, not in a cookie. To allow only your own sites, send back the caller's origin when it's on your list:

import { corsHeaders as supabaseCors } from 'npm:@supabase/supabase-js@^2/cors'

const allowed = ['https://myapp.com', 'http://localhost:3000']

function cors(req: Request) {
const origin = req.headers.get('Origin') ?? ''
return {
...supabaseCors,
'Access-Control-Allow-Origin': allowed.includes(origin) ? origin : allowed[0],
'Vary': 'Origin',
}
}

Then use cors(req) wherever the example uses corsHeaders. In our test, this worked from a listed address and was refused from one that wasn't. An origin is the scheme, the host and the port, with no path or trailing slash: https://myapp.com, not https://myapp.com/. Your site with and without www. counts as two origins.

## Check a deployed function from a terminal

curl doesn't enforce CORS, but it shows what your function answers to a preflight. Put in your project's address, the function's name and your site:

curl -i -X OPTIONS 'https://YOUR-PROJECT.supabase.co/functions/v1/hello' \
-H 'Origin: https://myapp.com' \
-H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: POST' \
-H 'Access-Control-Request-Headers: authorization, x-client-info, apikey, content-type'

In our test, Supabase's example answered with these lines:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
access-control-allow-origin: *
access-control-allow-headers: authorization, x-client-info, apikey, content-type, x-retry-count, traceparent, tracestate, baggage
access-control-allow-methods: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, OPTIONS

A status other than 200 is section 2, or section 1 when the access-control lines are missing too. A header your app sends but the list doesn't name is section 3. Don't run this check against 127.0.0.1:54321: there the local gateway answers instead of your function, and in our test it answered 200 for the function with no CORS code at all.

## If an AI tool built your app

Give your AI tool this prompt, with the full line from the console:

Calling a Supabase Edge Function from the browser fails with this CORS error: [paste the full console line]. In every Edge Function the app calls from the browser: import corsHeaders from 'npm:@supabase/supabase-js@^2/cors'. Answer OPTIONS requests first, before reading the body, checking the user's token or checking the method, with status 200 and corsHeaders. Add corsHeaders to every other response, errors included, and wrap the handler in try/catch so a thrown error also returns JSON with corsHeaders. If the app calls a function with a region or with custom headers, add those header names to Access-Control-Allow-Headers. Don't pin Access-Control-Allow-Origin to one address. Redeploy the functions afterwards. Don't change anything else.

## Not quite your error?

- The call fails with "Edge Function returned a non-2xx status code": Edge Function returned a non-2xx status code.

- The function answers 401 "Missing authorization header" or "Invalid JWT": Supabase Edge Function "Missing authorization header" (401).

- Sign-in fails with "Failed to fetch": Supabase auth "Failed to fetch".

- The line ends with "Permission was denied for this request to access the `loopback` address space": your live app calls the Supabase on your own computer.

## Still stuck?

Open the Network tab in your browser's developer tools, call the function again and look at its two requests: the preflight (method OPTIONS) and the real one. The preflight's status and response headers tell you which of sections 1 to 4 applies. If the real request went out too, your function ran: its logs in the Supabase dashboard, at the time of the call, name the error your app couldn't read.

guides.t: Supabase "Missing authorization header" Edge Function fix
guides.d: Your Edge Function answers 401 "Missing authorization header" and your code never runs. Who sends the header, who doesn't, and the two safe fixes.
guides.x:
Fix guide · updated 2026-11-15

## Supabase Edge Function "Missing authorization header" (401)

401 · {"code":"unauthorized_no_auth_header","message":"Missing authorization header"}

Your Edge Function answers 401 with "Missing authorization header", and the function's logs show nothing from your code. That's because your code never ran: Supabase checks every request before your function starts, and this one arrived without the header that check expects. Here's who sends that header, who doesn't, and the two safe ways to fix it.

## What the error means

Edge Functions have a check in front of your code called verify_jwt, on by default. It reads the Authorization header of every request. If there's none, the platform answers 401 and your function never starts (Supabase's docs, "Edge Function 401 error response"). The body is {"code":"unauthorized_no_auth_header","message":"Missing authorization header"}; Supabase's own docs also show an older shape, {"code":401,"message":"Missing authorization header"}.

Supabase's client adds the header for you: supabase.functions.invoke sends the signed-in user's token, or your project's key when nobody is signed in. So this error almost always comes from a caller that isn't your app's Supabase client.

## 1. A webhook or another service calls the function

Stripe, GitHub, Resend, a cron service, Zapier: none of them know about your Supabase login, so their requests arrive with no Authorization header and stop at the check. For these functions, turn the check off, and check the caller yourself in your code instead (for Stripe, the webhook signature; for others, a secret header only they know).

Three ways to turn it off for one function:

- Dashboard: Edge Functions → open the function → its details → turn off JWT verification.

- CLI: supabase functions deploy stripe-webhook --no-verify-jwt

- In your code: in supabase/config.toml, so every deploy uses it:

[functions.stripe-webhook]
verify_jwt = false

Our guide on Stripe webhooks in a Supabase Edge Function shows the signature check that has to replace it.

## 2. Your own code calls the function with fetch

If your frontend calls https://<project>.supabase.co/functions/v1/<name> with plain fetch or axios, nothing adds the header. Use the Supabase client instead, which adds it:

const { data, error } = await supabase.functions.invoke('my-function', {
body: { name: 'Ada' },
});

Never put your service role key or secret key in browser code to get past the check. Anyone can read it there, and it bypasses every security rule in your database.

## 3. "Invalid JWT" comes right after

Same check, other message: the header is there, but what's in it can't be verified. Usually it's an expired token (why the browser sent one: Supabase "JWT expired"), a token from another Supabase project, or a project that moved to Supabase's new signing keys, which the old check doesn't understand ("Invalid Token or Protected Header formatting"). Supabase's own advice is to turn the built-in check off and verify the user in your function's code.

## Turning the check off: what you take on

With verify_jwt off, anyone who finds the URL can call the function. That's fine when the code checks the caller: a Stripe signature, a secret header, or the user's token. For a function your signed-in users call, check the token at the top:

import { createClient } from 'npm:@supabase/supabase-js@2';

Deno.serve(async (req) => {
const supabase = createClient(Deno.env.get('SUPABASE_URL')!, Deno.env.get('SUPABASE_ANON_KEY')!, {
global: { headers: { Authorization: req.headers.get('Authorization') ?? '' } },
});
const { data: { user } } = await supabase.auth.getUser();
if (!user) return new Response('Unauthorized', { status: 401 });

// the rest of your function, for this user
});

Don't turn the check off on a function that reads or writes user data without a check like this one.

## Find out which 401 you have

- "Missing authorization header", "Invalid JWT" or "Invalid Token…": the check stopped the request. Your code didn't run, so it logged nothing.

- Any other body, or an empty one: your own code ran and returned 401. Search your function for 401, or for a third-party API whose 401 you pass along.

Supabase's knowledge base article "Edge Function 401 error response" has a SQL query for your logs that sorts recent 401s by cause.

## If an AI tool built your app

Give your AI tool this prompt:

Find every place in the frontend that calls a Supabase Edge Function with fetch or axios, and replace it with supabase.functions.invoke('<function name>', { body }), so the user's session token is sent. Don't put any service role or secret key in frontend code. List the Edge Functions that are called by outside services (webhooks such as Stripe), and don't change those callers. Don't change anything else.

Then, for each webhook function on that list, turn off JWT verification yourself (case 1) and make sure the function checks the caller's signature or secret.

## Not quite your error?

- The app only says "Edge Function returned a non-2xx status code": read the real error behind it.

- The browser's console says "has been blocked by CORS policy": Supabase Edge Function "blocked by CORS policy".

- Stripe shows 400 or 401 on your webhook: Stripe webhook errors with a Supabase Edge Function.

- The database refuses the function's query: Supabase "permission denied for table" (42501).

## Still stuck?

Call the function from a terminal with the header set, using your project's anon or publishable key, and compare: curl -X POST 'https://<project>.supabase.co/functions/v1/<name>' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <key>' --data '{}'. If that works and your app still gets 401, your app isn't sending the header: open the browser's Network tab and look at the request's headers.

guides.t: Supabase "Email address is invalid" | App Finishers
guides.d: Sign-up, magic link or password reset fails with Email address "x" is invalid (email_address_invalid)? What Supabase refuses, tested on real Auth, and the fix.
guides.x:
Fix guide · updated 2026-11-16

## Supabase "Email address is invalid"

AuthApiError: Email address "test@example.com" is invalid · email_address_invalid · 400

Sign-up, a magic link or a password reset fails with Email address "test@example.com" is invalid. The address is shaped like an email, and maybe it worked on your machine. We ran Supabase's real Auth server with its email check turned on, plus supabase-js 2.119, and tried 21 addresses and the calls that send email. Two surprises: the check only runs when Auth is about to send an email, and when a user changes their email, the message names the wrong address.

## What the error means

Before Supabase Auth sends any email (sign-up confirmation, magic link or code, password reset, invite, email change), it checks the address it's sending to. If the address fails, Auth sends nothing and answers:

400 {"code":"email_address_invalid","message":"Email address \"test@example.com\" is invalid"}

From curl, Postman or another language, without the version header supabase-js sends:

400 {"code":400,"error_code":"email_address_invalid","msg":"Email address \"test@example.com\" is invalid"}

Supabase's error-code docs sum it up as "Example and test domains are currently not supported". It's a different check from "Unable to validate email address: invalid format", which refuses addresses that aren't shaped like an email. This one refuses addresses that look fine but can't receive mail. It's in Auth since v2.165 (December 2024) and is off unless Auth starts with GOTRUE_MAILER_EMAIL_VALIDATION_EXTENDED=true. Hosted projects have it on. The Supabase CLI (v3.1.0) doesn't set it, so supabase start accepts test@example.com and your hosted project refuses it.

Nothing is saved when it fails. In our test, refused sign-ups, magic-link sign-ups and invites left no user behind, so the person can just try again with the right address.

## 1. A test or example address

These are refused without any network lookup (from Auth's validateclient.go; every one we tried was refused):

- Domains: example.com, example.net, example.org, test.com, email.com, anonymous.com, and the typos gamil.com and gamai.com.

- Any domain ending in .test, .example, .invalid, .local or .localhost. That includes company network names like ana@company.local.

- A domain with no dot: ana@localhost, ana@mycompany.

- Four exact addresses: test@gmail.com, example@gmail.com, someone@gmail.com, test@email.com.

Capitals don't help: Test@Example.COM was refused, and the message showed it in lower case, because Auth lowercases the address first.

To test your app, use addresses that really receive mail. Gmail and many other providers deliver you+test1@yourdomain.com to you@yourdomain.com, so one inbox gives you as many test accounts as you need. For automated tests, create users on the server with auth.admin.createUser({ email, password, email_confirm: true }) and get links with auth.admin.generateLink(): neither sends an email, so neither is checked. In our test, owner@example.com was created this way and signed in with its password.

## 2. A short Gmail address

At gmail.com, the part before the @ must be at least 6 characters, because Gmail itself requires 6. A comment in Auth's code says this rule cut bounced emails by 23%. Dots and +tags count as characters:

ana@gmail.com // refused
ana.b@gmail.com // refused (5 characters)
ana+1@gmail.com // refused (5 characters)
ana+test@gmail.com // accepted (8 characters)
anabelle@gmail.com // accepted

A real Gmail user rarely has an address this short, so a refusal here usually means a test address or a typo.

## 3. A domain that doesn't exist

For other domains, Auth asks DNS whether the domain has a mail server (MX record), and if not, whether it exists at all. We gave Auth a DNS server of our own to see each case:

- A domain that doesn't exist, like the typo ana@gmail.con: refused.

- A domain with a mail server: accepted. A domain with only a website address (no MX record): accepted too, since mail can go to that host.

- A DNS server that fails or doesn't answer: accepted. Auth waits up to 3 seconds, then lets the address through. It refuses only when DNS clearly answers that the domain has no mail server and no address.

Big providers (gmail.com, outlook.com, yahoo.com, icloud.com and others) skip the DNS lookup. So when a real person gets this error, it's almost always a typo in the domain. Tell them that in plain words (code below).

## 4. It only happens when Auth sends an email

The check sits in the code that sends email, so the same address passes or fails depending on the call. In our test, with @example.com addresses:

- signUp() with Confirm email on: refused. With Confirm email off, no email is sent: quick@example.com signed up and got a session, then got this error on resetPasswordForEmail() and signInWithOtp().

- signInWithOtp(), resend({ type: 'signup' }) and auth.admin.inviteUserByEmail(): refused.

- resetPasswordForEmail(): refused when the account exists, ok when it doesn't, because Auth sends nothing then (open issue supabase/auth#2702).

- signInWithPassword(), auth.admin.createUser() and auth.admin.generateLink(): never checked.

So an account created while Confirm email was off, or by a seed script, can sign in for weeks and then hit this error the first time it needs a reset link.

## 5. Changing an email: the message names the wrong address

When a signed-in user changes their email, Auth checks the new address (and the current one too, with the default secure email change). But the message names the current address. In our test:

// signed in as ana.real@realmail.dev
supabase.auth.updateUser({ email: 'ana.new@example.com' })
// Email address "ana.real@realmail.dev" is invalid

// signed in anonymously (a guest adding an email)
supabase.auth.updateUser({ email: 'guest@example.com' })
// Email address "" is invalid

The current address is fine. It's the new one that was refused: the same users changed to an address on a real domain without error. The empty "" for guests is open issue supabase/auth#2847. So on a change-email form, ignore the address in the message and tell the user their new address can't receive email.

## Show a message people understand

Check the error code, not the message, and say what to do:

const { error } = await supabase.auth.signUp({ email, password })
if (error?.code === 'email_address_invalid') {
setError("We can't send email to this address. Check it for typos, or use another one.")
} else if (error) {
setError(error.message)
}

On the change-email form, use "We can't send email to your new address."

## A real address that's still refused

If the address passes every rule above and the domain receives mail, the refusal isn't explained by Auth's open-source code. People report hosted projects refusing real-looking Gmail addresses (supabase/supabase#53456 on sign-up, #52484 on a password reset), and the code can also ask a separate validation service before sending. Only Supabase can see that, so contact Supabase support with the request time and the address.

## If an AI tool built your app

Give your AI tool this prompt:

When Supabase Auth returns the error code email_address_invalid (from signUp, signInWithOtp, resetPasswordForEmail, resend or updateUser), show "We can't send email to this address. Check it for typos, or use another one." next to the email field instead of the raw message. On the change-email form, say it's the new address that can't receive email. Don't use example.com, test.com or other fake addresses in seed data or tests. Don't change anything else.

## Not quite your error?

- "Unable to validate email address: invalid format": the address isn't shaped like an email.

- "Email address "x" cannot be used as it is not authorized", or "Error sending confirmation email": Supabase's built-in email only sends to your team.

- "email rate limit exceeded": too many emails in an hour.

- "missing email or phone": the email never reached the request.

## Still stuck?

Open the failed request in your browser's Network tab. The path tells you which call sent the email (signup, otp, recover, user, resend), and the payload shows the address Auth got. Check that address for a typo, a test domain or a short Gmail name before you look anywhere else.

guides.t: Supabase "Email not confirmed" error | App Finishers
guides.d: Login fails with "Email not confirmed"? Why Supabase blocks it, why the confirmation email never arrives, and the fix for each case.
guides.x:
Fix guide · updated 2026-11-15

## Supabase "Email not confirmed" error

AuthApiError: Email not confirmed · email_not_confirmed · Email address not authorized · email rate limit exceeded

Someone signs up for your app, tries to log in, and gets "Email not confirmed". Or since you went live, every new user hits it. Their password is fine. What's missing is one date on their account: the moment they confirmed their email address. Here's how Supabase decides, and the fix for each way it goes wrong.

## What the error means

We read the sign-in code in Supabase Auth, the server behind supabase.auth (internal/api/token.go). For an email and a password, it checks the password first. A wrong password gets "Invalid login credentials", even on an account that was never confirmed. Only when the password is right does it look at the account's email_confirmed_at. If that's empty, the answer is HTTP 400 with the code email_not_confirmed and the message "Email not confirmed".

So the error tells you two things: the person typed the right password, and their address was never confirmed. Either they haven't clicked the link yet, the link never reached them, or you changed a setting and expected it to fix accounts that already exist. Six cases cover it.

## 1. They haven't clicked the link yet

On hosted Supabase projects, users must confirm their email before they can sign in. That's the default, and you change it on the Auth Providers page of your dashboard, under Email. With it on, signUp() creates the account unconfirmed, sends the confirmation email, and returns no session. That part works as designed. The bug is a login form that shows the raw error and leaves the user stuck. Catch the code, say what to do, and offer a new link:

const { error } = await supabase.auth.signInWithPassword({ email, password });
if (error?.code === 'email_not_confirmed') {
// Say: "Check your inbox for the confirmation link", with a "Send it again" button
}

// The "Send it again" button:
const { error: resendError } = await supabase.auth.resend({
type: 'signup',
email,
options: { emailRedirectTo: 'https://yourapp.com/welcome' },
});

For an address that is already confirmed, resend answers OK and sends nothing (we checked internal/api/resend.go), so the button is safe to show.

## 2. The email never left Supabase

This is the usual cause once real people sign up. Until you set up your own email sending (custom SMTP), Supabase's built-in service only delivers to the members of your Supabase organization. Every other address fails with "Email address not authorized". It also sends only 2 emails an hour for the whole project (Supabase's docs, today's value; they say it can change). You test with your own address, it works, you launch, and nobody else ever gets a link. They can't confirm, so they can't log in.

The fix is custom SMTP: an email service such as Resend, Postmark, Brevo or Amazon SES, entered on your project's SMTP settings page (Authentication). After that, Supabase sends to every address, starting at 30 emails an hour, which you can raise under Authentication → Rate Limits. Our guide on "Error sending confirmation email" walks through the setup and its usual traps, and if you picked Resend, read "You can only send testing emails to your own email address" first.

## 3. Too many emails, too fast

Two limits stop new confirmation emails, and both answer HTTP 429 with the code over_email_send_rate_limit:

- Per address: "For security purposes, you can only request this after N seconds." Supabase won't send a second email to the same person within a short window (60 seconds unless your project sets another).

- Per project: "email rate limit exceeded". The project used up its hourly allowance: 2 an hour on the built-in service, and whatever your Rate Limits page says with custom SMTP.

Signing up again with the same unconfirmed address doesn't fail with an error about the account. Supabase leaves the account as it is and sends the confirmation again, which counts against the hourly limit (within 60 seconds of the last one, it answers "For security purposes…" instead). A user who signs up again every few minutes because the email hasn't come, or a test script, can use up the hour for everybody. Show the "Send it again" button with a short countdown, and set up custom SMTP before launch.

## 4. They clicked, landed on a broken page, and gave up

Supabase confirms the address the moment the link is opened, before it sends the browser anywhere (internal/api/verify.go). If your Site URL is still http://localhost:3000, or the address you passed as emailRedirectTo isn't in your allowed list, the user lands on a dead page. Their account is confirmed all the same, and they can log in. They just don't know it.

Set your real address as the Site URL and add every address your app redirects to under Authentication → URL Configuration, then pass that address as emailRedirectTo in signUp(). The full walkthrough is in Supabase login redirects to localhost.

## 5. You turned off "Confirm email" and old users are still stuck

Turning the setting off only changes sign-ups from then on: a new account is confirmed as it's created. Accounts made before the change keep an empty email_confirmed_at, and the sign-in check from the top of this page still applies to them, so they keep getting "Email not confirmed". We checked both sides in Supabase Auth's code (signup.go and token.go).

Confirm those accounts from a server, with the admin API and your service role key. Never put that key in browser code:

// Server only: an Edge Function, an API route or a one-off script
import { createClient } from '@supabase/supabase-js';

const admin = createClient(process.env.SUPABASE_URL, process.env.SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY);
const { error } = await admin.auth.admin.updateUserById(userId, { email_confirm: true });

This runs on your server or in an Edge Function, never in the browser: there, every auth.admin call fails with "User not allowed".

Only do this for addresses you trust: confirming skips the proof that the person owns the inbox. If your app should stay open to the public, keep "Confirm email" on and fix the email delivery instead (case 2).

## 6. Something opened the link before the user did

Some company mail filters open every link in a message to scan it. The confirmation link works once, so the scanner uses it up: the account is usually confirmed by that visit, and the user's own click then shows "Email link is invalid or has expired". Tell them to just try logging in. If it keeps happening, our guide on "Email link is invalid or has expired" shows how to switch to a code the user types instead of a link.

## If an AI tool built your app

Apps built with Lovable, Bolt or Replit on Supabase often ship with all of this at once: the built-in email service, the Site URL still on the preview or localhost, and a login form that prints the raw error. Before launch, give your AI tool this prompt:

On the login form, handle the Supabase error code email_not_confirmed: show "Check your inbox for the confirmation link" and a "Send it again" button that calls supabase.auth.resend({ type: 'signup', email, options: { emailRedirectTo: window.location.origin } }), with a 60-second countdown after each send. Show the 429 messages in plain words instead of the raw error. Pass emailRedirectTo in signUp too. Don't change anything else.

Then do the two dashboard steps yourself, since the AI can't: custom SMTP (case 2) and URL Configuration (case 4).

## Not quite your error?

- The confirmation email never arrives and sign-up shows an error: Supabase "Error sending confirmation email".

- The link says it's invalid or expired: Supabase "Email link is invalid or has expired".

- The link sends users to localhost: Supabase login redirects to localhost.

- Sign-up fails with "Database error saving new user": Supabase "Database error saving new user".

## Still stuck?

Look at the account itself in the SQL editor of your Supabase dashboard:

select email, email_confirmed_at, confirmation_sent_at
from auth.users
where email = 'person@example.com';

An empty email_confirmed_at means the address was never confirmed, and confirmation_sent_at says when Supabase last tried to send the link. Then open the Auth logs at that time: a send that failed is there with its reason, such as "Email address not authorized" or a rate limit, and so is the click on the link if it ever reached Supabase.

## Supabase "email rate limit exceeded" error

AuthApiError: email rate limit exceeded · over_email_send_rate_limit · 429

You tested your sign-up form a few times and Supabase now answers "email rate limit exceeded". Or your app is live and new users can't sign up or reset their password. Your code isn't broken: Supabase caps how many emails your project sends, and on its built-in email service the cap is 2 an hour for the whole project. Here's what the error means, what counts against the limit, and how to fix it for good.

## What the error means

We read the email code in Supabase Auth (internal/api/mail.go). Two different limits answer with HTTP 429 and the same code, over_email_send_rate_limit:

- "email rate limit exceeded" is the limit for the whole project. Your project has sent its allowance of emails for the hour, and Supabase refuses every new one, for every user, until the count goes back down.

- "For security purposes, you can only request this after N seconds." is the limit for one person. The same address asked for the same kind of email too soon. The default wait is 60 seconds, and N is what's left of it.

The first one is the one that hurts: one user, or one afternoon of testing, can use up the hour for everybody.

## 1. You're still on Supabase's built-in email service

This is the cause almost every time. Until you connect your own email provider, Supabase sends with a built-in service meant for trying things out. It sends only 2 emails an hour for the whole project (Supabase's docs, today's value; they say it can change without notice), and only to members of your Supabase organization. Any other address gets Email address "…" cannot be used as it is not authorized.

Every email Supabase Auth sends counts against those 2: a sign-up confirmation, a magic link or one-time code, a password reset, an invite, an email change. Three test sign-ups in an hour are enough.

The fix is custom SMTP: an email service such as Resend, Postmark, Brevo or Amazon SES, entered under Authentication → SMTP Settings (under Emails). After that, Supabase sends to every address, starting at 30 emails an hour. To raise that, go to Authentication → Rate Limits → Rate limit for sending emails. On the built-in service that field is locked: the dashboard says "The built-in email service has a fixed rate limit." Our guide on "Error sending confirmation email" walks through the SMTP setup step by step.

## 2. Your app sends more emails than you think

Each of these sends a new email, and each one counts:

- Signing up again with an address that isn't confirmed yet. Supabase doesn't refuse it: it sends the confirmation again (we read signup.go). A user who signs up again every few minutes because the first email hasn't come uses one more email each time.

- A form that submits twice. The first request sends the email. The second usually gets "For security purposes…", and the user sees that error even though the email is on its way.

- A "Resend email" button with no wait. Impatient users press it until something happens.

- An email sent when a page loads. Code that calls signInWithOtp or resetPasswordForEmail in a useEffect or on page load sends again on every visit and every reload.

For test accounts, skip the sign-up form. Create them from a server with your service role key (never in browser code). createUser never sends an email, so nothing counts:

import { createClient } from '@supabase/supabase-js';

const admin = createClient(process.env.SUPABASE_URL, process.env.SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY);
await admin.auth.admin.createUser({
email: 'test1@example.com',
password: 'a-long-password',
email_confirm: true, // already confirmed: no email needed
});

## 3. "For security purposes, you can only request this after N seconds."

This one is about one address, not the whole project. Supabase remembers when it last sent each kind of email to a person and refuses another of the same kind until the wait is over: one timer for the confirmation, one for the email change, and one shared by the password reset and the magic link. So a magic link right after a reset email is refused too.

Nothing is wrong. Show the user a countdown and turn the button back on when it ends. Once you use custom SMTP, you can change the 60 seconds under Authentication → Rate Limits → Minimum interval per user.

## 4. "Resend" says it worked, but no email arrives

Not a rate limit, but it often comes right after one. supabase.auth.resend({ type: 'signup', email }) answers with success and sends nothing when the address is already confirmed, or when no account uses that address at all (we read resend.go). Answering the same way whether or not the account exists also keeps strangers from using the form to find out who has an account. If the person is already confirmed, they can simply sign in. Our guide on "Email not confirmed" shows how to check an account in the SQL editor.

## Turning off "Confirm email" is not the fix

With "Confirm email" off, sign-ups stop sending confirmation emails, so the error goes away for them. Supabase's code even skips the hourly count in that case today, but a comment in that same code says this will be removed. And a live app without confirmation lets anyone sign up with an address they don't own, and still needs email for password resets. Use it for a quick test, then turn it back on and set up custom SMTP.

## If an AI tool built your app

Give your AI tool this prompt, so users see a clear message instead of a raw error:

When a Supabase auth call returns the error code over_email_send_rate_limit (HTTP 429), don't retry it automatically. If the message starts with "For security purposes", read the number of seconds in it, show "Please wait N seconds before asking for another email", and disable the button with a countdown until then. Otherwise show "We can't send more emails right now. Please try again in a few minutes." After any email is sent, disable the "Resend" button for 60 seconds with a countdown. Make sure the sign-up, magic link and password reset forms can't be submitted twice while a request is running, and that no email is sent on page load. Don't change anything else.

Then do the dashboard step yourself, since the AI can't: custom SMTP (case 1), and the hourly number under Authentication → Rate Limits.

## Not quite your error?

- Emails never arrive and the logs say "not authorized": Supabase "Error sending confirmation email".

- Password resets or magic links fail with "Error sending recovery email" or "Error sending magic link email" (each failed try still counts against the hourly limit): Supabase "Error sending recovery email".

- Supabase refuses the address itself with Email address "x" is invalid: Supabase "Email address is invalid".

- Sign-in answers "Email not confirmed": Supabase "Email not confirmed".

- The link in the email says it's invalid or expired: Supabase "Email link is invalid or has expired".

- Sign-ins or sign-ups answer "Request rate limit reached" (HTTP 429): Supabase "Request rate limit reached".

- Your provider says you can only send testing emails to yourself: Resend "You can only send testing emails to your own email address".

## Still stuck?

Open the Auth logs in your Supabase dashboard at the time of the error. Each refused email is there with its 429 and its message, so you can see which limit you hit and which request caused it: a sign-up, a reset, a magic link. If you already use custom SMTP and still see "email rate limit exceeded", compare the number under Authentication → Rate Limits with how many emails your logs show in the last hour. If your email provider itself refuses a message (its own daily limit, an unverified domain), the error is a different one, "Error sending confirmation email" or similar, and the provider's own logs say why.

## Supabase "Error running hook URI" (Custom Access Token hook)

AuthRetryableFetchError: Error running hook URI: pg-functions://postgres/public/custom_access_token_hook · 500

Sign-in fails with Error running hook URI after you, or your AI tool, turned on a Custom Access Token hook: the database function that adds something like a user role to the login token. The message only names the hook. Supabase writes the real reason in its logs. We ran Supabase's real Auth server with supabase-js 2.119, broke the hook in each common way, and wrote down what each one shows. Three surprises: the docs' revoke line, run without the grant line above it, locks everyone out; a hook that works in the SQL editor can fail for Auth, because Auth looks for your tables in another schema; and a missing row level security policy gives no error at all, only an empty role.

## What the error means

Once the hook is on, Supabase Auth calls your function each time it creates an access token: at every sign-in, and again at every token refresh (about once an hour with the default settings). If the function fails, Auth creates no token and answers with a 500. In supabase-js 2.119 it arrives as AuthRetryableFetchError, with status 500 and error.code undefined, and with the same message whatever went wrong:

Error running hook URI: pg-functions://postgres/public/custom_access_token_hook

When the function ran but gave back something Auth can't use, the same 500 comes with a more precise message: output claims do not conform to the expected schema or output claims field is missing. Section 5 covers those.

## 1. Read the real reason in the logs

Supabase dashboard → Logs. Set Log Type to Auth and Level to error, then open the line for the failed sign-in (path /token). Under Raw JSON, the error field holds the reason. One of ours:

{"msg": "request completed", "path": "/token", "status": 500,
"error": "ERROR: permission denied for function custom_access_token_hook (SQLSTATE 42501)", …}

In our test, the Postgres log showed the same error, next to the statement Auth ran: select "public"."custom_access_token_hook"($1);. Find the start of your error field here:

- permission denied for function custom_access_token_hook: section 2.

- permission denied for table …: section 3.

- relation "…" does not exist: section 4.

- output claims do not conform to the expected schema or output claims field is missing: section 5.

- canceling statement due to statement timeout: section 6.

- function public.custom_access_token_hook(unknown) does not exist or … is not unique: section 7.

- ERROR: followed by your own words and (SQLSTATE P0001): your function raised that error itself. Section 9 shows a better way.

No error at all, but your claim is always null? That's section 3 too.

## 2. "permission denied for function": Auth isn't allowed to run it

Auth runs your function as its own database role, supabase_auth_admin. A new function can be run by every role, so a fresh hook works without any grant. Supabase's examples follow it with a revoke line, so your app's users can't call the function through the API. That revoke also takes away Auth's access, unless the grant line ran too. In our test, every sign-in failed. Run all three lines:

grant execute on function public.custom_access_token_hook to supabase_auth_admin;
grant usage on schema public to supabase_auth_admin;
revoke execute on function public.custom_access_token_hook from authenticated, anon, public;

These are the lines the dashboard runs for you when you pick a Postgres function in Authentication → Auth Hooks (we read its code). If you set the hook up with the Supabase CLI's config.toml or with a migration, nothing runs them for you, so put them in the migration.

## 3. "permission denied for table", or a role that's always null

The function also reads your tables as supabase_auth_admin, and Supabase's defaults never give that role access to them. So any table you, a migration or an AI tool created is closed to it. Grant it (use your own table name):

grant select on table public.user_roles to supabase_auth_admin;

If row level security is on for that table (it should be), the hook needs a policy too. Without one there's no error at all: the read finds no rows. In our test the sign-in worked and the token said "user_role": null for everyone, admins included. A policy written for authenticated, like "users can read their own role", doesn't count: Postgres only applies a policy to the roles it names.

create policy "Auth can read user roles" on public.user_roles
as permissive for select to supabase_auth_admin using (true);

## 4. "relation … does not exist": works in the SQL editor, fails for Auth

Supabase sets Auth's role to look for tables in the auth schema, not in public. So a hook that reads from user_roles, without public., works when you test it in the SQL editor and fails for Auth with relation "user_roles" does not exist. One of the examples on Supabase's own hook page, "Add admin role", reads from profiles this way. Write public. in front of every table the hook uses, and every type or function of your own:

select role into user_role from public.user_roles
where user_id = (event->>'user_id')::uuid;

Adding set search_path = public to the function, after language plpgsql, also worked in our test.

## 5. "output claims …": what the function gave back

Auth expects your function to return the event it received, with claims changed. Each mistake has its own message, in the app and in the log:

- output claims do not conform to the expected schema: - (root): Invalid type. Expected: object, given: null: the function returned NULL. The usual cause is jsonb_set with a NULL value, which makes the whole result NULL. In our test it failed only for users with no row in the roles table, so it looked like "new users can't sign in". Wrap the value: coalesce(to_jsonb(user_role), 'null').

- output claims field is missing: the function returned the claims instead of the whole event. End it with return jsonb_set(event, '{claims}', claims);.

- output claims do not conform to the expected schema: - (root): email is required, and more lines like it: the function built new claims from scratch. Auth needs aud, exp, iat, sub, email, phone, role, aal, session_id and is_anonymous. Start from event->'claims' and add to it.

- output claims do not conform to the expected schema: - app_metadata: Invalid type. Expected: object, given: string: the function replaced a standard claim with another kind of value. Put your value in a claim of your own, like user_role.

A complete hook that avoids all four, with the grants from sections 2 and 3. It worked in our test, for users with and without a role:

create or replace function public.custom_access_token_hook(event jsonb)
returns jsonb
language plpgsql
stable
as $$
declare
claims jsonb := event->'claims';
user_role text;
begin
select role into user_role from public.user_roles
where user_id = (event->>'user_id')::uuid;

claims := jsonb_set(claims, '{user_role}', coalesce(to_jsonb(user_role), 'null'));
return jsonb_set(event, '{claims}', claims);
end;
$$;

## 6. "canceling statement due to statement timeout": 2 seconds

Auth gives the hook 2 seconds. In our test a hook that took 1.5 seconds worked, and one that took 3 seconds failed after 2 with canceling statement due to statement timeout. Every sign-in also waits for the hook, so a slow one slows every login. Keep it to one quick lookup by user id, on a column with an index or a primary key.

## 7. "function … does not exist" or "is not unique"

The hook's URI names one schema and one function: pg-functions://postgres/public/custom_access_token_hook means public.custom_access_token_hook. If that function was renamed, deleted or created in another schema, Auth fails with function public.custom_access_token_hook(unknown) does not exist. The (unknown) is normal: Auth doesn't say what type its value is. Create the function again, or pick the right one in Authentication → Auth Hooks.

If two functions have that name, for example one that takes json and one that takes jsonb, Auth can't choose and fails with … is not unique. Delete the one you don't use:

drop function public.custom_access_token_hook(json);

## 8. Sign-in works, then every query fails with role "admin" does not exist

Don't put your app's role in the role claim. Supabase uses role to choose the database role for every request. In our test, a hook that set role to "admin" let the user sign in, then every query failed with status 401, code 22023: role "admin" does not exist. Users without a row in the roles table kept authenticated and had no problem, so it looked like a bug only admins hit. Use a claim of your own, like user_role, and read it in your policies with auth.jwt() ->> 'user_role'.

## 9. Blocking a sign-in on purpose: return an error, don't raise one

Some hooks refuse certain users, for example a suspended account. With raise exception 'Account suspended', the app only gets the usual Error running hook URI… with status 500, and supabase-js treats it as a temporary failure. Return an error object instead:

return jsonb_build_object('error', jsonb_build_object(
'http_code', 403, 'message', 'Account suspended'));

In our test the app then got AuthApiError with status 403 and your message. Without http_code, it's a 500 again, with your message.

## 10. People who were already signed in

The hook runs at every refresh too, so a broken hook also hits people who are already signed in, at their next refresh. In our test, with an expired access token: after a 500 (sections 2 to 7), supabase-js tried the refresh 8 times over 26 seconds, then getSession() returned the error and kept the stored session. After the 403 from section 9, it stopped after one try, removed the session and sent a SIGNED_OUT event. So a broken hook doesn't sign anyone out, but nobody gets a new token until you fix it.

## Test the hook by hand

The SQL editor doesn't run as Auth's role, so a missing grant or policy won't show there. Ask Postgres instead (change user_roles to your table). Both columns must say true:

select
has_function_privilege('supabase_auth_admin', 'public.custom_access_token_hook(jsonb)', 'execute') as can_run_hook,
has_table_privilege('supabase_auth_admin', 'public.user_roles', 'select') as can_read_table;

With row level security on, this list needs a line with SELECT (or ALL) and supabase_auth_admin in roles:

select policyname, cmd, roles from pg_policies where tablename = 'user_roles';

Then run the function the way Auth does: with Auth's schema, within 2 seconds, for a real user. Put in the email of someone who can't sign in. The rollback at the end undoes anything the function changed:

begin;
set local search_path = auth;
set local statement_timeout = '2s';
select public.custom_access_token_hook(jsonb_build_object(
'user_id', id,
'authentication_method', 'password',
'claims', jsonb_build_object(
'aud', 'authenticated', 'role', 'authenticated', 'sub', id,
'email', email, 'phone', coalesce(phone, ''),
'iss', 'test', 'iat', 1700000000, 'exp', 2000000000,
'aal', 'aal1', 'session_id', gen_random_uuid(),
'is_anonymous', is_anonymous,
'app_metadata', raw_app_meta_data, 'user_metadata', raw_user_meta_data
)
)) as hook_output
from auth.users
where email = 'someone@example.com';
rollback;

A working hook gives one row with a claims key that holds your claim. An error here is the one Auth hits (sections 4 and 6). NULL, or no claims key, is section 5. In our test, without the set local search_path line, a hook missing public. worked here and still failed for Auth: that line is what makes the test honest.

## If an AI tool built your app

Read the error field first (section 1), then give your tool this prompt with it:

Supabase sign-in fails because my Custom Access Token hook, public.custom_access_token_hook, errors with: "PASTE THE ERROR FIELD FROM THE AUTH LOG". Fix only that function and its permissions, in a new migration: write public. in front of every table it reads; start from event->'claims', add our claim with jsonb_set and coalesce(..., 'null'), and return jsonb_set(event, '{claims}', claims); never change the role claim, use a claim named user_role; grant execute on the function and select on each table it reads to supabase_auth_admin, add a select policy for supabase_auth_admin on those tables, and revoke execute on the function from authenticated, anon, public. Don't change anything else.

## Not quite your error?

- "Database error saving new user": a function that runs at sign-up is failing.

- "permission denied for table" in your app's own queries: the grants for your app's users.

- "Invalid Refresh Token: Refresh Token Not Found": the stored session is gone.

- "JWT expired": an old token reached the database.

## Still stuck?

Turn the hook off in Authentication → Auth Hooks. Sign-ins work again, without your custom claim, so anything that reads it (like a policy on user_role) acts as if it's missing. Fix the function with the tests above, then turn the hook back on.

## Supabase: "Error sending confirmation email"

Error sending confirmation email · Email address not authorized

Sign-up worked every time while you were testing. Then real people try it and get Error sending confirmation email, or Email address not authorized, or the email simply never arrives. Nothing is wrong with your code. Supabase's built-in email was never meant for real users.

## Why it happens

Supabase's built-in email service is for testing only, and it has two limits that hit the moment you launch:

- It only delivers to members of your Supabase team. Everyone else gets Email address not authorized.

- It sends about 2 emails per hour for the whole project, with no delivery guarantee. Supabase can change that number without notice. Past the limit, users see email rate limit exceeded.

You tested with your own address, which is on your team, so everything looked fine. If you already connected your own email provider and still see Error sending confirmation email, the provider refused the message: jump to step 5.

## The fix: connect a real email provider

### 1. Pick a provider

Supabase's docs list Resend, Amazon SES, Postmark, Twilio SendGrid, ZeptoMail and Brevo. Several have free plans big enough for a new app. Resend and Postmark are the quickest to set up.

### 2. Verify your domain with the provider

The provider gives you a few DNS records (usually SPF and DKIM). Add them where your domain's DNS lives (Cloudflare, Namecheap, GoDaddy…) and wait for the provider to show the domain as verified. This step is what keeps your emails out of spam folders.

### 3. Enter the SMTP details in Supabase

Supabase dashboard → Authentication → SMTP Settings (under Emails) → enable custom SMTP and fill in:

- Host and port: from your provider (port 465 or 587)

- Username and password: the SMTP credentials your provider gives you (often an API key)

- Sender email: an address on the domain you verified, like no-reply@yourapp.com

- Sender name: your app's name

### 4. Raise the rate limit

Right after you save, Supabase starts you at 30 emails per hour. If you expect more sign-ups than that, go to Authentication → Rate Limits and raise it.

### 5. Test, and read the log if it fails

Sign up with an address that isn't on your team. If it still fails, Supabase → Logs (Auth) shows the exact answer from your provider. The usual causes:

- the sender address isn't on the verified domain,

- a wrong password or API key,

- a port that doesn't match the encryption (465 = SSL, 587 = STARTTLS),

- the domain isn't verified yet at the provider.

Each answer from your provider, and what it means, is in our guide to "Error sending recovery email": the same failure, on password resets and magic links.

## The shortcut, and why to avoid it

You can turn off Confirm email in Supabase's email provider settings so sign-ups no longer need an email at all. That's fine for a quick test, but on a live app it lets anyone sign up with fake addresses and leaves users with no way to reset a password. Connect a real provider instead. It takes about 15 minutes.

## Still not arriving?

If emails send but land in spam, your domain records (SPF, DKIM, and ideally DMARC) need fixing. If the confirmation link sends people to localhost, see our guide on login redirects to localhost. If Supabase answers Email address "x" is invalid once your provider is connected, the address itself was refused: see Supabase "Email address is invalid".
