## Supabase "Error sending recovery email"

AuthRetryableFetchError: Error sending recovery email · Error sending magic link email · 500

The password reset or the magic link button fails with Error sending recovery email or Error sending magic link email. Supabase tried to hand the email to your email provider and the provider said no, or never answered. The message doesn't say why, but Supabase's Auth log does. We ran Supabase's real Auth server against a test mail server that fails in each common way, with supabase-js 2.119, and wrote down what each failure looks like. Three surprises: a reset for an address with no account always "works", every failed attempt still counts against your hourly email limit, and a slow mail server can deliver an email whose link is already dead.

## What the error means

Supabase Auth builds the email, connects to the SMTP server in your settings (Resend, Postmark, Brevo, Amazon SES…) and sends it. If any step fails, it answers with a 500 that only says which email failed:

500 {"code":"unexpected_failure","message":"Error sending recovery email"}

From curl, Postman or another language, without the version header supabase-js sends:

500 {"code":500,"error_code":"unexpected_failure","msg":"Error sending recovery email","error_id":"…"}

In supabase-js 2.119 it arrives as AuthRetryableFetchError with status 500, and error.code is undefined. The same failure gets a different name depending on the email Auth was sending. In our test, with the mail server refusing the password:

- resetPasswordForEmail(): Error sending recovery email, also for an account that isn't confirmed yet.

- signInWithOtp() for a confirmed user: Error sending magic link email. For a new user, or one who never confirmed, Auth sends a sign-up confirmation instead, so the message is Error sending confirmation email.

- signUp() and resend({ type: 'signup' }): Error sending confirmation email.

- updateUser({ email }): Error sending email change email. reauthenticate(): Error sending reauthentication email. auth.admin.inviteUserByEmail(): Error sending invite email.

All of them have the same causes and the same fix. If you never set up your own email provider, read our guide to "Error sending confirmation email" first: Supabase's built-in email only sends to your team and refuses everyone else with "Email address not authorized".

## 1. Read the real reason in the Auth log

Supabase dashboard → Logs. Set Log Type to Auth and Level to error, then open the line for your request: path /recover for a password reset, /otp for a magic link. Under Raw JSON, the error field holds what the mail server answered. One of ours:

{"msg": "request completed", "path": "/recover", "status": 500,
"error_code": "unexpected_failure",
"error": "535 \"5.7.8 Authentication credentials invalid\"", …}

Find the start of your error field here. The number is a standard SMTP code. The words after it are your provider's own, so they're more precise than ours:

- 535 …: the SMTP username or password is wrong. Copy both again from your provider. For Resend, the username is resend and the password is an API key. If you deleted or replaced that key, put the new one in.

- gomail: could not send email 1: 550 … (or another code starting with 5, like 554): the login worked, but the provider refused this email. Its words say why. The usual one: the Sender email in Supabase isn't on the domain you verified with the provider. Also common: an account still in test mode, like Resend's "You can only send testing emails to your own email address".

- gomail: could not send email 1: 451 … (any code starting with 4): a temporary refusal, often a sending limit at the provider. Check your provider's dashboard for limits, then try again.

- unencrypted connection: the server didn't offer encryption on that port, so Auth refused to send your password over it. Check the host and port against your provider's SMTP page.

- tls: first record does not look like a TLS handshake: port 465 on a server that doesn't use TLS on that port. Use 587.

- tls: failed to verify certificate: x509: certificate is valid for …, not …: the host name doesn't match the server's certificate. Use the exact host from your provider, not an IP address or a name of your own pointing to it.

- dial tcp …: connect: connection refused, EOF, or a 421: nothing answered at that host and port, or the server hung up at once. Check the host and port.

- context deadline exceeded, with status 504: the server didn't answer within Auth's 10-second limit. Your app got a different message for this one, see section 3.

Change the settings under Authentication → SMTP Settings, save, and try again. There's no need to wait: a failed attempt doesn't start the 60-second wait between two emails to the same person.

## 2. Port 465 is the only TLS port Supabase knows

Auth's mail code turns on TLS from the first byte only when the port is exactly 465. On any other port it starts unencrypted and switches to encryption with STARTTLS. So:

- 465: TLS from the start. Worked in our test.

- 587 (and the other ports, like 2587): starts plain, then STARTTLS. 587 worked in our test.

- 2465: Resend lists it as TLS from the start, like 465. Supabase doesn't know that, so it waits for a hello the server never sends. After 10 seconds your app gets Processing this request timed out, please retry after a moment. (status 504). Use 465 or 587 instead.

## 3. "Processing this request timed out": the email may still arrive, with a dead link

When the mail server is slow or silent, Auth gives up after 10 seconds and answers:

504 {"code":"request_timeout","message":"Processing this request timed out, please retry after a moment."}

It doesn't stop the sending, though. Our test server waited 12 seconds before saying hello. The app got the 504 at 10 seconds, and the reset email still arrived two seconds later. Its link didn't work: Email link is invalid or has expired, because Auth had already given up and saved nothing for that link. So users who saw the error and then got the email anyway hit the expired-link error. Once your mail settings are fixed, they need to ask for a new email.

A wrong port (section 2), or a mail server that accepts the connection but doesn't answer, ends the same way.

## 4. Why it "works" when you test it

- A made-up address. resetPasswordForEmail() for an address with no account answers ok and sends nothing, so it never touches your mail server. Auth answers the same either way, so the form doesn't reveal who has an account. Test the reset with a real account.

- Confirm email turned off. Then signUp() sends no email and works fine, while password resets and magic links still need your mail server and fail. In our test, signInWithOtp() for a new address created a confirmed user and then failed with Error sending magic link email. With Confirm email on, the same call left no user behind.

## 5. Failed attempts still use up your hourly email limit

With Confirm email on (the default), Supabase counts an email against the project's hourly limit before it tries to send it (30 an hour by default once you use your own SMTP). A failed send counts too. We set the limit to 3: two failed resets and one that worked used it up, and the next request got email rate limit exceeded without even trying the mail server. So after an afternoon of failures, users can stay blocked for the rest of the hour even though your settings are fixed. Raise the limit in Authentication → Rate Limits, or see our guide to "email rate limit exceeded".

## 6. Help a locked-out user right now

On your server, with the secret service-role key, auth.admin.generateLink() returns the link without sending any email. It worked in our test while the mail server was refusing everything:

const { data, error } = await supabaseAdmin.auth.admin.generateLink({
type: 'recovery', // or 'magiclink'
email: 'user@theirdomain.com',
})
// data.properties.action_link = the link the email would have contained

That link signs the person in, so only give it to someone you've confirmed owns the account. It's a stopgap while you fix the settings, not a way around them.

## Show a message people understand

Check error.status, not error.code (it's empty for these errors in supabase-js 2.119):

const { error } = await supabase.auth.resetPasswordForEmail(email, { redirectTo })
if (error && (error.status === 500 || error.status === 504)) {
setError("We couldn't send the email right now. Please try again in a few minutes.")
} else if (error) {
setError(error.message)
} else {
setNotice('If an account exists for this address, we sent a link.')
}

## If an AI tool built your app

This error comes from the email settings in your Supabase dashboard, so no code change fixes it, and an AI tool that rewrites your login flow will make things worse. Fix the settings first (sections 1 and 2), then give your tool this prompt for the message:

When supabase.auth.resetPasswordForEmail or signInWithOtp returns an error with status 500 or 504 ("Error sending recovery email", "Error sending magic link email" or "Processing this request timed out"), show "We couldn't send the email right now. Please try again in a few minutes." instead of the raw message. Don't treat it as a network error and don't retry automatically. Don't change the sign-in flow or anything else.

## Using a Send Email hook instead of SMTP?

Then you won't see these messages. Auth passes on what your hook said. In our test: a hook that answered 500 gave Unexpected status code returned from hook: 500, a hook that never answered gave Failed to reach hook after maximum retries (422, after 3 tries), and a hook that answered { "error": { "http_code": 400, "message": "…" } } passed its own message to the app. The reason is in your hook's logs, for example your Edge Function's logs.

## Not quite your error?

- "Error sending confirmation email" or "Email address "x" cannot be used as it is not authorized": Supabase's built-in email only sends to your team.

- "email rate limit exceeded" or "For security purposes, you can only request this after N seconds": too many emails.

- "Email address "x" is invalid": Supabase refused the address itself.

- "Email link is invalid or has expired": the link was used, replaced or too old.

## Still stuck?

Put the same host, port, username and password into another email program, or your provider's own test tool. If it fails there too, the problem is at the provider: contact their support with the time of the failed request, and they can read the refusal in their own logs. If it works there and Supabase still fails, compare the Sender email and the port, the two settings other programs fill in for you.

guides.t: Supabase "infinite recursion detected in policy": fix
guides.d: A 500 with error 42P17 means a security policy looks something up in its own table, or two tables' policies look each other up. Find the policy and fix it.
guides.x:
Fix guide · updated 2026-11-09

## Infinite recursion detected in policy for relation (Supabase): find the policy and break the loop

infinite recursion detected in policy for relation "..." · 42P17 · 500

A page stays empty or shows an error. In the browser's Network tab, the request to /rest/v1/ for one of your tables returns a 500, and the error from Supabase reads infinite recursion detected in policy for relation "profiles", code 42P17, with your own table's name in the quotes. Your data is fine. One of your table's security policies (row level security) has a loop in it, and Postgres refuses to run it.

## 1. What the loop is

A policy decides which rows each user can see. To check a row, Postgres runs the policy. If the policy looks something up in its own table, Postgres has to run the policy again to check that lookup, and again for the next one, forever. So it stops right away with this error. Two tables whose policies look each other up make the same loop.

We reproduced it on Postgres 16, with Supabase's roles. What it breaks:

- Every signed-in user the policy applies to gets the error, not only admins. In our test, a normal user got the same 500 as the admin.

- Every request that reads the table fails: loading it, updating or deleting rows, and adding a row when the app asks for it back (.insert(...).select()). A plain insert went through.

- The Supabase dashboard looks fine. The Table Editor and the SQL editor use the postgres role by default, and Supabase gives that role the right to skip policies (bypassrls), so you see all your rows there while the app gets a 500.

## 2. Find the policy

Run this in the SQL editor (Supabase's dashboard), or ask your AI tool to list the policies of the table named in the error:

select tablename, policyname, cmd, qual, with_check
from pg_policies
where schemaname = 'public'
order by tablename, policyname;

Look at the policies of the table in the error, mainly those whose cmd is SELECT or ALL. You'll find one of two shapes.

A policy that looks up its own table. The usual one is an admin check on profiles:

create policy "Admins can view all profiles" on public.profiles
for select to authenticated
using (
exists (
select 1 from public.profiles
where id = auth.uid() and role = 'admin'
)
);

In the pg_policies list, Postgres shows the table's own name after FROM, with _1 added: FROM profiles profiles_1. Team features make the same shape: a policy on team_members that lets members see their teammates by looking up team_members.

Two tables that look each other up. Supabase's own example is a sharing feature: the policy on lists reads list_members to find who a list is shared with, and the policy on list_members reads lists to find who owns it. The error names whichever table the app asked for first: in our test, loading lists reported "lists", and loading list_members reported "list_members".

## 3. Break the loop with a security definer function

Supabase's documented fix moves the lookup into a function marked security definer. Such a function runs as the role that created it, postgres on Supabase, which isn't held back by policies. The lookup inside it doesn't run the policy again, so the loop is gone. For the admin check:

create schema if not exists private;

create or replace function private.is_admin()
returns boolean
language sql
stable
security definer
set search_path = ''
as $$
select exists (
select 1 from public.profiles
where id = (select auth.uid()) and role = 'admin'
)
$$;

revoke execute on function private.is_admin() from public;
grant usage on schema private to authenticated;
grant execute on function private.is_admin() to authenticated;

drop policy "Admins can view all profiles" on public.profiles;
create policy "Admins can view all profiles" on public.profiles
for select to authenticated
using ( (select private.is_admin()) );

In our test, the admin then saw every profile and a normal user saw only their own, through their existing "view own profile" policy. For teams, the function returns the caller's teams, and every policy that needs them calls it. Use the same type as your team_id column:

create or replace function private.my_team_ids()
returns setof uuid
language sql
stable
security definer
set search_path = ''
as $$
select team_id from public.team_members
where user_id = (select auth.uid())
$$;

revoke execute on function private.my_team_ids() from public;
grant usage on schema private to authenticated;
grant execute on function private.my_team_ids() to authenticated;

drop policy "Members can view their team" on public.team_members;
create policy "Members can view their team" on public.team_members
for select to authenticated
using ( team_id in (select private.my_team_ids()) );

A member then saw everyone on their own team and nobody else. Policies on other tables, like projects or tasks, can use the same team_id in (select private.my_team_ids()) test. That also breaks the two-table loop: both policies call the function instead of reading each other's table. Run the SQL in the SQL editor, or give it to your AI tool and ask it to apply it as a migration, with your own table and policy names.

Three details matter:

- The private schema. A security definer function in a schema your API exposes, like public, can be called by anyone through the API with the creator's rights. Supabase's docs say never to put one there. Your policies can still call a function in a schema the API doesn't expose.

- set search_path = '' stops a caller from swapping in their own objects. Every name inside then needs its schema: public.profiles, not profiles.

- (select ...) around the call, as in Supabase's examples, lets Postgres run the function once per request instead of once per row.

## 4. Errors you may see after the fix

permission denied for function is_admin (42501, a 403 in the app). The grant execute line is missing. Policies run with the rights of the user making the request, so that user needs the right to run the function.

stack depth limit exceeded (a 500). The function was created without security definer, so its lookup goes through the same policy again and the loop is back. It doesn't always show: in our test it failed only when the table had no "view own row" policy. So it can work for months, then break when someone edits a policy. Add security definer either way.

relation "profiles" does not exist. With set search_path = '', a table name without its schema isn't found. Write public.profiles.

## 5. Fixes that make it worse

Turning row level security off on the table, or replacing the policy's condition with true, makes the error go away because nothing is checked anymore. Every signed-in user, and often anyone with your app's public key, can then read and change every row. Using the service role key (or a secret key) in the app does the same thing: that key skips every policy, and anyone who opens your site can copy it. If your AI tool proposes one of these, ask it for the security definer function instead.

## 6. Test it as a real user

The dashboard skips policies, so test as a signed-in user. Run this in the SQL editor with the ID of an admin, then with the ID of a normal user (from Authentication → Users):

begin;
set local role authenticated;
set local request.jwt.claim.sub = 'PUT-THE-USER-ID-HERE';
select * from public.profiles;
rollback;

Both should return rows with no error, and the normal user should see only what they're allowed to. Then reload the page in your app.

## Still stuck?

Write down the full error, the output of the pg_policies query for the table in the error, and the tables its policies read. That's what anyone helping you will ask for first, and following the lookups from one policy to the next usually shows where the loop closes.

guides.t: Fix Supabase invalid input syntax for type uuid "undefined"
guides.d: A Supabase query fails with invalid input syntax for type uuid: "undefined" (22P02). Which variable was empty when the query ran, and how to wait for it.
guides.x:
Fix guide · updated 2026-11-16

## Supabase invalid input syntax for type uuid: "undefined" (22P02)

{"code":"22P02","details":null,"hint":null,"message":"invalid input syntax for type uuid: \"undefined\""}

A page of your app loads nothing, and the request behind it failed with invalid input syntax for type uuid: "undefined", code 22P02, HTTP 400. The database received the word "undefined" where it expected an ID: the variable your code put in the filter was empty when the query ran. We ran Supabase's Data API (PostgREST 13) ourselves, with the requests supabase-js builds (version 2.119, November 2026). Here's how to find the empty variable, and how to make the query wait for it.

## What the error means

supabase-js writes each filter into the request's address: .eq('user_id', value) becomes user_id=eq. followed by the value as text. JavaScript writes an empty value as the word itself, so the database gets "undefined" or "null" to compare with a uuid column, and refuses. In our test:

- .eq('id', undefined) sent id=eq.undefined and got invalid input syntax for type uuid: "undefined",

- .eq('id', null) sent id=eq.null and got the same error with "null",

- .in('id', [undefined, …]), .single(), .update() and .delete() with an undefined ID all got the same error,

- an integer column says invalid input syntax for type integer: "undefined" instead.

Nothing is wrong with your table or your policies. The fix is in the code that runs the query.

## The one-minute check

Open your browser's Network tab, reload, and click the failing request (it shows 400). Its address names the table and the column, for example /rest/v1/profiles?select=*&user_id=eq.undefined. Search your code for that table, find the filter on that column, and log the value just before the query:

console.log('user_id filter =', userId) // the variable your .eq() uses

If it prints undefined or null, one of the causes below applies. If it prints something that isn't an ID, see the last one.

## 1. The user isn't loaded yet

A query filters on user?.id and runs on the first render, before Supabase has loaded the session, so user is still null. Get the user first, and stop if there isn't one:

const { data: { user } } = await supabase.auth.getUser()
if (!user) return // not signed in (yet): don't query
const { data, error } = await supabase.from('profiles').select('*').eq('user_id', user.id)

In React, keep user?.id in the effect's dependencies and return early while it's missing. With React Query, add enabled: !!user?.id so the query waits.

## 2. A URL parameter with another name, or the word "undefined" in the URL

The route is /projects/:projectId but the page reads useParams().id: that's undefined. Use the same name in both places. Or the link to the page was built while its ID was missing, and the address itself says /projects/undefined: the page then reads the text "undefined", and the query fails the same way. Fix the code that builds the link, and check the parameter before querying:

const { projectId } = useParams()
if (!projectId || projectId === 'undefined') return // show "Not found" instead

## 3. The ID comes from data that hasn't arrived

A second query uses a field from the first one, like profile?.team_id, and runs before the first one has answered. Run it only once that value exists: in the first query's result, or with enabled: !!profile?.team_id in React Query.

## 4. The wrong field name

The row has user_id, but the code reads row.userId or row.uuid: a field that doesn't exist is undefined. Log the whole object (console.log(row)) and use the key it really has.

## 5. null on purpose: use .is()

If you want the rows where a column is empty, .eq('team_id', null) fails with "null". Use .is(), which our test answered normally:

const { data, error } = await supabase.from('profiles').select('*').is('team_id', null)

## 6. A value that isn't a uuid

If the message quotes something else, like invalid input syntax for type uuid: "123" or a name, the variable isn't empty: it's the wrong value for that column. A number from another table, a slug from the URL, an email address. Filter on the column that holds that value, for example .eq('slug', slug), or look up the row's uuid first.

## Don't hide it with .match()

.match({ id: undefined }) doesn't fail: supabase-js drops keys whose value is undefined, so the request goes out with no filter at all. In our test it returned every row of the table. Never switch to .match() to make this error go away, and above all not before .update() or .delete(). Make the query wait for the value instead.

## If an AI tool built your app

Give your AI tool this prompt, with the table and column from the Network tab:

A Supabase query on the profiles table fails with invalid input syntax for type uuid: "undefined" because its user_id filter is undefined when it runs. Find every Supabase query whose filter value can be undefined or null at that moment (user?.id, route params, fields from another query). Don't run those queries until the value exists: return early, or use enabled: !!value in React Query. Use .is(column, null) where null is meant. Don't replace .eq() with .match(). Don't change anything else.

## Not quite your error?

- An rpc() call with an undefined argument sends no argument at all, and gets a 404 "Could not find the function … without parameters": Supabase "Could not find the function in the schema cache" (PGRST202).

- An insert() with an undefined value leaves that column out. In our test it then failed with null value in column "user_id" … violates not-null constraint (23502). If a policy checks user_id, you may get Supabase RLS: "new row violates row-level security policy" instead.

- The ID is right but .single() finds no row: Supabase 406 and PGRST116: "Cannot coerce the result to a single JSON object".

- The user is never loaded, even after waiting: Supabase "Auth session missing!" error.

- The same undefined in a Realtime filter (filter: `user_id=eq.${user?.id}`) doesn't fail loudly: the channel still says SUBSCRIBED and no event ever comes. See Supabase Realtime not working: SUBSCRIBED but no events.

## Still stuck?

Look at the failing request's address again: each column=eq.undefined in it is one filter with an empty value, so there may be more than one. Log every variable used in that query's filters on the same line, and reload: the one that prints undefined is the one to wait for.

guides.t: Supabase "Invalid login credentials" error | App Finishers
guides.d: "Invalid login credentials" though the password looks right? The five cases Supabase hides behind one message, and how to find yours.
guides.x:
Fix guide · updated 2026-11-15

## Supabase "Invalid login credentials" error

AuthApiError: Invalid login credentials · invalid_credentials · 400

The user is sure of their email and password, and Supabase still answers "Invalid login credentials". Sometimes it's every user, right after you published. Supabase uses this one message for several different problems, on purpose, so the message alone won't tell you which one you have. Here's the list, and a two-minute check that tells them apart.

## What the error means

We read the sign-in code in Supabase Auth (internal/api/token.go). An email and password sign-in answers HTTP 400 with the code invalid_credentials and "Invalid login credentials" when:

- no account has that email in this Supabase project,

- the account exists but has no password at all,

- the password doesn't match the one stored,

- a password hook you added rejected the attempt,

- the password was changed while this sign-in was being checked.

The first three are the real causes. Supabase gives them all the same answer so a stranger can't use your login form to test which emails have an account. That's good security, and it's also why you have to look at the account yourself (see "Find your case in two minutes" below). Upper or lower case in the email is never the problem: Supabase compares emails in lower case.

## 1. The account isn't in the project your app talks to

This is the most common one in apps built with AI tools. You look at the users in one Supabase project, but your app is connected to another: a preview and a live version with different settings, a remix that made a new project, or a .env file from an older setup. For that other project, the account doesn't exist, so the answer is "Invalid login credentials".

Check the address your app uses: it's the URL passed to createClient(), often in VITE_SUPABASE_URL or NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL. It looks like https://abcdefgh.supabase.co. Those 8 letters are the project's reference, and the dashboard shows the same reference in its own address bar. If they differ, you're looking at the wrong project, or your app is.

## 2. The account has no password

People who signed up with Google or GitHub, with a magic link, with a one-time code, or who were invited and never finished, have no password stored. Supabase checks for one before anything else, and with none it answers "Invalid login credentials", even if they type a password they use elsewhere.

They can sign in the way they signed up. Or they can set a password through your reset flow: send the email, and on your reset page save the new password.

// "Forgot password?" link
await supabase.auth.resetPasswordForEmail(email, { redirectTo: 'https://yourapp.com/reset' });

// On https://yourapp.com/reset, once the link has logged them in
const { error } = await supabase.auth.updateUser({ password: newPassword });

If your app offers Google and email at once, say it on the login form: "Signed up with Google? Use the Google button."

## 3. The password really is different

Supabase compares exactly what your form sends. A password manager filling an old password, Caps Lock, a form that adds or keeps a space, or a password changed on another device will all fail. Before digging into code, reset the password of one test account and sign in with the new one. If that works, the system is fine and the problem is what was typed.

## 4. You created the users yourself, with SQL or a seed script

Supabase stores a hash of the password in auth.users.encrypted_password and checks it with bcrypt (argon2 and Firebase scrypt hashes are also accepted, for imports). An AI-written script that inserts users straight into auth.users often puts the password there as plain text, or skips it. Those accounts can never sign in, whatever is typed. A script can also put a random value in instance_id: Auth only looks for users whose instance_id is all zeros, so in our test such an account got Invalid login credentials with the right password (the fix is in our guide to "Database error querying schema").

Create users through Supabase instead, from a server with your service role key (never in browser code):

import { createClient } from '@supabase/supabase-js';

const admin = createClient(process.env.SUPABASE_URL, process.env.SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY);
const { error } = await admin.auth.admin.createUser({
email: 'person@example.com',
password: 'a-long-password',
email_confirm: true, // skip the confirmation email for accounts you create yourself
});

For accounts that already exist with a broken password, send them a reset (case 2), or set a new one from the server with admin.auth.admin.updateUserById(userId, { password }). If that call fails with Database error loading user, the row has NULL columns: fix them first with our guide to "Database error querying schema".

## 5. A password hook, or bad timing

If you added a "password verification attempt" hook (Authentication → Hooks), it can reject a sign-in, and Supabase then answers with this code and your hook's message (by default "Further password verification attempts will be rejected."). And if the password is changed at the very moment someone signs in, Supabase refuses that sign-in rather than let the old password through. Both are rare. If you never set up a hook, skip this one.

## Find your case in two minutes

In the Supabase dashboard of the project your app really uses (case 1), open the SQL editor and run:

select email,
email_confirmed_at,
coalesce(encrypted_password, '') <> '' as has_password,
raw_app_meta_data->>'provider' as signed_up_with
from auth.users
where lower(email) = lower('person@example.com');

- No row: no account in this project. Case 1, or the person never signed up.

- has_password is false: case 2. signed_up_with says how they did sign up.

- A password and a confirmed email: case 3, or case 4 if you created the account by script. A reset tells them apart.

- A password but no email_confirmed_at: once the right password is typed, Supabase will answer "Email not confirmed" instead. See our guide on "Email not confirmed".

## If an AI tool built your app

Give your AI tool this prompt, so your users see a useful message instead of a dead end:

On the login form, when Supabase returns the error code invalid_credentials, show "Wrong email or password" with a "Forgot password?" link that calls supabase.auth.resetPasswordForEmail(email, { redirectTo: window.location.origin + '/reset' }). Add a /reset page that saves the new password with supabase.auth.updateUser({ password }). If the app also has Google sign-in, add the line "Signed up with Google? Use the Google button." Don't change anything else.

Then check case 1 yourself: the Supabase URL in your app's settings must be the project you look at in the dashboard.

## Not quite your error?

- The password is right but the account isn't confirmed: Supabase "Email not confirmed".

- The form says "missing email or phone": Supabase "missing email or phone".

- Sign-up itself fails: Supabase "Database error saving new user".

- Sign-up says the email is taken: Supabase "User already registered".

- The second sign-in attempt fails with "captcha protection: request disallowed": Supabase "captcha protection: request disallowed".

- Users get logged out at random: Supabase "Invalid Refresh Token: Refresh Token Not Found".

- The reset page says "Auth session missing!": Supabase "Auth session missing!".

## Still stuck?

Open the Auth logs in your Supabase dashboard at the time of the failed sign-in. You'll see the request with invalid_credentials, but not which case it was: Supabase keeps that private by design. The SQL check above is how you find out. If the row looks right and a fresh password still fails, look at what your form really sends: log the email and the password's length (never the password) just before signInWithPassword.

guides.t: Supabase "Invalid path specified in request URL" PGRST125
guides.d: Sign-up, login or a query fails with "Invalid path specified in request URL" (PGRST125). Usually it's the Supabase URL in your app. The fixes.
p: invalid path specified in request url
guides.x:
Fix guide · updated 2026-11-15

## Supabase "Invalid path specified in request URL" (PGRST125)

404 · {"code":"PGRST125","details":null,"hint":null,"message":"Invalid path specified in request URL"}

Sign-up fails, login fails, or a database query comes back with "Invalid path specified in request URL", sometimes with the code PGRST125. The message comes from PostgREST, the part of Supabase that answers database requests at /rest/v1/. It means your app called an address with the wrong shape. Most of the time it's one setting, the Supabase URL in your app, and the fix takes a few minutes.

## What the error means

After /rest/v1/, PostgREST accepts only three shapes of address:

- one table or view name: /rest/v1/todos

- rpc/ and one function name: /rest/v1/rpc/my_function

- nothing at all (the API's own description)

Anything else gets a 404 with the code PGRST125 and this message, whatever the method: GET, POST, PATCH or DELETE. Filters, sorting and paging go after the ?, never in the path. We ran PostgREST 14.18, the version in Supabase's self-hosted setup: /todos/5, /todos/, /api/todos and /rest/v1/todos all got PGRST125, while /todos?id=eq.5 worked.

So open your browser's developer tools, Network tab, make the error happen again, and look at the failing request's address:

- /rest/v1/ appears twice, or /auth/v1/ or /storage/v1/ comes after it: see section 1.

- An id or a schema name in the path, like /rest/v1/todos/5: see section 2.

- A slash at the end, or an address your code builds by hand: see section 3.

## 1. Your app's Supabase URL ends with /rest/v1

The Supabase client needs the Project URL alone, like https://abcdefghijklmnopqrst.supabase.co. But the Supabase dashboard also shows an API URL, on Project Settings → Data API, and that one ends with /rest/v1/. Paste it into your app and the client puts it in front of every request. We tested it with supabase-js 2.119.0:

- a query goes to …supabase.co/rest/v1/rest/v1/todos

- sign-up goes to …/rest/v1/auth/v1/signup, login to …/rest/v1/auth/v1/token

- a Storage call goes to …/rest/v1/storage/v1/…

All of them land on PostgREST, which answers PGRST125. That's why a login form can show a database error: signUp and signInWithPassword return an AuthApiError with this message and status 404. Edge Function calls only say "Edge Function returned a non-2xx status code", with the same message in the response behind it (how to read it).

The fix:

- Copy the Project URL: click Connect at the top of your Supabase dashboard, or look on your project's home page. It ends with .supabase.co, with nothing after it.

- Put it where your app reads it. Lovable: src/integrations/supabase/client.ts or VITE_SUPABASE_URL. Bolt and other Vite apps: VITE_SUPABASE_URL. Next.js: NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL.

- Hosting on Vercel or Netlify? Fix the variable there too, then redeploy: the build bakes the value into your app.

To make this mistake loud next time, check the address before you create the client. A wrong value then fails at startup with a clear message, not at login with a cryptic one:

const url = import.meta.env.VITE_SUPABASE_URL;
// The Project URL only: https://<project-ref>.supabase.co, nothing after it
if (new URL(url).pathname !== '/') {
throw new Error(`VITE_SUPABASE_URL has a path, use the Project URL only: ${url}`);
}

In Next.js, use process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL. The check also accepts a custom domain, since it only looks at what comes after the domain.

## 2. An id or a schema name in the path

Supabase's database API doesn't take ids in the path, the way many REST APIs do: /rest/v1/todos/5 doesn't exist. The id goes in a filter. This catches hand-written fetch calls and the HTTP steps of n8n, Make or Zapier:

GET /rest/v1/todos?id=eq.5
PATCH /rest/v1/todos?id=eq.5 body: {"done": true}
DELETE /rest/v1/todos?id=eq.5

Keep the filter on every PATCH and DELETE: it's what limits the change to that one row. With supabase-js, from() takes a table name only:

// Wrong: PGRST125
await supabase.from('todos/5').select();

// Right
await supabase.from('todos').select().eq('id', 5);
await supabase.from('todos').update({ done: true }).eq('id', 5);

Same for a schema: /rest/v1/api/todos and from('api/todos') both get PGRST125. The schema goes in a header. With supabase-js, write supabase.schema('api').from('todos'). With plain HTTP, send Accept-Profile: api on GET and Content-Profile: api on POST, PATCH and DELETE. The schema must also be in the Exposed schemas list, on Project Settings → Data API. If it isn't, the error becomes PGRST106 "Invalid schema: api".

## 3. A slash too many, or another service's path

A slash at the end also gets PGRST125: /rest/v1/todos/ or /rest/v1/rpc/my_function/. It usually comes from code that builds the address by hand, like `${SUPABASE_URL}/rest/v1/${table}/`. Remove the last slash.

Each Supabase service has its own address, right after .supabase.co: /rest/v1/ for the database, /auth/v1/ for logins, /storage/v1/ for files and /functions/v1/ for Edge Functions. An Edge Function or Storage address placed behind /rest/v1/ gets PGRST125, because PostgREST reads it as a table address.

## Which "path" error do you have?

- "Invalid path specified in request URL" (PGRST125): the request reached the database API, but the address has the wrong shape. This page.

- {"error":"requested path is invalid"}: the address matches no Supabase service at all, often a login or email link that sends people to your Supabase address. See Supabase "requested path is invalid".

- "Could not find the table 'public.todos' in the schema cache" (PGRST205): the shape is right, the name isn't. Check the spelling, the schema, and that the table exists: see Supabase "Could not find the table" (PGRST205).

- "Invalid schema" (PGRST106): the schema isn't exposed (section 2).

## If an AI tool built your app

Give your AI tool this prompt:

Find where the Supabase client is created and where its URL comes from (.env, client.ts or a hardcoded value). The URL must be the Project URL only, like https://<project-ref>.supabase.co, with nothing after .supabase.co: remove any /rest/v1 or other path, and add a check at startup that throws a clear error if the URL has a path. Then find every hand-written call to /rest/v1/ (fetch, axios, webhooks): the path must be /rest/v1/<table> or /rest/v1/rpc/<function>, with no id or schema in the path (ids go in filters like ?id=eq.5, schemas in the Accept-Profile or Content-Profile header) and no slash at the end. In supabase-js, from() must get a table name only. Don't change anything else.

Then fix the same variable in your host's settings (Vercel, Netlify) and redeploy.

## Still stuck?

Take the failing address from the Network tab and remove https://<project-ref>.supabase.co/rest/v1/ from the front. What's left, up to the ?, must be a table name, or rpc/ and a function name. Anything else, even one extra slash, is the bug.

guides.t: Supabase "JWT expired" (PGRST303) | App Finishers
guides.d: Supabase requests fail with "JWT expired" (PGRST303, HTTP 401) about an hour after login. supabase-js refreshes its own token: find the old copy your app sends.
p: token has invalid claims: token is expired
guides.x:
Fix guide · updated 2026-11-16

## Supabase "JWT expired" (PGRST303)

{"code":"PGRST303","details":null,"hint":null,"message":"JWT expired"}

Requests to your Supabase tables fail with "JWT expired", code PGRST303, HTTP 401, often about an hour after the user logged in. Storage says the same thing as "exp" claim timestamp check failed, and Auth as token has invalid claims: token is expired. We reproduced all three with Supabase's real Auth, Data API and Storage servers and the real supabase-js client (2.119, November 2026). The surprise: supabase-js doesn't send an expired token by itself. Something else in the app does.

## What the error means

When a user is signed in, each request carries their access token, a JWT. It has an expiry time, one hour after it was issued unless you changed that setting. Past it, Supabase refuses the token:

- the Data API (tables, views, rpc()): HTTP 401, PGRST303, "JWT expired". The version we tested still accepted a token 29 seconds late and refused it at 31 seconds;

- Storage: HTTP 400 with "statusCode":"403" and "exp" claim timestamp check failed, already 10 seconds late;

- Auth, for example supabase.auth.getUser(token): HTTP 403, bad_jwt, "invalid JWT: unable to parse or verify signature, token has invalid claims: token is expired", also 10 seconds late.

Nothing is wrong with the user's account. The session also holds a refresh token, and trading it for a new access token is the normal way out.

## Why supabase-js usually doesn't hit it

Before each request, supabase-js checks the session it keeps. If the access token runs out within the next 90 seconds, it refreshes first, then sends the request with the new token. In our test, a session that had expired 10 minutes earlier still worked with the background refresh switched off, which is what supabase-js does in a hidden browser tab: it called the refresh endpoint, then the table. supabase.functions.invoke() did the same.

When the refresh fails, for example because the user signed out on every device, supabase-js doesn't send the expired token either. It drops the session, fires SIGNED_OUT, and sends the request with your public key instead. In our test that gave an empty list, no error, and only a console warning: "Invalid Refresh Token: Refresh Token Not Found".

So "JWT expired" means the token didn't come from supabase-js's own session handling. These are the causes we reproduced.

## Cause 1: a token saved and sent by hand

The app keeps a copy of the access token from login and puts it on requests itself. supabase-js refreshes its session, but nobody updates the copy. An hour later, every request with it fails. In our test, each of these sent the expired token:

- a client created with global: { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } }. The header wins: the client had a fresh session inside and still sent the old token, then got "JWT expired" from the table and "exp" claim timestamp check failed from Storage;

- a client created with accessToken: async () => savedToken;

- supabase.functions.invoke('name', { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } }): a header you pass is sent as it is.

The same goes for a fetch() with a token kept in React state, a variable, your own localStorage key or a database row, and for a token pasted into Postman, n8n, Make, a cron job or a .env file: it works for an hour, then stops.

## Cause 2: the device clock is behind

supabase-js decides whether the token has expired with the device's own clock. With the clock 2 hours behind, it kept sending a token the server had considered expired for 10 minutes, didn't try to refresh it, and got "JWT expired". The same account works on other devices. With the clock 2 hours ahead, nothing failed, but supabase-js refreshed the session before every single request.

## Cause 3: server code passing the caller's token along

An Edge Function or API route that takes the user's token from the request and uses it is only as fresh as what the browser sent. If the browser sent a saved token (cause 1), supabase.auth.getUser(token) answers 403 bad_jwt "token is expired", and a client built with that header gets "JWT expired" from your tables. With JWT verification on, an Edge Function stops the request before your code runs: see Supabase Edge Function "Missing authorization header" (401), which covers "Invalid JWT".

## The one-minute check

Find out which token the failing request carried. In the browser's developer tools, open the Network tab, click the failing request, and copy its Authorization request header, the part after "Bearer ". Then, in the console:

const t = 'paste the token here';
const { exp } = JSON.parse(atob(t.split('.')[1].replace(/-/g, '+').replace(/_/g, '/')));
console.log(Math.round(Date.now() / 1000 - exp), 'seconds past expiry, by this device clock');

- A positive number, often in the thousands: the request carried an old token that supabase-js would have refreshed. Something in your code sends its own copy (cause 1, or cause 3 on a server). Search the code for Authorization, access_token and accessToken.

- A negative number while the server says "JWT expired": this device's clock is behind (cause 2).

Decode tokens in your own console, not on a website: until it expires, a token works like a password.

## Fix 1: let supabase-js add the token

In browser code, create one client with your project URL and public key, and don't set Authorization yourself: no global.headers.Authorization, no headers on functions.invoke(). supabase-js then sends the current token and refreshes it when needed. In our test, a client holding a session that had expired 10 minutes earlier refreshed it and got the rows; with the header set, the same request failed.

export const supabase = createClient(SUPABASE_URL, SUPABASE_ANON_KEY);

const { data, error } = await supabase.from('todos').select('title');
const res = await supabase.functions.invoke('send-invoice', { body: { id } });

## Fix 2: when you need the token, read it at call time

For a fetch() to your own API or to another service, get the token from supabase-js right before the call, every time. getSession() refreshes an expiring session first: in our test, a session expired for 10 minutes came back with a token good for another hour.

const { data: { session } } = await supabase.auth.getSession();
const res = await fetch('/api/report', {
headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${session?.access_token}` },
});

Don't keep the token in state, context or a variable for later.

## Fix 3: jobs that run later keep the refresh token

A worker or scheduled job that acts for a user later can't use a saved access token. Save the refresh token, give both to setSession(), and supabase-js refreshes before the first request. In our test, setSession() with an expired access token and a valid refresh token refreshed first, then read the user's rows. Each refresh token works only once, so save the new session it returns:

const { data, error } = await supabase.auth.setSession({ access_token, refresh_token });
// save data.session.refresh_token for the next run

A job that doesn't need to act as one user can use the service role key instead, on the server only. Never put that key in browser code: it bypasses every security rule in your database.

## Fix 4: a device with the wrong clock

If only one user or one device gets the error, have them turn on automatic date and time. Nothing in your code needs to change.

## If an AI tool built your app

Give your AI tool this prompt:

My Supabase requests fail with "JWT expired" (PGRST303) about an hour after login. Find every place where the code sets an Authorization header or keeps a user's access token itself: createClient with global.headers.Authorization, the accessToken option, functions.invoke with headers, fetch calls with a Bearer token, and tokens saved in state, context, localStorage or the database. Remove the hand-made headers so supabase-js adds the current token itself, and where a token is really needed, read it with supabase.auth.getSession() right before the call. Keep a single Supabase client for the whole app. Show me each change before making it.

## Not quite your error?

- Lists come back empty after a while and the console warns "Invalid Refresh Token: Refresh Token Not Found": Supabase "Invalid Refresh Token: Refresh Token Not Found".

- "Auth session missing!": Supabase "Auth session missing!" error.

- A code typed from an email says "Token has expired or is invalid": Supabase "Token has expired or is invalid" (email OTP).

- A signed Storage link stops working with "exp" claim timestamp check failed and InvalidJWT: the link itself expired, see Supabase Storage "Object not found".

- PGRST301 "No suitable key or wrong key type": the token isn't expired, the server can't verify it at all. In our test, a token signed with another project's secret got this. Check that the app's Supabase URL and key belong to the project the user signed in to.

## Still stuck?

Decode the failing token as above and also print its iat, the time it was issued. If it's older than the session your app is showing, the request used a copy saved at that time: find where your code stored it.

guides.t: Supabase login redirects to localhost after deploy
guides.d: Google sign-in or the email link sends users to localhost:3000 after deploy? Fix the Site URL, Redirect URLs, your code and Google's callback.
guides.x:
Fix guide · updated 2026-11-07

## Supabase login redirects to localhost after deploy

http://localhost:3000/#access_token=… · This site can't be reached

Your app is live. A user taps Sign in with Google, or the link in their confirmation email, and lands on http://localhost:3000 with This site can't be reached. Or they land on your old Lovable preview instead of your real site. This is one of the most common problems right after a first deploy, and the fix takes a few minutes.

## Why it happens

After a login, Supabase decides where to send the user. It only sends people to addresses on an approved list. If the address your app asks for isn't on that list, Supabase uses the Site URL instead, and on many projects that's still http://localhost:3000 from development. So the fix is to tell Supabase your real address, in two places, and make your code ask for it.

## 1. Set the Site URL to your real domain

Supabase dashboard → Authentication → URL Configuration → Site URL: put your live address, for example https://yourapp.com. Save.

## 2. Add your addresses to Redirect URLs

Same page, Redirect URLs → Add URL. Add every address users should come back to, with /** at the end so every page on it is allowed:

https://yourapp.com/**
https://www.yourapp.com/**
http://localhost:3000/**

Keep the localhost line only if you also run the app on your computer. Using preview deployments? Supabase accepts wildcards, for example https://*-yourteam.vercel.app/** for Vercel previews. For your Lovable preview, copy its address from the browser bar and add /**.

## 3. Make your code ask for the right address

Tell Supabase where to come back after each kind of login. Using the current page's address means the same code works in preview and in production, as long as both are on the list:

// Google (or any OAuth provider)
await supabase.auth.signInWithOAuth({
provider: "google",
options: { redirectTo: `${window.location.origin}/` },
});

// Email + password sign-up: where the confirmation link sends people
await supabase.auth.signUp({
email,
password,
options: { emailRedirectTo: `${window.location.origin}/` },
});

Search your project for signInWithOAuth, signUp and signInWithOtp and check each one.

## 4. For Google sign-in: fix the callback in Google Cloud

Google Cloud Console → APIs & Services → Credentials → your OAuth client:

- Authorized redirect URIs must contain your Supabase callback, not your site: https://<your-project-ref>.supabase.co/auth/v1/callback (Supabase shows the exact address in Authentication → Providers → Google).

- Authorized JavaScript origins: your site, for example https://yourapp.com.

Seeing Error 403: access_denied for everyone except you? Your Google consent screen is still in Testing mode, which only lets listed test users in. Publish it to production in the OAuth consent screen settings.

## Two more things that look like the same bug

- {"error":"requested path is invalid"}: the link sent people to your Supabase project address itself instead of your app. Same fix: the Site URL must be your app's address.

- Old emails still go to the wrong place. Links in emails sent before the fix keep their old address. Send a new confirmation or magic link to test.

If your project runs on Lovable Cloud rather than your own Supabase project, the same two settings exist there: look for the URL and redirect settings in its authentication section.

## Still landing in the wrong place?

Supabase → Authentication → Logs shows each login attempt and where it tried to send the user. If sign-in now works but the app shows no data afterwards, that's a different problem, covered in our row-level security guide.

guides.t: Supabase "missing email or phone" | App Finishers
guides.d: Login fails with "missing email or phone" though the email was typed? It never reached the request. Every cause, tested on real Supabase Auth, and the fix.
p: one of email or phone must be set
type provided requires an email address
must provide either an email or phone number
guides.x:
Fix guide · updated 2026-11-16

## Supabase "missing email or phone"

AuthApiError: missing email or phone · validation_failed · 400

Your login form fails with "missing email or phone", and the person did type their email. We ran Supabase's real Auth server and supabase-js 2.119 on our machine and tried every way a sign-in can lose the email on the way. The answer is always the same: the email was not in the request. The surprise: a phone login fails the same way when the object you pass also has an email key, even an empty one.

## What the error means

supabase.auth.signInWithPassword() sends POST /auth/v1/token?grant_type=password. Supabase Auth reads three fields from the JSON body: email, phone and password. When email and phone are both empty or missing, it stops there, before it looks at the password or for an account. This is what the browser's Network tab shows:

400 {"code":"validation_failed","message":"missing email or phone"}

From curl, Postman or another language, without the version header supabase-js sends, the same error looks like this:

400 {"code":400,"error_code":"validation_failed","msg":"missing email or phone"}

So no account was checked and the password played no part: in our test, an empty password got this same error. The bug is in the request, not in the user.

## 1. The email was empty when the call ran

Each of these got "missing email or phone" in our test:

supabase.auth.signInWithPassword({ email: '', password }) // empty state
supabase.auth.signInWithPassword({ email: undefined, password }) // wrong variable or field name
supabase.auth.signInWithPassword({ email: null, password }) // formData.get('email') found no such field

An undefined email isn't even sent: the request body only had the password. The usual causes: the input isn't wired to the state your code reads (in React, a value with no onChange), the handler reads form.mail when the field is called email, or, with a server action, the input has no name="email", so formData.get('email') returns null.

Read the value from the form when it's submitted, trim it, and don't call Supabase without it:

<form onSubmit={onSubmit}>
<input name="email" type="email" autoComplete="email" required />
<input name="password" type="password" autoComplete="current-password" required />
</form>

async function onSubmit(event) {
event.preventDefault()
const form = new FormData(event.currentTarget)
const email = String(form.get('email') ?? '').trim()
const password = String(form.get('password') ?? '')
if (!email) return setError('Enter your email address.')
const { error } = await supabase.auth.signInWithPassword({ email, password })
if (error) setError(error.message)
}

The trim matters for the next error: in our test, " ana@lab.test " with spaces got "Invalid login credentials", because Supabase doesn't trim. Capitals were fine: Ana@Lab.test signed in.

## 2. Phone login: an email key in the same object wins

supabase-js picks the email path when the object has an email key, whatever its value, and then sends only the email. In our test, the phone number wasn't in the request at all:

supabase.auth.signInWithPassword({ email: '', phone: '+15555550100', password }) // missing email or phone
supabase.auth.signInWithPassword({ email: undefined, phone: '+15555550100', password }) // missing email or phone

This happens with one login form for both, which passes all its fields. Build the object with one key only:

const credentials = usePhone ? { phone, password } : { email, password }
const { error } = await supabase.auth.signInWithPassword(credentials)

A phone and password sign-in also needs the Phone provider turned on (Authentication → Sign In / Providers). With it off, the answer is 422 phone_provider_disabled "Phone logins are disabled".

## 3. You call the Auth API without supabase-js

From curl, Postman, Dart or Flutter, Python, or an API call in a no-code tool, Auth only reads email, phone and password at the top level of a JSON body. In our test:

- {"username": "...", "password": "..."}, the usual OAuth habit: missing email or phone.

- {"user": {"email": "...", "password": "..."}}, nested: missing email or phone.

- {}: missing email or phone.

- {"EMAIL": "..."} signed in. The case of the key doesn't matter, its name does. A JSON body with no Content-Type header signed in too.

- A form-encoded body (application/x-www-form-urlencoded, what OAuth clients send): 400 bad_json "Could not parse request body as JSON: unexpected end of JSON input". Auth reads the form while looking for grant_type, and no JSON is left after that.

- An empty body: the same bad_json. JSON encoded twice, so the body is a string: "cannot unmarshal string into Go value of type api.PasswordGrantParams".

The request that works:

curl -X POST 'https://YOUR-PROJECT.supabase.co/auth/v1/token?grant_type=password' \
-H 'apikey: YOUR-PUBLISHABLE-OR-ANON-KEY' \
-H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
-d '{"email":"ana@example.com","password":"your-password"}'

## 4. Mistakes that never reach Supabase

supabase-js checks the object before it sends anything. These made no request at all in our test, so your Supabase logs won't show them:

- signInWithPassword({ username, password }) or { Email, password }: AuthInvalidCredentialsError "You must provide either an email or phone number and a password". Here the key's case does matter.

- signInWithPassword(email, password), two arguments instead of one object: it throws TypeError: Cannot use 'in' operator to search for 'email' in ana@lab.test. It's thrown, not returned in error, so the page crashes unless you catch it.

And two that do reach Supabase but get 400 bad_json instead: an email that is an object (an input element, an event, { value }), and a custom global.fetch in createClient that passes on the method and headers but not the body. Pass everything on: fetch(url, { ...init, headers }).

## The same empty email on other calls

An empty email gets a different message on each Auth call. All are 400 validation_failed except sign-up, and the fix is the same as in part 1:

- signInWithOtp({ email: '' }): "One of email or phone must be set".

- resetPasswordForEmail(''): "Password recovery requires an email".

- resend({ type: 'signup', email: '' }): "Type provided requires an email address".

- verifyOtp({ email: '', token, type: 'email' }): "Only an email address or phone number should be provided on verify", although neither was.

- signUp({ email: '', password }): 422 "Anonymous sign-ins are disabled", see that guide.

## If an AI tool built your app

Give your AI tool this prompt:

On the login form, read the email and password from the form when it is submitted (each input needs a name attribute), trim the email, and if it's empty show "Enter your email address." and don't call Supabase. Pass supabase.auth.signInWithPassword one object with either { email, password } or { phone, password }, never both keys. Don't change anything else.

## Not quite your error?

- The email arrives but the sign-in is refused: Supabase "Invalid login credentials".

- The account exists but isn't confirmed: Supabase "Email not confirmed".

- Sign-up refuses the address: Supabase "Unable to validate email address: invalid format".

- Sign-up with an empty email: Supabase "Anonymous sign-ins are disabled".

## Still stuck?

Open the failed token?grant_type=password request in your browser's Network tab and look at its payload. If it shows "email":"" or no email at all, the bug is in the code that builds the object: log that object right before you call signInWithPassword.

guides.t: Supabase "New password should be different" error
guides.d: Password reset fails with "New password should be different from the old password" (same_password). Why, and the other password errors on that page.
p: new password should be different from the old password
guides.x:
Fix guide · updated 2026-11-15

## Supabase "New password should be different from the old password"

AuthApiError: New password should be different from the old password. · same_password · 422

A user resets their password and Supabase refuses: "New password should be different from the old password." Sometimes it's a person who never really lost their password. Sometimes it's your reset page sending the password twice. Here's when Supabase answers this, and the other password errors that show up on the same page.

## What the error means

We read the password-change code in Supabase Auth (internal/api/user.go). When you call supabase.auth.updateUser({ password }) for an account that already has a password, Supabase compares the new one with the stored one. If they match, it refuses with HTTP 422, code same_password. Nothing is broken: the password stays what it was, and the person can sign in with it.

## 1. The person chose their current password

The common case on a reset page: the person hadn't really forgotten their password, or their password manager filled in the old one. Show a friendly message instead of the raw error: "That's already your password. You can sign in with it.", with a sign-in link.

## 2. Your reset page sends the password twice

If the person typed a brand-new password and still sees this error, your page probably called updateUser twice. The first call changed the password; the second one sent the same password again and got same_password. A double-clicked button or a call inside a useEffect that runs again does it. Disable the button while the request runs, call updateUser only from the submit handler, and leave the page (or show "Password changed") after the first success.

## The other password errors on the same page

- "Password should be at least 6 characters." (weak_password): shorter than your project's Minimum password length, in the Email provider settings. The number in the message is your project's setting.

- "Password should contain at least one character of each: …" (weak_password): your project requires certain kinds of characters, and the message lists them.

- "Password is known to be weak and easy to guess, please choose a different one." (weak_password): Prevent use of leaked passwords is on, and this password is on HaveIBeenPwned's list of leaked passwords.

- "Password update requires reauthentication" (reauthentication_needed): Secure password change is on, and the person's session is more than 24 hours old. Call supabase.auth.reauthenticate(), which sends them a code, then updateUser({ password, nonce: code }).

- "Current password required when setting new password." (current_password_required, or current_password_mismatch when it's wrong): Require current password when updating is on. Supabase's API takes it as current_password. A reset link is exempt: during a password recovery, Supabase doesn't ask for the current one.

All of these settings sit in your Supabase dashboard under Authentication → Sign In / Providers → Email.

## If an AI tool built your app

Give your AI tool this prompt:

On the reset-password page, call supabase.auth.updateUser({ password }) only from the form's submit handler, disable the button while the request runs, and don't call it again after it succeeds: show "Password changed" with a sign-in link. Map these Supabase error codes to messages: same_password → "That's already your password. You can sign in with it." with a sign-in link; weak_password → show the error's own message; reauthentication_needed → call supabase.auth.reauthenticate(), say "We sent you a code to confirm it's you", ask for the code, then retry updateUser({ password, nonce: code }). Don't change anything else.

## Not quite your error?

- The new password is refused as too short or too weak: Supabase "Password should be at least 6 characters".

- The reset page says "Auth session missing!": Supabase "Auth session missing!".

- The reset link says it's invalid or expired: Supabase "Email link is invalid or has expired".

- Sign-in fails right after the reset: Supabase "Invalid login credentials".

- The reset email never comes: Supabase "email rate limit exceeded".

## Still stuck?

Open the Auth logs in your Supabase dashboard at the time of the error: each refused password change is there with its code. If same_password shows up for a password the person swears is new, count how many times your page called updateUser in a row: two calls a second apart is the double submit from case 2.

## Supabase "new row for relation … violates check constraint" (23514)

{"code":"23514","details":null,"hint":null,"message":"new row for relation \"orders\" violates check constraint \"orders_status_check\""}

An insert or update from your app fails with "new row for relation "orders" violates check constraint "orders_status_check"", code 23514, HTTP 400. A check rule on the table refused the row, and the message names the table and the rule. We reproduced the usual ways it happens with the request code of supabase-js (postgrest-js 2.119) against Postgres 16 and Supabase's Data API (PostgREST 13), November 2026.

## What the error means

A check constraint is a rule the database tests on every row it writes, such as "status is one of pending, paid, shipped, cancelled" or "amount is above 0". When the new row breaks the rule, nothing is written.

The last name in the message is the rule. A rule written on one column is named after the table and the column: orders_status_check is the rule on orders.status. A rule written for the whole table keeps the name it was given, such as sale_below_price. The one-minute check below shows what any rule says.

On most Supabase tables, row level security (RLS) is on, and then the error's details are empty. With the service role key, or on a table without RLS, they show the whole row: "Failing row contains (8, 11111111-…, Paid, 10)." Keep details out of messages your users see: it lists every value in the row.

If the row also breaks your RLS policy, you get "new row violates row-level security policy" (HTTP 403) instead. In our test, the policy check came first. See Supabase RLS: "new row violates row-level security policy".

## Cause 1: a value that isn't on the allowed list

AI tools often write a status column as a list of allowed words, and the list is exact, capitals included. In our test, with the list pending, paid, shipped, cancelled, the values 'Paid', 'PAID' and 'completed' all failed on orders_status_check, in an insert, an update and an upsert alike. The usual story: the screen shows "Paid" and sends it as it is, or a new status such as "refunded" was added to the app but never to the database.

## Cause 2: a number or a length out of range

Rules like amount > 0, age >= 13 or char_length(username) between 3 and 20 fail on the edge cases. In our test, amount: 0, age: 12, a two-letter username and an empty string '' were all refused. Numbers sent as text, like '12' from a form field, are converted first and then checked the same way.

## Cause 3: a rule between two columns

A rule can compare columns, such as "the sale price is below the price". Then changing one column can break it. In our test, a product had price 10 and sale price 8, and update({ price: 5 }) failed on sale_below_price, though the update never touched the sale price.

## Cause 4: the rule is on the column's type

If the message reads "value for domain email_address violates check constraint "email_address_check"", the rule sits on a custom type (a domain) that the column uses, not on the table. In our test, insert({ email: 'bob@' }) got that message, code 23514, HTTP 400. The table's own rules don't include it; the second query in the one-minute check finds it.

## Cause 5: a new rule over old rows

This one comes from a migration or the SQL Editor, not from your app: "check constraint "amount_cap" of relation "orders" is violated by some row", also code 23514. A rule added with alter table … add constraint is tested against every row already in the table, and an old row broke it, so nothing changed. Fix 4 adds the rule anyway and deals with the old rows after.

## Two things that surprise people

- One bad row stops the whole batch. In our test, an insert() of two rows, one good and one with status 'done', failed with 23514 and neither row was written.

- An empty value passes a check. In our test, amount: null went in although the rule says amount > 0, and so did age: null. A check only judges values that are there. To require a value, the column needs not null too (Fix 5).

## The one-minute check

Note the table and the rule's name in the message. Then, in the SQL Editor, list the table's rules:

select conname, pg_get_constraintdef(oid)
from pg_constraint
where conrelid = 'public.orders'::regclass and contype = 'c';

In our test it printed CHECK ((status = ANY (ARRAY['pending'::text, 'paid'::text, …]))) for orders_status_check: the allowed words, exactly as the database compares them. For a rule on a domain:

select conname, pg_get_constraintdef(oid)
from pg_constraint
where contypid = 'public.email_address'::regtype;

Then open the failing request in your browser's Network tab and compare its body with the rule: a capital letter, a zero, a name that's too short, or a column the update changed.

## Fix 1: send a value the rule allows

If the rule is right, fix what the app sends. Show a label on screen and send the stored word:

<select name="status">
<option value="paid">Paid</option>
<option value="shipped">Shipped</option>
</select>

Check the same rule in the form before saving, and catch the code, so a refused save shows a clear message instead of failing quietly:

const { error } = await supabase.from('orders').insert(order);
if (error?.code === '23514') {
// error.message names the rule, e.g. orders_status_check
showError("Some values aren't allowed. Check the status and the amount.");
}

## Fix 2: update the rule when the app is right

If "refunded" is a real status now, add it to the rule. Drop and re-add the rule in one statement:

alter table public.orders
drop constraint orders_status_check,
add constraint orders_status_check
check (status in ('pending', 'paid', 'shipped', 'cancelled', 'refunded'));

In our test, the update to 'refunded' that had failed went through afterwards. Put the change in a migration, so every copy of your database gets it.

## Fix 3: change linked columns together

For a rule between columns, send both values in the same update, so the row is valid once it's written:

await supabase.from('products').update({ price: 5, sale_price: 4 }).eq('id', id);

In our test, this update went through where update({ price: 5 }) alone had failed.

## Fix 4: add a rule to a table that has old rows

Add it with not valid: new and changed rows are checked at once, old rows are left alone. Then find the old rows that break it, fix them, and validate:

alter table public.orders add constraint amount_cap check (amount < 1000) not valid;

select id, amount from public.orders where not (amount < 1000);

alter table public.orders validate constraint amount_cap;

In our test, the rule went in with not valid, a new row over the cap was refused at once, the old row stayed, and validate failed with "is violated by some row" until the old row was fixed.

## Fix 5: require a value as well

A check doesn't stop empty values. If the amount must be there, add not null too. Fill the empty rows first with the right value for your data, or the change fails with "column "amount" of relation "orders" contains null values" (23502):

update public.orders set amount = 1 where amount is null;
alter table public.orders alter column amount set not null;

In our test, an insert with an empty amount then failed with 23502, the not-null error: Supabase "null value in column … violates not-null constraint" (23502).

## If an AI tool built your app

Give your AI tool this prompt, with the table and the rule from your error:

My Supabase insert fails with "new row for relation "orders" violates check constraint "orders_status_check"" (23514). Show me that rule's definition from the migrations or pg_constraint. Then find every insert, update and upsert on that table and compare what each one sends with the rule: exact words and capitals for allowed lists, ranges and lengths, and rules between two columns. If the app is right and the rule is out of date, write a migration that drops and re-adds the rule in one alter table statement. If the rule is right, change what the app sends, check the same rule in the form, and show a clear message when error.code is '23514'. Show me each change before making it.

## Not quite your error?

- "null value in column … violates not-null constraint": Supabase "null value in column … violates not-null constraint" (23502).

- "value too long for type character varying": Supabase "value too long for type character varying" (22001).

- "new row violates row-level security policy": Supabase RLS: "new row violates row-level security policy".

- "duplicate key value violates unique constraint": Supabase "duplicate key value violates unique constraint" (23505).

- "violates foreign key constraint": Supabase "violates foreign key constraint" (23503).

- "invalid input syntax for type uuid": Supabase invalid input syntax for type uuid: "undefined" (22P02).

## Still stuck?

Copy the request body from the Network tab and try the same insert in the SQL Editor with those values. Change one value at a time until the row goes in: the last one you changed is the one that broke the rule.
