## Supabase RLS: "new row violates row-level security policy"

new row violates row-level security policy for table "profiles"

Your app tries to save something, and Supabase answers with error 42501:

new row violates row-level security policy for table "profiles"

Row-level security (RLS) is Supabase's lock on each table. When it's on, nobody can read or write a row unless a policy says they can. This error means the lock is working: no policy allows this user to save this row. Here are the four reasons that happens, and the fix for each.

Seeing permission denied for table instead, also with code 42501? That's not RLS: since October 30, 2026, new tables need an explicit grant. See Supabase "permission denied for table" (42501).

## 1. There's no policy for inserting at all

AI builders often create a policy to read rows and forget the one to add them.

Check: Supabase dashboard → Authentication → Policies → your table. Is there a policy for INSERT?

Fix: in the SQL editor, add one. This version lets signed-in users add rows that belong to them:

create policy "Users can add their own rows"
on public.profiles
for insert
to authenticated
with check ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );

Replace profiles and user_id with your table and the column that stores the owner.

## 2. The user isn't actually signed in

The policy above is for authenticated users. If the request goes out before login finishes, or the session expired, Supabase treats it as an anonymous visitor (anon), and the policy doesn't apply.

Check: right before the insert, log the session:

const { data: { session } } = await supabase.auth.getSession();
console.log(session?.user?.id); // undefined = not signed in

Fix: only save after sign-in is confirmed, and send logged-out users to the login page instead of letting the request fail.

## 3. The owner column is empty

The policy checks that user_id equals the signed-in user. If your code never fills in user_id, the column is empty, the check fails, and you get the same error.

Fix: let the database fill it in automatically:

alter table public.profiles
alter column user_id set default auth.uid();

Now every new row gets the signed-in user's id, even if your code forgets. If an empty column isn't one the policy checks, the error is "null value in column … violates not-null constraint" instead: see Supabase "null value in column … violates not-null constraint" (23502).

## 4. You read the row back right after saving it

Code like .insert(row).select() saves the row and then asks for it back. Asking for it back is a read, so it also needs a SELECT policy. Without one, the whole request fails with the same message, even though your insert policy is fine.

Fix: add a read policy for the owner:

create policy "Users can read their own rows"
on public.profiles
for select
to authenticated
using ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );

Using .upsert()? That can also update existing rows, so it needs an UPDATE policy too.

## Signed in, but the app shows no data

No error at all, just empty lists. That's RLS too: when no SELECT policy matches, Supabase doesn't complain, it simply returns zero rows. It often shows up right after deploy, because the preview may have been reading the data in a way your live app can't.

Fix: add the read policy from step 4 for each table the page loads, with the right owner column.

A missing read policy also silences Realtime: postgres_changes events for those rows never arrive, and nothing reports an error. See Supabase Realtime not working: SUBSCRIBED but no events.

## The warning "RLS Disabled in Public"

Supabase's Security Advisor shows RLS Disabled in Public when a table has no row-level security at all. That table is open: anyone with your public key can read and change every row. Turn it on (Table Editor → the table → Enable RLS, or alter table public.your_table enable row level security;) and add policies right away, or your app will stop seeing that table's data.

## The fix you must never use

You'll find advice to just turn RLS off. Don't. Your Supabase key is inside your app, so anyone can find it in their browser. With RLS off, that key lets any visitor read, change or delete every row in the table: every user's data, not just their own. The error goes away and your customers' data becomes public.

The right fix is always a policy that matches who should be allowed to do what.

## Still failing?

The Supabase dashboard's Logs → Postgres shows the exact request that was refused. If your tables have several owners, teams or roles, the policies get trickier, and that's the kind of thing we fix every day.

## Supabase "null value in column … violates not-null constraint" (23502)

{"code":"23502","details":null,"hint":null,"message":"null value in column \"user_id\" of relation \"notes\" violates not-null constraint"}

An insert or update from your app fails with "null value in column "user_id" of relation "notes" violates not-null constraint", code 23502, HTTP 400. The column is marked not null, and the row reached it empty. The message names the column and the table. We reproduced the usual ways it happens with the request code of supabase-js (postgrest-js 2.119) against Postgres 16 and Supabase's Data API (PostgREST 13), November 2026.

## What the error means

A not null column refuses an empty value. The row got one because your code left the column out and it has no default, because your code sent null, because the default itself gave null, or because supabase-js filled in null for you. The causes below cover each case.

On most Supabase tables, row level security (RLS) is on, and then the error's details are empty. With the service role key, or on a table without RLS, they show the row: "Failing row contains (3, null, hi)."

One exception: if the empty column is the one your RLS policy checks, such as user_id = auth.uid(), you get "new row violates row-level security policy" instead. In our test, the policy check came first. See Supabase RLS: "new row violates row-level security policy".

## Cause 1: the column isn't sent and has no default

The code inserts { body } into a table whose user_id is not null with no default. In our test, with the service role key that's 23502 on user_id. Watch out for user_id: user?.id while the user hasn't loaded yet: undefined values are dropped from the request, so supabase-js sent exactly {"body":"hi"}, the same as leaving the column out.

## Cause 2: your code sends null

A default only fills a column that the insert leaves out. It never replaces a null you send. In our test, done had the default false, and insert({ title, done: null }) still failed on done. So did update({ done: null }).

The same goes for id: null. On an id column created as generated by default as identity, it failed with 23502 on "id". On one created as generated always, it failed with "cannot insert a non-DEFAULT value into column "id"" (code 428C9). Leave id out of inserts and the database numbers the row.

## Cause 3: several rows with different keys

When you insert an array, supabase-js sends one list of columns for the whole batch, every key that appears in any row. A row that doesn't have one of those keys gets null for it, not the default. In our test, insert([{ title: 'd' }, { title: 'e', done: true }]) failed on done for the first row, even though done has a default.

## Cause 4: an upsert to change one field

upsert() is an insert that turns into an update when the row exists, and the row to insert has to be complete. In our test, upsert({ id: 1, done: true }) to tick an existing todo failed with 23502 on title, although the row with id 1 was there.

## Cause 5: auth.uid() as the default, and nobody signed in

default auth.uid() fills the column with the signed-in user's id. With no session, auth.uid() is null. In our test, a guestbook table whose insert policy lets everyone write failed with 23502 on user_id for a visitor who wasn't signed in. With a policy for signed-in users only, the same request got the RLS error instead.

## The one-minute check

Note the column and the table in the message. Then, in the SQL Editor, see which columns are required and which have a default:

select column_name, is_nullable, column_default
from information_schema.columns
where table_schema = 'public' and table_name = 'todos'
order by ordinal_position;

Then open the failing request in your browser's Network tab and look at what was sent. The column is missing (cause 1 or 5), it's null (cause 2), the body is an array (cause 3), or the request has Prefer: resolution=merge-duplicates, which is what upsert() sends (cause 4).

## Fix 1: give owner columns a default

For a column that holds the owner, let the database fill it:

alter table public.notes alter column user_id set default auth.uid();

In our test, insert({ title }) by a signed-in user then got the user's id in user_id, and the RLS policy still checked it. Leave the column out of the insert: sending user_id: null still fails.

## Fix 2: wait for the user, then send the real value

Don't insert before the session has loaded. Read the user first, and stop if there isn't one:

const { data: { user } } = await supabase.auth.getUser();
if (!user) return; // show the login screen instead
const { error } = await supabase.from('notes').insert({ body, user_id: user.id });

## Fix 3: batches with defaults

Pass defaultToNull: false, or give every row the same keys. In our test, the batch that failed went in with the option: supabase-js asked for the defaults (Prefer: missing=default) and the first row got done = false.

await supabase.from('todos').insert(rows, { defaultToNull: false });

## Fix 4: change one field with update()

To edit a row that exists, use update() with a filter. In our test, it changed the one field and nothing else. An upsert() worked too once it carried every required column.

await supabase.from('todos').update({ done: true }).eq('id', id);

## Fix 5: allow empty, if empty is fine

If the column can really be empty, such as an optional note, drop the rule instead:

alter table public.todos alter column note drop not null;

Don't do this for owner columns like user_id: a row without an owner is a row nobody's policies can reach.

## If an AI tool built your app

Give your AI tool this prompt, with the column and table from your error:

My Supabase insert fails with "null value in column "user_id" of relation "notes" violates not-null constraint" (23502). Find every insert, upsert and update on that table. Don't send null or undefined for that column: give owner columns a default of auth.uid() in a migration and leave them out of the insert, wait for the signed-in user before inserting, leave id out of inserts, use update().eq('id', id) to change one field instead of upsert(), and pass { defaultToNull: false } when inserting an array of rows with different keys. Show me each change before making it.

## Not quite your error?

- "new row violates row-level security policy": Supabase RLS: "new row violates row-level security policy".

- The error comes from sign-up, as "Database error saving new user": Database error saving new user (Supabase).

- "invalid input syntax for type uuid: "undefined"": Supabase invalid input syntax for type uuid: "undefined" (22P02).

- "duplicate key value violates unique constraint": Supabase "duplicate key value violates unique constraint" (23505).

- "violates foreign key constraint": Supabase "violates foreign key constraint" (23503).

- "new row for relation … violates check constraint": Supabase "new row for relation … violates check constraint" (23514).

- "value too long for type character varying": Supabase "value too long for type character varying" (22001).

## Still stuck?

Copy the request body from the Network tab and try the same insert in the SQL Editor with those values. Change one value at a time until the row goes in: the last one you changed is the empty one.

## Supabase "operator does not exist: uuid = text" (42883)

ERROR: operator does not exist: uuid = text. HINT: No operator matches the given name and argument types. You might need to add explicit type casts.

A migration, a policy you create in the SQL Editor, or a supabase.rpc() call fails with operator does not exist: uuid = text (code 42883), and the hint "You might need to add explicit type casts". Somewhere a uuid is compared with text, and Postgres won't compare two different types for you. We reproduced each case on Postgres 16, with the same types as Supabase's auth.uid() and auth.jwt(), and behind Supabase's Data API (PostgREST 13), November 2026. In every case, one side was text: a user_id column created as text, auth.jwt() ->> 'sub', or a function parameter declared as text.

## What the error means

auth.uid() returns a uuid, like the ids in auth.users and the columns that store them. auth.jwt() ->> 'sub' returns the same id as text. Postgres has no = between uuid and text. In our test:

- a policy using (auth.uid() = user_id) on a text user_id was refused when we created it: "uuid = text",

- a policy using (auth.jwt() ->> 'sub' = id) on a uuid id was refused with "text = uuid": the order follows your expression,

- a view joining profiles.id = notes.user_id, uuid with text, wasn't created,

- a function comparing a text parameter with a uuid column was created fine, then failed each time it was called.

## The one-minute check

In the SQL Editor, list the types of your id columns:

select table_name, column_name, data_type from information_schema.columns
where table_schema = 'public' and (column_name = 'id' or column_name like '%\_id')
order by table_name, column_name;

A user_id (or owner_id, author_id) that says text while the ids it holds are uuids is the usual suspect.

## Fix 1: make the column a uuid

The lasting fix. Changing the type failed at first in our test, with "cannot alter type of a column used in a policy definition": drop the policies that use the column, change it, then create them again:

drop policy "own notes" on public.notes;
alter table public.notes alter column user_id type uuid using user_id::uuid;
create policy "own notes" on public.notes for select
using ((select auth.uid()) = user_id);

The alter fails if a row holds something that isn't a uuid. Find those rows first:

select user_id from public.notes where user_id !~ '^[0-9a-fA-F-]{36}$';

While you're at it, a foreign key to auth.users (id) keeps the column honest. Choose its delete rule first: Supabase "Database error deleting user" explains why.

## Fix 2: cast the other side

If you can't change the column yet, cast the uuid to text, which our test accepted:

create policy "own notes" on public.notes for select
using ((select auth.uid())::text = user_id);

Cast auth.uid(), not the column. user_id::uuid breaks the whole query as soon as one row holds something that isn't a uuid, and a cast on the column also keeps Postgres from using an index on it.

For auth.jwt() ->> 'sub' compared with a uuid column, use auth.uid() instead: it's the same user id, already a uuid. For a join, cast on the text side, p.id::text = n.user_id, until the column is fixed.

## A function called with rpc(): declare the parameter uuid

A PL/pgSQL function that compares a text parameter with a uuid column is created without complaint and fails when it runs. In our test, rpc() on such a function answered HTTP 404, with "code":"42883" and this message. The function exists: the Data API reports error 42883 as a 404. Declaring the parameter as uuid fixed it (200):

create function public.note_count(p_user uuid) returns bigint ...

Changing a parameter's type creates a second function next to the old one, so drop the old one: drop function public.note_count(text);.

## "operator does not exist: text ->> unknown"

Same error code, other cause: ->> used on a text column that holds JSON. In our test, meta ->> 'color' on a text column failed this way. ->> works on json and jsonb: change the column to jsonb (alter table public.notes alter column meta type jsonb using meta::jsonb;), or cast in the query, meta::jsonb ->> 'color'.

## If an AI tool built your app

Give your AI tool this prompt:

Our Supabase database fails with operator does not exist: uuid = text (42883). Find every column that stores a user id or another uuid id but is typed text, and write a migration that changes it to uuid: check first that every value is a valid uuid, and drop and recreate the policies that use the column. In policies, compare (select auth.uid()) with uuid columns. Declare function parameters that hold ids as uuid, and drop the old text versions. Show me the SQL before running it. Don't change anything else.

## Not quite your error?

- "invalid input syntax for type uuid": a value isn't a uuid at all: Supabase invalid input syntax for type uuid: "undefined" (22P02).

- "column reference … is ambiguous" in a function: Supabase: column reference "id" is ambiguous (42702).

- rpc() answers 404 with PGRST202: then the function really isn't found: Supabase "Could not find the function in the schema cache" (PGRST202).

## Still stuck?

Look under the error for the LINE marker: the caret (^) points at the comparison. The two words around the = in the message are the two types, left and right. Change the side that isn't what you meant.

## Supabase "Password should be at least 6 characters"

AuthWeakPasswordError: Password should be at least 6 characters. · weak_password · 422

A new user picks a password and sign-up fails with "Password should be at least 6 characters." The same error, weak_password, also comes back from reset-password pages and from your server's admin calls, sometimes with a message about required characters or leaked passwords instead. We ran Supabase's real Auth server and supabase-js 2.119 on our machine with each password setting to see exactly what it refuses. Here's what we found, and how to make your form say it before Supabase does.

## What the error means

Supabase Auth checks every new password against your project's rules: on signUp, on updateUser({ password }) (reset page, account settings), and, in our test, on the admin calls made with the service key too (auth.admin.createUser, auth.admin.updateUserById). A password that falls short gets HTTP 422 with the code weak_password. This is what the browser's Network tab shows:

422 {"code":"weak_password","message":"Password should be at least 6 characters.","weak_password":{"reasons":["length"]}}

supabase-js turns it into an AuthWeakPasswordError. Its reasons array says what was wrong:

- length: shorter than your minimum. "Password should be at least 6 characters." The number is your project's setting.

- characters: a required kind of character is missing. "Password should contain at least one character of each: …"

- pwned: the password is on a list of leaked passwords. "Password is known to be weak and easy to guess, please choose a different one."

When several apply, Supabase joins the sentences into one message. In our test, abc123 with a minimum of 8 and the "lowercase, uppercase letters and digits" rule got both sentences and reasons: ["length", "characters"].

All three rules are set in your Supabase dashboard under Authentication → Sign In / Providers → Email. In local development they live in supabase/config.toml under [auth]: minimum_password_length and password_requirements. Restart the local stack after you change them.

## 1. "Password should be at least 6 characters"

The password is shorter than Minimum password length. 6 is the default, and also the lowest it goes: the dashboard doesn't accept less, and when we set 4 directly on the Auth server, it still asked for 6. Supabase recommends 8 or more.

Supabase counts characters, not bytes: abcdé (5 characters) was refused at 6. An emoji counts as one character, while JavaScript's password.length counts it as two. Three emoji passed a password.length >= 6 check in JavaScript, and Supabase refused them. Count with [...password].length if your form checks first.

If the number in the message isn't the one in your dashboard, your app talks to a different project, or to your local Supabase. The message always quotes the setting of the server that answered.

## 2. "Password should contain at least one character of each: …"

Your project has Password requirements set. Each group between the commas needs at least one character from it. The three settings give these messages:

- Letters and digits: "…of each: abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ, 0123456789." Any letter plus a digit.

- Lowercase, uppercase letters and digits: "…of each: abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz, ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ, 0123456789."

- Lowercase, uppercase letters, digits and symbols: the same, plus !@#$%^&*()_+-=[]{};'\:"|<>?,./`~

Only those symbols count. In our test, a space, € or é added to Abcdef1 was refused, and !, @, : or \ passed.

That message is hard to read on a sign-up form. Show the rule in plain words under the password field instead (the prompt below does it).

## 3. "Password is known to be weak and easy to guess"

Prevent use of leaked passwords is on. Supabase checks the password against HaveIBeenPwned's list of leaked passwords, and reasons contains pwned. Supabase lists this setting on the Pro plan and above. The check needs the internet, so it isn't part of our offline test; the message comes from Supabase Auth's code. Say it plainly on your form: "This password has appeared in a data breach. Choose another one."

## 4. Raising the minimum doesn't lock anyone out

Existing users whose password no longer meets your rules still sign in. In our test, a user created with 123456 under the defaults signed in fine after we raised the minimum to 8 and required lowercase, uppercase letters and digits. supabase-js added data.weakPassword to the result, with the same message and reasons. That's your chance to ask for a new password:

const { data, error } = await supabase.auth.signInWithPassword({ email, password });
if (!error && data.weakPassword) {
// Signed in, but this password no longer meets your rules.
// Show data.weakPassword.message and a link to your change-password page.
}

The new password then goes through updateUser({ password }), which applies the current rules.

## 5. The look-alikes on the same form

- "Password cannot be longer than 72 characters" (HTTP 400, validation_failed). This limit counts bytes, not characters: 72 × a passed and 73 failed, but 40 × é failed too (80 bytes), while 36 × é passed (72 bytes). Letters with accents take 2 bytes, emoji 4. Long passphrases in other languages hit it first.

- "Signup requires a valid password" (HTTP 400, validation_failed): the password sent was empty. Check that the field's value actually reaches your signUp call.

## Make your form say it first

Check the same rules before you call Supabase, so people see the rule while they type instead of an error afterwards. Keep Supabase's answer as the final word: if error still comes back, show its message.

// Same values as Authentication → Sign In / Providers → Email
const MIN_LENGTH = 8;
const REQUIRED = [/[a-z]/, /[A-Z]/, /[0-9]/]; // "Lowercase, uppercase letters and digits"

function passwordProblem(password) {
if ([...password].length < MIN_LENGTH) return `Use at least ${MIN_LENGTH} characters.`;
if (!REQUIRED.every((r) => r.test(password))) return 'Use a lowercase letter, an uppercase letter and a digit.';
if (new TextEncoder().encode(password).length > 72) return 'That password is too long.';
return null;
}

## If an AI tool built your app

Give your AI tool this prompt, after changing the first sentence to match your settings:

My Supabase project requires passwords of at least 8 characters with a lowercase letter, an uppercase letter and a digit. On the sign-up, reset-password and change-password forms, show that rule under the password field before the person submits, and check it before calling Supabase (count characters with [...password].length). When Supabase returns an error with code weak_password, read error.reasons: "length" → "Use at least 8 characters.", "characters" → "Use a lowercase letter, an uppercase letter and a digit.", "pwned" → "This password has appeared in a data breach. Choose another one." When signInWithPassword succeeds and data.weakPassword is set, let the person in and show a banner asking them to choose a new password, with a link to the change-password page. Don't change anything else.

## Not quite your error?

- The reset page says the new password must be different: Supabase "New password should be different from the old password".

- Sign-up says the email is taken: Supabase "User already registered".

- Sign-up refuses the email address: Supabase "Unable to validate email address: invalid format".

- Sign-up is closed for everyone: Supabase "Signups not allowed for this instance".

- Sign-up says "Anonymous sign-ins are disabled": Supabase "Anonymous sign-ins are disabled".

- Sign-in fails with the right password: Supabase "Invalid login credentials".

## Still stuck?

Open the Auth logs in your Supabase dashboard at the time of the error: each refused password is there with weak_password. If the message quotes a number your dashboard doesn't show, compare the Supabase URL in your app's settings with the dashboard's: the rule that answered belongs to another project.

guides.t: Supabase "permission denied for table" (42501): safe fix
guides.d: Since October 30, 2026 new Supabase tables need a grant before your app can reach them. Add the right grant per role, without the GRANT ALL trap.
guides.x:
Fix guide · updated 2026-11-08

## Supabase "permission denied for table" (42501) since October 30: the safe fix

permission denied for table profiles · code 42501 · permission denied for sequence

Your app worked, then you added a table, and now Supabase answers 401 or 403 with permission denied for table profiles (code 42501). Nothing is wrong with your RLS. Since October 30, 2026, Supabase no longer opens new tables to your app automatically: each one needs an explicit GRANT first. Here's the safe fix, the error that often comes next, and the quick fix that reopens your data to anyone.

## What changed on October 30

Until this change, every table you created in the public schema was reachable through Supabase's Data API right away: anon, authenticated and service_role got select, insert, update and delete on it by default. Supabase announced the switch on April 28, 2026, made it the default for new projects from May 30, and applied it to all existing projects on October 30.

- Tables that already existed keep their grants. Your app breaks the first time someone adds a table: you, a migration, or an AI tool like Lovable, Bolt or Cursor.

- It hits everything that goes through the Data API: supabase-js and the other client libraries, REST calls to /rest/v1/, and GraphQL. Code that connects to Postgres directly, with a connection string, isn't affected.

- Tables in auth, storage, realtime and your own custom schemas keep their current grants and defaults.

## Is it this error, or an RLS error?

Two different problems share the code 42501, and the API answers both with 401 when the user is signed out and 403 when signed in. Read the message:

- permission denied for table profiles: the role has no grant on the table. Postgres refuses before RLS even runs. This guide.

- new row violates row-level security policy for table "profiles": the grant is there, but an RLS policy refused the row. See new row violates row-level security policy.

- A query that returns no rows and no error: RLS again, with no policy letting that user see the rows.

The API's answer also carries a hint naming the missing privilege, for example GRANT SELECT ON public.your_table TO anon;. It tells you what's missing. It doesn't tell you whether that role should have it.

## The fix: grant each role what it needs, together with RLS

Supabase calls these three steps a unit: the grant, RLS, and the policies. Run them in the SQL Editor or put them in the migration that creates the table. Example for a profiles table:

-- 1. Grants: only the roles and actions your app uses
grant select, insert, update, delete on public.profiles to authenticated;
grant select, insert, update, delete on public.profiles to service_role;
-- grant select on public.profiles to anon; -- only if signed-out visitors must read it

-- 2. RLS on
alter table public.profiles enable row level security;

-- 3. Policies: which rows each user may touch
create policy "own profile" on public.profiles
for all to authenticated
using (auth.uid() = id) with check (auth.uid() = id);

Which role is which:

- anon: signed-out visitors, using your public key. Anyone can use that key, so grant anon only what a stranger may see.

- authenticated: signed-in users. Most app tables need grants here.

- service_role: your server code and edge functions, with the secret key. It skips RLS but still needs the grant. In our test, a new table without one refused it with the same error.

We rebuilt Supabase's three roles on a test PostgreSQL 16 database and ran each step. With RLS and a correct policy but no grant, the insert failed with permission denied for table. After the grant, it went through.

## Next error: "permission denied for sequence"

Once the table grant is in, inserts can fail again with permission denied for sequence todos_id_seq. The table's id is a serial column, which draws numbers from a separate sequence, and the new default doesn't grant that either. Grant it to the roles that insert:

grant usage on sequence public.todos_id_seq to authenticated;

Ids made with generated ... as identity or a uuid default don't need this. In our test, the identity-column table took inserts with the table grant alone.

## Don't fix it with GRANT ALL

Two quick fixes make the error disappear, and an AI assistant may offer either one:

- grant all on all tables in schema public to anon, authenticated; opens every table at once, including the ones you meant to keep private.

- Turning auto-exposure back on (alter default privileges ... grant ... on tables to anon, authenticated, service_role). Supabase documents this as a rollback, but it brings back the exact risk the change removes: every future table becomes reachable the moment it exists.

A grant only decides who may touch a table. RLS decides which rows. If any table lacks RLS, the grant opens all of it to anyone with your public key. We tested the rollback: we restored the defaults, then created a table without RLS. A signed-out user (anon) read its private row and wrote a new one. Grant table by table instead, and only to the roles that need it.

## Find every table that needs a grant

Paste this in the SQL Editor. It lists each table in public, whether RLS is on, and what each role can do:

select c.relname as table_name,
c.relrowsecurity as rls_on,
has_table_privilege('anon', c.oid, 'select') as anon_select,
has_table_privilege('authenticated', c.oid, 'select') as auth_select,
has_table_privilege('authenticated', c.oid, 'insert') as auth_insert
from pg_class c
join pg_namespace n on n.oid = c.relnamespace
where n.nspname = 'public' and c.relkind in ('r', 'p')
order by 1;

A table your app uses with false in the role's column needs a grant. A table with rls_on = false and true under anon_select is readable by anyone: turn RLS on before anything else. Supabase also flags tables in the Security Advisor, and shows a Data API exposure badge in the Table Editor.

## If an AI tool builds your database

Lovable, Bolt, Cursor and Claude Code create tables through migrations. If a migration has no GRANT, the new table stays closed. Tell the AI once, in its project instructions or in your next prompt:

For every new table in the public schema, add explicit GRANT statements in the same migration as ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY and the policies. Grant only the roles that need access: authenticated for signed-in features, service_role for server code, anon only for data signed-out visitors must read. Never grant to anon by default, and never use GRANT ALL.

Then check its migration for those three parts before you accept it. If you use Supabase's own agent skill, Supabase says it already includes the grants step.

## Functions work differently

Your database functions (the ones you call with rpc()) don't follow the table rule: in Postgres, every new function can be executed by PUBLIC, meaning every role. That's also why revoke execute on function ... from anon alone doesn't lock a function. In our test, anon still ran it through PUBLIC. To really lock one, revoke from both, then grant back the roles that need it:

revoke execute on function public.my_function from public, anon;
grant execute on function public.my_function to authenticated;

If several functions share that name, add the argument types, for example public.my_function(uuid).

## Still stuck?

Check that you're editing the right project: the Supabase URL in your app's settings should match the project open in the dashboard. Then run the audit query again after each grant. Supabase has a support form for this change, linked at the end of their changelog post, with its full timeline and SQL.

guides.t: Supabase Realtime not working: SUBSCRIBED but no events
guides.d: Realtime says SUBSCRIBED but postgres_changes never fires? The real error is in a system message. Find it and fix the cause, tested on real Realtime.
p: unable to subscribe to changes with given parameters
please check realtime is enabled for the given connect parameters
an exception happened so please check your connect parameters
error 400: bad request, no primary key
guides.x:
Fix guide · updated 2026-11-17

## Supabase Realtime postgres_changes not working: SUBSCRIBED but no events (the real causes, tested)

SUBSCRIBED but no events · Unable to subscribe to changes with given parameters · Error parsing `filter` params · cannot add `postgres_changes` callbacks after `subscribe()`

Your channel says SUBSCRIBED, a row changes in the database, and your postgres_changes callback never runs. Nothing looks wrong because the subscribe callback only tells you that the channel joined. Whether Realtime can actually watch your table comes a moment later, in a separate system message that most apps never listen to. Add one listener, read that message, and match it to the sections below. We ran every case on Supabase Realtime v2.167.0 (the version the Supabase CLI runs) with supabase-js 2.119, in November 2026.

## 1. Make the hidden message visible

Add a system listener next to your postgres_changes one, and log both arguments of the subscribe callback:

const channel = supabase
.channel('todos-feed')
.on('system', {}, (msg) => console.log('realtime system:', msg))
.on('postgres_changes', { event: '*', schema: 'public', table: 'todos' }, (payload) => console.log(payload))
.subscribe((status, err) => console.log('status:', status, err))

Reload the page and look at the browser console. In our tests, the subscribe callback said SUBSCRIBED in every case of this page, even the broken ones. The system message is what tells them apart:

- status: 'ok', message: 'Subscribed to PostgreSQL': Realtime is watching the table. If your events still don't arrive, something filters them out: sections 4 to 7.

- status: 'error', Unable to subscribe to changes with given parameters. Please check Realtime is enabled…: section 2.

- status: 'error', An exception happened… or Error parsing `filter` params: section 3.

If the status is CHANNEL_ERROR or TIMED_OUT instead, the channel didn't join at all, and err holds the reason. CLOSED means the channel was closed, by your own cleanup or by the server.

## 2. "Unable to subscribe to changes": the table isn't in the Realtime publication

Realtime only watches the tables listed in a publication called supabase_realtime. Creating a table and turning on Realtime for it are two separate steps. When the table isn't listed, the system message says:

Unable to subscribe to changes with given parameters. Please check Realtime is enabled for the given connect parameters: [event: *, schema: public, table: notes, filters: [], select: nil]

See which tables are listed in the SQL Editor:

select schemaname, tablename from pg_publication_tables where pubname = 'supabase_realtime';

Add yours (or use Database → Publications → supabase_realtime in the dashboard):

alter publication supabase_realtime add table public.notes;

Then subscribe again. In our test, the channel opened before the fix stayed silent: Realtime doesn't retry after this error. A new subscription got the next insert right away. Reloading the page is enough.

The same message comes back when the name doesn't match exactly. In our test, table: 'Todos' for a table named todos gave it. Names are case-sensitive: copy the schema and table name from the table list.

## 3. A filter Realtime can't read

A filter built before the user is loaded, like filter: `user_id=eq.${user?.id}`, sends the word undefined. In our test, the system message said:

Unable to subscribe to changes with given parameters. An exception happened so please check your connect parameters: [event: *, schema: public, table: todos, filters: [{"user_id", "eq", "undefined", false}], select: nil]. Exception: ERROR 22P02 (invalid_text_representation) invalid input syntax for type uuid: "undefined"

Don't open the channel until you have the ID. In React, return early from the effect while user is missing, and put user?.id in its dependencies so it runs again once the user arrives. The same empty-variable problem in ordinary queries is covered in invalid input syntax for type uuid: "undefined".

A filter written like SQL, user_id = ${id} or user_id=${id}, gave this, with your value in the brackets:

Error parsing `filter` params: [" 6f1c2a9e-…"]

Realtime doesn't retry after these errors either: fix the filter, then open the channel again. The format is column=operator.value, with no spaces: user_id=eq.${id}. The usual operators are eq, neq, lt, lte, gt, gte and in (status=in.(open,done)).

## 4. "Subscribed to PostgreSQL" but nothing arrives: Row Level Security

For every INSERT and UPDATE, Realtime checks whether the subscriber could read the new row, as that user, with your RLS policies. If not, the event isn't sent, and nothing tells you. In our tests:

- A signed-in user never got events for another user's rows. That's RLS doing its job.

- A table with RLS on and only an insert policy, no select policy, sent nothing, not even for the user's own rows. A select run as that user returned 0 rows for the same table.

- A client that wasn't signed in (the anon key) got nothing from a policy written to authenticated.

To check, run the same select with the same client: await supabase.from('posts').select('*'). If data is empty while the table has rows, the policy is what hides them. The fix is a select policy that lets the user read the rows they should see:

create policy "read own posts" on public.posts
for select to authenticated
using (user_id = auth.uid());

In our test, the next insert arrived on the channel that was already open, without subscribing again: policies are checked on each event.

One thing that looks like a fix but isn't: in our test, a client created with the service_role key received every row, other users' rows included, because that key skips RLS. Never put it in the browser. If your server gets events with that key while your app gets none, that's the sign your users can't read those rows.

## 5. Signed in after subscribing

If the channel opens before the user is signed in, it starts with the anon key and gets nothing from policies written for signed-in users. At sign-in, supabase-js passed the new token to Realtime by itself, and a second Subscribed to PostgreSQL message arrived 1.1 to 1.8 seconds later in our five runs. A row written 0.2 seconds after the sign-in was lost every time; one written 4 seconds after arrived every time. Realtime's source waits a random 1 to 3 seconds before it subscribes again with the new token.

So open the channel after sign-in, for example in an effect that depends on the user's ID. If you can't, treat the second Subscribed to PostgreSQL message as the moment your events start.

## 6. UPDATE and DELETE events that don't come

An update that hides the row. For an UPDATE, Realtime checks the new version of the row only. Our policy hid archived rows: moving a row from open to archived sent nothing to its owner, and moving it back sent the event. If your app needs to know when a row leaves the list, the user must still be allowed to read the row after the change.

DELETE with a filter. By default, Postgres only records the primary key of a deleted row. In our test, a DELETE subscription with filter: `user_id=eq.${id}` got nothing. After this, it got the next delete:

alter table public.todos replica identity full;

A filter on the primary key (id=eq.14) worked without it.

RLS doesn't apply to DELETE. Realtime can't check a row that no longer exists. In our test, every subscriber of the table got every DELETE, other users' rows included, with only the ID in payload.old. Don't put anything in the primary key that other users shouldn't see.

Empty payload.old. With the default setting, payload.old holds only the primary key, for updates and deletes. With replica identity full, our UPDATE events carried the whole old row, even with RLS on. DELETE events on a table with RLS still carried only the ID.

## 7. Rows written right after SUBSCRIBED

When Realtime has just started watching your database (the first subscriber after a quiet period or a restart), it needs a moment after the join before it really captures changes. On a freshly started Realtime, SUBSCRIBED came after about 40 ms in our tests, but Subscribed to PostgreSQL only after 2 to 2.8 seconds. Rows written in that gap never arrived: in each run, every write made in the first second after SUBSCRIBED was lost, and every write made after the ok message arrived. On a Realtime already serving other channels, rows written the moment SUBSCRIBED came all arrived (3 of 3).

This bites tests, demos and pages that insert a row right after subscribing to see it appear. Write only after the system message says ok:

supabase
.channel('todos-feed')
.on('system', {}, (msg) => {
if (msg.extension === 'postgres_changes' && msg.status === 'ok') startWriting()
})
.on('postgres_changes', { event: 'INSERT', schema: 'public', table: 'todos' }, onInsert)
.subscribe()

supabase-js 2.119 also has a channel option meant for this: supabase.channel('todos-feed', { config: { postgres_changes_options: { wait: true } } }) holds SUBSCRIBED back until Realtime has subscribed. It didn't make early writes safe every time. SUBSCRIBED and the ok message came together, 170 to 280 ms after the call. In two of our five runs, rows written in the next 250 ms were still lost; in the other three, none were. Either way, load the current rows with a normal query once you're subscribed. A missed event then costs you nothing.

## 8. React: "cannot add `postgres_changes` callbacks … after `subscribe()`"

This error is thrown when .on('postgres_changes', …) is called on a channel that has already been subscribed:

Error: cannot add `postgres_changes` callbacks for realtime:todo-feed after `subscribe()`.

supabase.channel('todo-feed') hands back the channel that's already open under that name. So an effect that runs a second time without removing the first channel crashes with this error. Remove the channel in the effect's cleanup:

useEffect(() => {
if (!user) return
const channel = supabase
.channel(`todos-${user.id}`)
.on('postgres_changes', { event: '*', schema: 'public', table: 'todos', filter: `user_id=eq.${user.id}` }, onChange)
.subscribe()
return () => { supabase.removeChannel(channel) }
}, [user?.id])

In our test, a cleanup followed at once by a new channel with the same name worked, and so did the sequence React StrictMode runs in development (subscribe, clean up, subscribe again, all at once).

## 9. Events that arrive empty

If the callback runs but payload.new is {}, read payload.errors. We saw two:

- ["Error 401: Unauthorized"]: the role lost its read permission on the table. In our test, revoke select on public.todos from authenticated caused it, and grant select on public.todos to authenticated; fixed it.

- ["Error 400: Bad Request, no primary key"]: the table has no primary key. Add one.

## If an AI tool built your app

Give your tool this prompt:

My Supabase Realtime subscription (postgres_changes) says SUBSCRIBED but the callback never runs. Add .on('system', {}, (msg) => console.log(msg)) to the channel and log (status, err) in .subscribe(). Then check, in this order: the table is in the supabase_realtime publication (alter publication supabase_realtime add table public.TABLE); the subscriber has a SELECT policy on the table that matches the rows (RLS); the filter uses column=eq.value with no undefined value; the channel is opened after the user is signed in and removed in the useEffect cleanup. Show me the SQL to run in the Supabase SQL Editor and the corrected subscription code.

## Not quite your error?

- Your writes fail with "new row violates row-level security policy": the insert policy is missing.

- "permission denied for table" on ordinary queries: the role has no grant on the table.

- Queries fail with invalid input syntax for type uuid: "undefined": a variable was empty when the query ran.

- "JWT expired" on your requests: the session token wasn't refreshed.

## Still stuck?

Strip the subscription down to { event: '*', schema: 'public', table: 'your_table' }, no filter, and write a row from the SQL Editor once the system message says ok. If that row arrives, put your filter back. If it doesn't, the cause is the publication (section 2) or RLS (section 4). Realtime doesn't promise to deliver every event: if missing one would hurt, use the event as a signal to fetch the data again.

guides.t: Supabase "relation … does not exist" (42P01) | App Finishers
guides.d: "relation … does not exist" (42P01, HTTP 404) comes from SQL inside your Supabase database, not your request. Find the function or policy, then fix the name.
guides.x:
Fix guide · updated 2026-11-16

## Supabase "relation … does not exist" (42P01)

{"code":"42P01","details":null,"hint":null,"message":"relation \"public.orders\" does not exist"}

A Supabase call fails with "relation "public.orders" does not exist", code 42P01. Through supabase-js it comes back as HTTP 404, which looks like a missing page or function. The name in the message is a table or view that some SQL tried to read, and Postgres found nothing by that name. We reproduced every case below on Postgres 16 behind Supabase's Data API (PostgREST 13), November 2026.

## What the error means

When your app asks for a table that doesn't exist, with supabase.from('orders'), the answer is a different error: "Could not find the table 'public.orders' in the schema cache" (PGRST205). So 42P01 comes from SQL that runs inside the database: a function you call with rpc(), a function a policy calls, a trigger, or a migration you run.

The table in the message isn't always the one you asked for. In our test, reading profiles failed with "relation "public.admins" does not exist": a policy on profiles called a function that read admins, and admins had been dropped.

Check the code, not just the 404: "Could not find the function" (PGRST202) is a 404 too.

## When Postgres catches it

- When you create them: SQL functions, views and policies. In our test, all three were refused at creation when they read a missing table, so the error shows up in your migration or in the SQL Editor, and nothing gets created.

- Only when they run: functions written in language plpgsql. In our test, one that read a missing table was created without complaint and failed at the first rpc().

Postgres also lets you drop or rename a table that a plpgsql function uses. In our test, drop table went through, while a view on another table blocked its drop with "cannot drop table staff because other objects depend on it".

## Cause 1: the table really isn't there

It was never created (a migration that didn't run, or one run on another project), or it was dropped or renamed after the function was written. If the message has the schema, like public.orders, and the check below finds nothing, this is your case.

## Cause 2: search_path = '' without schema names

Supabase's database linter warns "Function Search Path Mutable" on functions that don't set a search_path, and recommends set search_path = ''. Its own docs add the catch: after that, every table in the function needs its schema. In our test, a function with set search_path = '' that read from profiles failed with "relation "profiles" does not exist", and public.profiles worked. As a SQL function, the same body was refused at creation.

set search_path = public also worked, and it also silences the warning: the linter only checks that the function sets a search path. Supabase's recommendation is still '' with full names.

## Cause 3: a capital letter in the table name

A table created as "Orders", with quotes, keeps its capital. Without quotes, Postgres reads every name in lower case. In our test, a function reading from orders failed with "relation "orders" does not exist", and public."Orders" worked. From supabase-js, from('orders') got PGRST205 with the hint "Perhaps you meant the table 'public.Orders'", and from('Orders') worked.

## Cause 4: the table is in another schema

A table kept out of the API in its own schema, say private.plans, has to be named with that schema. In our test, from plans failed with "relation "plans" does not exist", and from private.plans worked.

## The one-minute check

Look for the name in every schema, in any capitalization, in the SQL Editor:

select table_schema, table_name, table_type
from information_schema.tables
where lower(table_name) like '%orders%';

Then find the functions that mention it:

select p.oid::regprocedure as function_name
from pg_proc p join pg_namespace n on n.oid = p.pronamespace
where n.nspname = 'public' and p.prosrc ilike '%orders%';

Nothing in the first list: cause 1. Found with a capital letter: cause 3. Found in another schema: cause 4. Found in public, but the function has search_path = '' and no schema in the name: cause 2.

## Fix 1: name the schema in every function

Write the full name, public.orders, private.plans or public."Orders", and replace the function:

create or replace function public.order_count()
returns bigint
language plpgsql stable
set search_path = ''
as $$
begin
return (select count(*) from public.orders);
end $$;

This also works with set search_path = '', the setting the linter asks for.

## Fix 2: create the table, or follow the new name

If the table is missing, create it, or run the migration that creates it. If it was renamed, update every function that still uses the old name. The second query above lists them.

## Fix 3: migrations in order

Create a table before the functions, views and policies that read it. Since SQL functions, views and policies are checked at creation, a migration that creates them first fails with this error and stops.

## If an AI tool built your app

Give your AI tool this prompt, with the name from your error:

My Supabase app fails with relation "public.orders" does not exist (42P01). Find every database function, trigger function, view and RLS policy that reads this table. Check that the table exists, with this exact name and capitalization, and in which schema. Then write a migration that uses the full schema-qualified name everywhere (public.orders), keeps set search_path = '' on functions that have it, and creates any missing table before the objects that read it. Show me the SQL before running it.

## Not quite your error?

- "Could not find the table 'public.orders' in the schema cache": Supabase "Could not find the table in the schema cache" (PGRST205).

- It happens at sign-up, as "Database error saving new user": Database error saving new user (Supabase).

- It happens at sign-in, as "Error running hook URI": Supabase "Error running hook URI" (Custom Access Token hook).

- "Could not find the function … in the schema cache": Supabase "Could not find the function in the schema cache" (PGRST202).

- "permission denied for table": Supabase "permission denied for table" (42501).

## Still stuck?

Call the function in the SQL Editor, for example select public.order_count();. The error there ends with a CONTEXT line, such as "PL/pgSQL function order_count() line 1 at RETURN", which names the function and the line that read the missing table.

guides.t: Supabase "Request rate limit reached" (429) | App Finishers
guides.d: Supabase Auth answers 429 "Request rate limit reached" (over_request_rate_limit). Which calls count, how fast they come back, the server-side trap. Tested.
guides.x:
Fix guide · updated 2026-11-16

## Supabase "Request rate limit reached" (429)

AuthApiError: Request rate limit reached · over_request_rate_limit · 429

Sign-ins start failing with "Request rate limit reached", HTTP 429. Usually while you test, sometimes for all your users at once. Supabase Auth limits how often one IP address can call each of its endpoints. We ran Supabase's real Auth server with its default limits and supabase-js 2.119 on our machine to see which calls count, how fast they come back, and what a 429 does to someone who is already signed in.

## What the error means

Supabase Auth gives each IP address an allowance per endpoint. It holds about 30 requests and refills over time. When it's empty, the call gets HTTP 429 with the code over_request_rate_limit:

429 {"code":"over_request_rate_limit","message":"Request rate limit reached"}

In our test, the answer had no Retry-After header to say when to try again. What we measured with the default limits:

- Password sign-ins and session refreshes (/token) share one allowance: about 30 at once, then one more every 2 seconds (150 per 5 minutes). Wrong passwords count too: after 30 wrong ones, the right password got the 429 as well.

- Sign-ups (/signup): 30 at once, then one every 10 seconds (30 per 5 minutes).

- updateUser (/user) and email codes and links (verifyOtp, /verify): 30 at once each.

- Anonymous sign-ins: 30 per hour, see our anonymous sign-ins guide.

Each endpoint counts on its own: once sign-ups ran out, a password reset, a magic link, updateUser and a password sign-in from the same address still went through. Each IP address counts on its own too: the same sign-in from another address worked at once. The numbers are under Authentication → Rate Limits in your Supabase dashboard, where most of them can be raised.

## 1. You're testing sign-in or sign-up over and over

Thirty quick tries from your machine and that endpoint is closed. Automated tests get there first. You don't need to wait the full 5 minutes for one more try: a sign-in comes back every 2 seconds, a sign-up every 10. For a test suite, raise the limits under Authentication → Rate Limits, or space the calls out.

## 2. Your server makes the calls for everyone

If sign-in, sign-up or the session refresh runs on your server (a Next.js server action, an API route, middleware, an edge function), Supabase sees your server's IP address, not your visitors'. Then all your users share one allowance. In our test, 30 quick sign-ins from one address closed sign-in for everyone else at that address.

Supabase's fix is IP address forwarding. Turn on IP Address Forwarding under Authentication → Rate Limits, then have your server send each visitor's IP address in an Sb-Forwarded-For header on its Auth calls, as Supabase's rate-limit docs show:

global: { headers: { 'sb-forwarded-for': request.headers.get('x-forwarded-for') } }

Supabase's docs say the header only counts on requests made with a secret key (sb_secret_…), not the publishable key or the legacy anon and service_role keys. Keep that key in server code only. In our test, with forwarding on, Auth counted each forwarded address separately: 60 sign-ins from one server, each forwarding a different visitor's address, all went through.

## 3. Many people share one address

An office, a school or a mobile carrier can put many people behind one IP address, and they share every allowance above. Session refreshes count in the same allowance as password sign-ins, so a page that refreshes the session far more often than it needs to uses it up for everyone on that network. Open your browser's Network tab, filter on /auth/v1/, and count the token requests per page load: more than one is a loop to fix.

## 4. A 429 can sign people out

This is the costly case. In our test, a supabase-js 2.119 client whose access token had expired asked for a new one while the allowance was empty. getSession() came back with no session and the 429 error, and the client fired SIGNED_OUT. The person has to sign in again, which needs the same allowance. With some allowance left, the same steps gave TOKEN_REFRESHED.

Reading supabase-js's code, it only drops the session when the access token has already expired. A refresh that fails while the token is still valid keeps the session and tries again later. So leave autoRefreshToken on (the default in the browser), and the refresh happens before the token runs out.

## If an AI tool built your app

Give your AI tool this prompt:

In every Supabase Auth call (signInWithPassword, signUp, verifyOtp, updateUser, resetPasswordForEmail), when the error code is over_request_rate_limit (HTTP 429), show "Too many attempts. Please wait a minute and try again." instead of the raw error, and disable the submit button for 30 seconds. Make sure the app creates one Supabase client and reuses it, and that nothing calls signIn, signUp, refreshSession or updateUser in a loop or on every render. Don't change anything else.

If your sign-in runs on a server, the forwarding setting and the secret key (case 2) are yours to set up: the AI can't open your dashboard.

## Not quite your error?

- "email rate limit exceeded", or "For security purposes, you can only request this after … seconds": Supabase "email rate limit exceeded".

- Users are signed out with "Invalid Refresh Token": Supabase "Invalid Refresh Token: Refresh Token Not Found".

- Guest users can't sign in at all: Supabase "Anonymous sign-ins are disabled".

- Sign-in fails with the right password and no 429: Supabase "Invalid login credentials".

## Still stuck?

Find out which allowance runs out. In your browser's Network tab, the refused request's path says it: token (sign-ins and refreshes), signup, user or verify. If it happens to your users and not to you, and your sign-in runs on a server, start with case 2.

guides.t: Supabase "requested path is invalid" after login: the fix
guides.d: Login or email link ends on {"error":"requested path is invalid"}? Supabase sent the user to its own address. Set Site URL and Redirect URLs, then redirectTo.
guides.x:
Fix guide · updated 2026-11-07

## Supabase "requested path is invalid": what it means and the fix

{"error":"requested path is invalid"}

A user clicks Confirm your email, or signs in with Google, Apple or X, and lands on a page that only says {"error":"requested path is invalid"}. Or an upload or a database call in your app fails with the same words. It looks cryptic, but it always means the same thing: something sent the browser, or your code, to an address on your Supabase project that doesn't exist. Find what sent it there, and the fix takes a few minutes.

## What the error means

Your Supabase project lives at an address like https://abcdefghijklmnopqrst.supabase.co. That's your backend, not a website: it only answers specific paths such as /auth/v1/…, /rest/v1/… and /storage/v1/…. Open the bare address, or a path that doesn't exist, and Supabase answers with this error. So look at the address bar when it happens:

- It starts with https://…supabase.co right after an email link or a login: see section 1.

- It only happens with X (Twitter), Apple or Google login: see section 2.

- Your code gets it back from an upload, a query or an rpc() call: see section 3.

## 1. Logins and email links land on your Supabase address

Supabase has two addresses that are easy to mix up:

- The Project URL (click Connect at the top of the Supabase dashboard), like https://abcdefghijklmnopqrst.supabase.co. Your app's code talks to it.

- The Site URL (Authentication → URL Configuration). That's where Supabase sends people after a login or an email link. It must be your app, like https://yourapp.com.

If the Site URL holds the Project URL, every confirmation link and every login ends on this error. Fix it in three steps:

- Site URL: put your app's live address. Save.

- Redirect URLs, on the same page: add every address users should come back to, ending with /**, for example https://yourapp.com/**.

- Your code: tell Supabase to send people back to your app, never to Supabase.

// Email sign-up: where the confirmation link sends people
await supabase.auth.signUp({
email,
password,
options: { emailRedirectTo: `${window.location.origin}/` },
});

// Google, Apple, X…
await supabase.auth.signInWithOAuth({
provider: "google",
options: { redirectTo: `${window.location.origin}/` },
});

A common trap: putting https://…supabase.co/auth/v1/callback in redirectTo. That callback address belongs in Google's, Apple's or X's developer console. In your code, redirectTo must point back to your app.

Then send yourself a new confirmation email to test. Links in emails sent before the fix keep the old address.

## 2. Only X (Twitter), Apple or Google login fails

When the step at the provider fails, Supabase sends the user back to your app's address with the reason attached. If that address is wrong, you get this message instead of the real error. Look at the address bar anyway: the real reason is often written there, after error_description=. Fix section 1 first, then check two things:

- The callback in the provider's console is exactly https://<your-project-ref>.supabase.co/auth/v1/callback. Supabase shows it under Authentication → Providers, on that provider's page.

- The keys you pasted into Supabase are the ones for the login type you turned on. With X, it's easy to copy the wrong pair from its developer portal.

## 3. Your code gets the error from an upload or a query

Check the Supabase address your app uses. It must be exactly the Project URL, with nothing after .supabase.co: the Supabase library adds /rest/v1, /storage/v1 and the rest by itself, so anything extra ends up in front of every request. One case gives a different message: with /rest/v1 at the end of the address (the API URL shown on Project Settings → Data API), requests reach the database API and fail with "Invalid path specified in request URL" instead, sign-up and login included. See that guide.

- Lovable apps: the address is in src/integrations/supabase/client.ts or in VITE_SUPABASE_URL. Bolt and other Vite apps: VITE_SUPABASE_URL. Next.js: NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL.

- Hosting on Vercel or Netlify? Check the environment variables there too, then redeploy: the build bakes the value into your app.

- Using an S3 tool with Supabase Storage? Its endpoint must end with /storage/v1/s3.

If your project runs on Lovable Cloud rather than your own Supabase project, the same settings exist there: look in its authentication settings for the site and redirect addresses.

## Still stuck?

Supabase → Authentication → Logs shows each login attempt and where Supabase tried to send the user. If users now land on localhost instead, see our guide on Supabase login redirecting to localhost.

guides.t: Fix Supabase "Signups not allowed for this instance"
guides.d: New users get "Signups not allowed for this instance" (signup_disabled) on sign-up, Google login or magic link. The setting behind it, and the OTP variant.
guides.x:
Fix guide · updated 2026-11-15

## Supabase "Signups not allowed for this instance"

AuthApiError: Signups not allowed for this instance · signup_disabled · 422

A new user tries to sign up, or to log in with Google or a magic link for the first time, and Supabase answers "Signups not allowed for this instance". People who already have an account still get in. One switch in your Supabase project decides this, and it's easy to turn off without noticing. Here's where it is, the look-alike errors, and how to open sign-ups safely.

## What the error means

We read the Supabase Auth code. When your project doesn't allow new users, every path that would create an account stops with HTTP 422, code signup_disabled, "Signups not allowed for this instance":

- signUp with an email and password, or a phone number,

- signInWithOtp (magic link or code) for an email that has no account yet,

- Google, GitHub or any other OAuth login for someone who has no account yet,

- anonymous sign-ins.

People who already have an account aren't affected: they sign in as usual. And you can still create accounts yourself: invites and admin.auth.admin.createUser don't check this setting. Both need your secret key, so they run on your server: from the browser they fail with "User not allowed".

## 1. "Allow new users to sign up" is off

In the Supabase dashboard: Authentication → Sign In / Providers → User Signups → Allow new users to sign up. Turn it on, save, and try the sign-up again.

It's usually off on purpose at some point: to keep strangers out of a half-built app, during a demo, or because a template was invite-only. If your app should stay invite-only, leave it off and invite people from the Users page in Authentication instead.

## 2. Google login sends new users back with nothing on screen

With Google and the other OAuth providers, the error doesn't come back from a call in your code. Supabase sends the person back to your site with the error in the address, both in the query string and after the #:

https://yourapp.com/?error=access_denied&error_code=signup_disabled&error_description=Signups+not+allowed+for+this+instance

If your app ignores those parameters, the person lands back on the login page with no message and tries again, forever. Read error_code and error_description on the page Supabase redirects to, and show a message.

## 3. "Signups not allowed for otp"

A different code, otp_disabled, and a different cause: your code calls signInWithOtp with shouldCreateUser: false. Supabase then sends a link or code only to emails that already have an account, and answers HTTP 422 "Signups not allowed for otp" for a new one. That's the right setup for a login-only form. If the same form is also how people sign up, remove shouldCreateUser: false (it defaults to true):

await supabase.auth.signInWithOtp({
email,
options: { emailRedirectTo: window.location.origin }, // no shouldCreateUser: false
});

## 4. "Email signups are disabled"

If the Email provider itself is off (Authentication → Sign In / Providers → Email), email sign-ups answer HTTP 400 "Email signups are disabled" and magic links answer "Email logins are disabled", both with the code email_provider_disabled. Turn the Email provider back on if your app uses email at all.

## Is it safe to open sign-ups?

Yes, if your database is protected. Once sign-ups are open, anyone can create an account and get a valid login, so every table needs Row Level Security policies that limit what a signed-in user can read and write. Turning sign-ups off is often a patch over missing policies. Check with our security checklist for vibe-coded apps before you turn the switch back on.

## If an AI tool built your app

Give your AI tool this prompt, so people see a clear message instead of a raw error or nothing:

On the sign-up form and the magic link form, when Supabase returns the error code signup_disabled, show "Sign-ups are closed right now." instead of the raw error. On the page Supabase redirects to after Google login, read error_code and error_description from the URL (the query string and the part after #); if error_code is signup_disabled, show the same message, and for any other error show error_description. Don't change anything else.

Then make the real decision yourself in the dashboard: turn "Allow new users to sign up" on (case 1), or keep it off and invite people.

## Not quite your error?

- Sign-up says the email is taken: Supabase "User already registered".

- Sign-up says "Anonymous sign-ins are disabled": Supabase "Anonymous sign-ins are disabled".

- Sign-up fails for every new email with a database message: Supabase "Database error saving new user".

- Google login sends people to localhost: Supabase login redirects to localhost.

- Google shows "Error 400: redirect_uri_mismatch": Google login "redirect_uri_mismatch".

- Google login opens a page of JSON with "Unsupported provider": Supabase "Unsupported provider: provider is not enabled".

## Still stuck?

If the switch is on and new users still get "Signups not allowed for this instance", make sure your app talks to the project you changed: the Supabase URL in your app's settings must match the dashboard's (see case 1 of our "Invalid login credentials" guide). The Auth logs in your dashboard show each refused request and where it came from: sign-up, magic link or OAuth.

guides.t: Supabase Storage "Bucket not found" | App Finishers
guides.d: Images don't show or uploads fail with "Bucket not found", yet the bucket exists. The three causes we reproduced, one of them a private bucket, and each fix.
guides.x:
Fix guide · updated 2026-11-16

## Supabase Storage "Bucket not found"

{"statusCode":"404","error":"Bucket not found","message":"Bucket not found","code":"NoSuchBucket"}

Your app's images don't show, or an upload fails, and opening the file's address shows {"statusCode":"404","error":"Bucket not found"}. Often the bucket is right there in your dashboard. We ran Supabase Storage ourselves (version 1.95, November 2026) and tried the usual mistakes: it answers "Bucket not found" in three situations, and in one of them the bucket exists but is private. Here's how to tell which one you have, and the fix.

## What the error means

Supabase Storage looks a bucket up by its exact name. It answers "Bucket not found" when:

- a public file address (/object/public/…) points to a private bucket (case 1),

- no bucket has exactly that name in the project your app uses (case 2),

- your app asks about the bucket itself with getBucket() from the browser, where it isn't allowed to see buckets (case 3).

Despite the "404" in the message, the HTTP status is 400, so your browser's console shows 400 (Bad Request). That's normal for Supabase Storage: the real status sits in statusCode.

## The one-minute check

In the Supabase dashboard, open the SQL Editor and run:

select id, name, public from storage.buckets;

This lists every bucket with its exact name and whether it's public. Now find the bucket name your app uses: in the code it's supabase.storage.from('avatars'), and in a failing file address it comes right after /public/, like https://abcdefghijklmnop.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/avatars/photo.png. The part before .supabase.co is the project that answered: it must match the reference in your dashboard's address, after /project/.

## 1. Images don't show: a public link to a private bucket

getPublicUrl() never asks Supabase anything: it only writes an address, so it can't fail and it can't warn you. If the bucket is private, which is the default for new buckets, that address answers "Bucket not found" to everyone, you included. It's the most common version of this error: the upload works, the check above shows the bucket with public = false, and every image is broken.

First decide: should anyone with the link be able to see these files? Profile pictures, product photos and blog images, usually yes. Then make the bucket public: in Storage, edit the bucket and turn on Public bucket, or run:

update storage.buckets set public = true where id = 'avatars';

Public only opens reading. Uploads and deletes still need your storage policies.

For private files (invoices, ID scans, anything personal), keep the bucket private and give each viewer a link that expires:

const { data, error } = await supabase.storage
.from('documents')
.createSignedUrl(path, 60 * 60); // valid for one hour
// use data.signedUrl as the image or download address

A signed link only works for files the signed-in user may read under your policies. Without such a policy, Supabase answers "Object not found".

## 2. There's no bucket with that exact name

Names must match exactly, capitals included: avatars, Avatars, avatar and user-avatars are four different buckets. If the name in your code isn't in the check's list, one of these happened:

- Typo or different name. Change the code or the bucket, so the two match.

- Another project. Buckets live in each project's database. A remix, a staging copy or a new project for production starts without them.

- A migration that never ran. AI tools often create buckets in a SQL migration. If it wasn't applied to this project, the bucket doesn't exist here.

Create the bucket once, with the exact name your code uses: Storage → New bucket, turning on Public bucket if case 1 applies, or in SQL (the form Supabase's docs give):

insert into storage.buckets (id, name, public)
values ('avatars', 'avatars', true);

On an upload, "Bucket not found" means this case. Storage checks the bucket before your policies: in our test, an upload to a missing bucket said "Bucket not found" even without any permission, and an upload to a real bucket without a policy said "new row violates row-level security policy" instead.

## 3. getBucket() says it doesn't exist, listBuckets() is empty

From the browser, getBucket() and listBuckets() read the bucket list as your user, through Row Level Security. Storage turns Row Level Security on for that list and adds no policy to it, so getBucket('avatars') answers "Bucket not found" and listBuckets() returns an empty list, while the bucket exists. With the service key, the same getBucket worked in our test.

This usually comes from code that checks for the bucket and creates it if it's missing. The check fails, then createBucket() fails too, with "new row violates row-level security policy". Your app doesn't need either: delete that code, create the bucket once (case 2), and upload straight to it.

## "Object not found" instead?

The neighbour error, {"statusCode":"404","error":"not_found","message":"Object not found","code":"NoSuchKey"}, means Storage found no file at that path, or none your user may read:

- The bucket is public but the file path is wrong.

- A private file, read or signed without a policy that allows it.

- A wrong bucket name in a public address: Storage looks up the bucket and the file at the same time and reports whichever fails first. In our test the same wrong address answered "Object not found" once and "Bucket not found" the next time, so check the bucket name too.

All the causes, tested: Supabase Storage "Object not found".

## If an AI tool built your app

Give your AI tool this prompt:

List every supabase.storage.from('...') call in the app: the bucket name, and whether it uploads, downloads, uses getPublicUrl or uses createSignedUrl. Remove any code that calls getBucket, listBuckets or createBucket at runtime to check for or create a bucket. Don't change anything else.

Then compare its list with the one-minute check: every bucket name must exist exactly, and every bucket used with getPublicUrl must have public = true.

## Not quite your error?

- Uploads fail with "new row violates row-level security policy": Supabase Storage "new row violates row-level security policy".

- About to make a bucket public? Check what's in it first: security checklist for vibe-coded apps.

- Uploads fail with "The object exceeded the maximum allowed size": Supabase Storage "The object exceeded the maximum allowed size".

- Your app reads a table and gets "permission denied": Supabase "permission denied for table" (42501).

## Still stuck?

Copy the exact address that fails (from the browser's Network tab, or by opening the broken image in a new tab) and the result of the one-minute check. The bucket name and project in that address, next to the real list of buckets, settle almost every case. The Storage logs in your dashboard show each refused request too.

guides.t: Fix Supabase Storage "mime type is not supported"
guides.d: Uploads fail with "mime type text/plain;charset=UTF-8 is not supported" or application/octet-stream. Why the declared type is wrong, and the one-line fix.
guides.x:
Fix guide · updated 2026-11-16

## Supabase Storage "mime type … is not supported"

{"statusCode":"415","error":"invalid_mime_type","message":"mime type text/plain;charset=UTF-8 is not supported","code":"InvalidMimeType"}

An upload fails with "mime type text/plain;charset=UTF-8 is not supported", or with application/octet-stream, image/heic or image/webp in the middle. The bucket only accepts certain file types, and the type your upload declared isn't one of them. Often the picture is fine and only its label is wrong. We tested every case with the real supabase-js storage client (version 2.119) against Supabase Storage itself (version 1.95, November 2026).

## What the error means

A bucket can have a list of allowed file types. When it does, Storage compares the type the upload declares with that list and refuses anything else, with HTTP 400 and "statusCode":"415" in the body. It reads the label, not the file's content. The type in the message tells you which case you're in:

- text/plain;charset=UTF-8: your code uploads raw data without saying what it is (case 1),

- application/octet-stream: a Blob or File without a type (case 2),

- a real type such as image/heic, image/webp or image/jpg: it isn't on the bucket's list, or it's a typo (case 3).

## The one-minute check

In the SQL Editor, run:

select id, allowed_mime_types from storage.buckets;

Empty means the bucket takes any type. Otherwise, compare the list with the type in your error message.

## 1. "text/plain;charset=UTF-8": raw data without a contentType

Your code uploads a string, an ArrayBuffer or decoded base64, which is common in React Native and Expo apps and when an app converts an image by hand. For that kind of data, supabase-js can't know the type, so it sends its default, text/plain;charset=UTF-8. Its own documentation says to pass contentType whenever the data isn't a Blob, File or FormData:

const { error } = await supabase.storage
.from('images')
.upload(path, arrayBuffer, { contentType: 'image/png' })

In our test, the same upload failed without contentType and went through with it.

## 2. "application/octet-stream": a Blob or File without a type

For a Blob or a File, supabase-js sends the type stored in the object itself and ignores the contentType option. In our test, an untyped Blob uploaded with contentType: 'image/png' still went out as application/octet-stream and was refused. Give the object its type instead:

const blob = new Blob([data], { type: 'image/png' })
// or, from an existing blob: new File([oldBlob], 'photo.png', { type: 'image/png' })
const { error } = await supabase.storage.from('images').upload(path, blob)

A Blob built from raw bytes has no type unless you give it one. A File picked in the browser gets its type from the file name, and an extension the browser doesn't recognize leaves it empty too.

## 3. A real type that isn't on the list

The file declares a correct type, but the bucket doesn't allow it. The usual ones:

- image/heic: photos from iPhones,

- image/webp: many images saved from the web,
