- Payload: iss = your Issuer ID, iat = now, exp = at most 20 minutes later, aud = appstoreconnect-v1.

Any JWT library makes it in a few lines: PyJWT in Python, jose or jsonwebtoken in Node. Make a fresh token for each step if your upload takes long.

## Step 3: the three upload calls

All three go to https://api.appstoreconnect.apple.com. First, create a build upload, with your version, build number and app ID:

POST /v1/buildUploads
{"data": {"type": "buildUploads",
"attributes": {"cfBundleShortVersionString": "1.0", "cfBundleVersion": "7", "platform": "IOS"},
"relationships": {"app": {"data": {"type": "apps", "id": "YOUR_APP_ID"}}}}}

Second, reserve the file. Use the build upload's id from the first answer, plus the file's exact name and size in bytes:

POST /v1/buildUploadFiles
{"data": {"type": "buildUploadFiles",
"attributes": {"fileName": "MyApp.ipa", "fileSize": 48211234, "assetType": "ASSET", "uti": "com.apple.ipa"},
"relationships": {"buildUpload": {"data": {"type": "buildUploads", "id": "BUILD_UPLOAD_ID"}}}}}

The answer contains uploadOperations, a list of pieces. Each piece gives a method, a url, an offset, a length and requestHeaders. For each one, send that slice of your file (from offset, length bytes) to that URL, with exactly the headers listed for it.

Third, tell Apple the file is complete:

PATCH /v1/buildUploadFiles/FILE_ID
{"data": {"type": "buildUploadFiles", "id": "FILE_ID", "attributes": {"uploaded": true}}}

## Step 4: wait for processing, then submit

Read GET /v1/buildUploads/BUILD_UPLOAD_ID every minute or so. Its state shows the progress, plus any errors and warnings. When processing is done, the build appears under TestFlight in App Store Connect. From there it's the usual path: test it, add it to a version, submit for review.

## If Apple refuses the build

- Signing errors: the file was signed for development or ad hoc. It has to be rebuilt with an App Store distribution profile.

- Bundle ID or app not found: the app ID in the first call doesn't belong to the .ipa's bundle ID.

- Build number already used: raise cfBundleVersion in the app, rebuild, and use the new number in the first call.

- SDK or Xcode too old: the builder has to rebuild with Xcode 26 or later. No upload method gets around that.

- 401 on every call: the token. Check the Key ID, the Issuer ID, aud, and that exp is at most 20 minutes after iat. Also check that your computer's clock is right.

## Rather not write code?

Build services with Macs in the cloud can do the same upload with the same API key: GitHub Actions, Codemagic, or Expo's EAS for Expo apps. They need a bit of setup, and the free tiers have limits. If your builder offers its own "publish to App Store" button, try that first.

Still stuck after all this? Send us the project and we'll find it.

Sources: Apple Developer, Upload builds, Create a Build Upload, Create a Reservation for a Build Upload File, Commit a Build Upload File, Creating API Keys for App Store Connect API and Generating Tokens for API Requests.

guides.t: Security checklist for AI-built apps before launch
guides.d: Eight checks for apps built with Lovable, Bolt, Replit or Cursor: Supabase RLS, leaked keys, self-made admins, unsigned payments, open storage.
p: is public, but rls has not been enabled
guides.x:
Fix guide · updated 2026-11-07

## Security checklist for AI-built apps before you launch

RLS Disabled in Public · Table public.profiles is public, but RLS has not been enabled.

AI builders write an app in an afternoon. They also make the same security mistakes over and over, and public scans of launched AI-built apps keep finding them. Go through these eight checks before real users and real money arrive. Most take a few minutes.

## 1. Row-level security is on for every table

Your Supabase key is inside your app, so anyone can find it. Row-level security (RLS) is the only thing deciding what that key can read and change.

Check: Supabase dashboard → Advisors → Security Advisor. Every RLS Disabled in Public warning is a table anyone can read and edit right now.

Fix: enable RLS on each one, then add policies for who may read and write. With RLS on and no policies, nobody can use the table at all, so do both. Our row-level security guide has the SQL.

## 2. No policy says "everyone" on private data

A policy written as using (true) means anyone. That's fine for a public product list and a disaster for orders, messages or profiles.

Check: Authentication → Policies, every table. Private data should check the owner, like (select auth.uid()) = user_id.

## 3. No secret keys in the browser

Only the public anon or publishable Supabase key belongs in your app's code. Secret keys there are readable by every visitor.

Check: open your live site → browser developer tools → Sources, and search all files for service_role, sk_live_ (Stripe), sk- (OpenAI) and whsec_. Also check that none of these sit in a variable starting with VITE_.

Fix: if you find one, create a new key at the provider and delete the old one first, because the old one is already public. Then move that call into a server function (a Supabase Edge Function) that keeps the key on the server.

## 4. Users can't make themselves admin

A very common hole: the profiles table has a plan, role, credits or is_admin column, and users are allowed to update their own row. Then anyone can open the browser console and give themselves the paid plan.

Fix: only let users change the safe columns:

revoke update on public.profiles from authenticated;
grant update (full_name, avatar_url) on public.profiles to authenticated;

Replace the two names with the columns users may edit. Plans and roles then change only from your server, for example from your payment webhook.

## 5. Payments are confirmed by the server

An order must become "paid" only when your server receives Stripe's webhook with a valid signature. Never trust a "payment successful" page or a value the browser sends: both can be faked. See our Stripe webhook guide for a working, signed webhook.

## 6. Private files are in private buckets

In Supabase Storage, a bucket marked Public lets anyone with the link open its files. ID documents, invoices and private uploads belong in a private bucket, with policies saying who can read them.

## 7. Server functions check who is calling

Supabase Edge Functions check for a logged-in user by default. Keep that on for everything except webhooks, which check the sender's signature instead. Inside each function, use the user from the verified login, never a user id sent in the request body.

## 8. Login settings are tightened

- Email confirmation on, with a real email provider (see our email guide).

- Redirect URLs limited to your own domains (see our redirect guide).

- Sensible limits in Authentication → Rate Limits, so nobody can hammer your sign-up or password reset.

## Bonus: security headers

Ask your host to send basic security headers (Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options). On Netlify and Cloudflare Pages that's a _headers file; on Vercel, a headers section in vercel.json.

## Want this done for you?

We run this whole checklist on your app and fix what we find as part of our Launch fix: your app live, payments working, and customer data locked down.
